search.s: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.t: 1 Chapter 1 Concepts of diagnosis and identification Screening, identification, diagnosis and eligibility are four terms often used as if they were synonyms, yet they are in fact four distinct steps, each with its own question, its own tools and its own responsible party. In this chapter we sketch the conceptual map on which all the chapters of the book are organized, and we place it within its regulatory framework in Saudi Arabia. Scene from the teachers' lounge At the start of the school year, Munira, a teacher, received the files of the students in her third-grade class. In Abdullah's file was a hospital report stating that he had been “diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder.” Sultan's file held the result of a reading screening the school had conducted the previous month, marked “needs follow-up.” Reem's file was empty, but last year's teacher had left Munira a note: “Keep an eye on Reem. I think she's gifted.” Munira wonders: Is Abdullah entitled to special education services because he has a diagnosis? Does Sultan have a learning disability because the screening flagged him? And is one teacher's opinion enough to consider Reem gifted? The answer to all three questions is the same: “Not necessarily.” Why this is so becomes clear only once we draw careful distinctions between steps that are frequently confused in practice. That is the work of this chapter, and we will return to the three students at its close. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Determine the purpose of assessment in a given situation and the type of tool suited to it. Distinguish among screening, identification, diagnosis and eligibility determination by the question each step asks and the kind of evidence it requires. Compare the three models of disability in terms of the diagnostic question toward which each one points. Map the special education categories in Saudi regulations onto the categories of US law and onto medical classification systems. Identify which principle of fair assessment has been violated in a given assessment situation. Build a RIOT/ICEL matrix for gathering evidence about a referred student, indicating the source of each piece of information in it. Plan a conversation with a family about a teacher's concern, following a structured sequence of steps. Detect common errors in a given assessment situation and propose ways to avoid them. Judge whether the available evidence is sufficient to move from one step of the assessment pathway to the next, and justify that judgment.

search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.t: Every school year, teachers and assessment and diagnosis teams make decisions that bear directly on the paths of particular students: who is referred for assessment, who meets the criteria for a given category, and who needs special education services or a gifted program. Many of the errors in these decisions stem less from the limitations of the tools than from confusing distinct steps that go by similar names. A screening result is treated as a diagnosis, a medical diagnosis is taken as an educational eligibility decision, and a single teacher's opinion is deemed sufficient to judge a student gifted, just as Munira finds in the opening scene. For this reason we open the book by pinning down concepts before turning to tools and categories, since it is the question each step asks that determines the kind of evidence required, who is responsible for it, and how much of it is enough to move on to the next step. We begin the chapter with the purposes of assessment, starting from the premise that assessment is a means of making decisions (Section 1.1). We then distinguish among screening, identification, diagnosis and eligibility determination (Section 1.2), and among measurement, testing and assessment (Section 1.3). Next we present the models of disability and the question toward which each points (Section 1.4), followed by medical and educational classification systems and the regulatory framework in Saudi Arabia (Section 1.5). We then turn to the principles of fair assessment (Section 1.6), the RIOT/ICEL framework for organizing sources of evidence (Section 1.7), and the roles of the team and the family (Section 1.8), and we close with the general assessment pathway and its common errors (Section 1.9).

search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.s: 1.1 Why do we assess? The purposes of assessment
search.t: Assessment is a means of making a decision. The first question an assessor asks, therefore, is “What decision do I need to make?” Only after that comes the question “Which test should I give?” A tool that is excellent for one decision may be useless for another. Specialists in educational measurement identify several purposes of assessment, each with its own question (Salvia et al., 2017): Table 1.1: Purposes of assessment, the question each purpose answers, and an example of a tool for it. Purpose Question it answers Example of a tool Screening Who needs a closer look? A short screening checklist given to all kindergarten children Diagnosis and classification Does the student have a disability, a disorder or giftedness? Of what kind? A comprehensive battery: intelligence, achievement, adaptive behavior and observation Eligibility determination and placement Is the student entitled to special services? In what setting should they be provided? A team decision based on the diagnosis and its impact on learning Instructional planning What should we teach? Where should we start? Criterion-referenced tests (which compare a student's performance with a defined level of mastery rather than with the performance of peers), and error analysis Progress monitoring Is the student learning? Is the plan working? Brief, repeated measures such as curriculum-based measurement ( Curriculum-Based Measurement, CBM ) Program evaluation Is the program meeting its goals for its students as a whole? Aggregated data on the program's students across years In this book we focus on the first two purposes, with some attention to the third. The teacher, however, is present in all of them, because diagnostic information must ultimately feed into instructional planning; otherwise it loses its value.

search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.t: Picture these four steps as a funnel: at the top are all students, and at the bottom are those who receive special services. The funnel narrows at each layer, because each step asks a more precise question than the one before it and requires stronger evidence. Screening A quick procedure applied to everyone, asking: Who needs a closer look? A worrying result or a documented observation Identification and referral Initial gathering of evidence and attempts at classroom support, followed by referral of students about whom concern persists Referral with family consent Diagnosis A comprehensive assessment that answers: Are the criteria for a particular category met? A diagnosis with an impact on learning Eligibility determination The team's decision: Does the student need special services? Which ones? Figure 1.1: From screening to eligibility. The number of students shrinks at each layer, while the depth of the questions and the strength of the evidence required increase. Screening Screening is applied to an entire group, such as all first graders, using a short tool that does not require a specialist. Its aim is to ensure that no child who needs a closer look slips past us. Screening tools are therefore preferably high in sensitivity ( Sensitivity ), that is, able to capture the largest possible proportion of those who actually have the problem, even if they also flag some who do not, because the cost of missing a child is greater than the cost of examining a child who turns out not to need it. Sensitivity alone, however, is not enough to judge a screening tool. The tool also needs acceptable specificity ( Specificity ), meaning the ability to rule out those who do not have the problem; otherwise it will swamp the team with unnecessary referrals. A school principal will care about a third question as well: if a student's result is negative, how likely is it that the student truly does not have the problem? This is the negative predictive value ( Negative predictive value ), the most important question to ask of a screening, because it measures how confident we can be that we have not missed anyone. Its magnitude, like that of the positive predictive value, depends jointly on the properties of the tool and on the prevalence of the problem in the group screened (Chapter 2 works through these concepts with numbers in Section 2.6). Misconception: “The screening flagged him, so the problem is confirmed” A positive screening result is an invitation to look more closely; diagnosis is a later stage that requires broader evidence. Screening tools are deliberately designed to catch more than they should, and when a problem is rare in a group, many of those flagged by the screening may in fact be free of it. The reverse holds as well: a negative result is no certificate of health. If the teacher's or the family's concern persists, a documented observation is reason enough to move on to the identification stage. Identification and referral After screening, or after a teacher's observation, the identification stage ( Identification ) begins: the stage of gathering initial evidence. At this stage the teacher and the school try to provide support within the classroom, whether by adjusting the method of instruction or by offering additional small-group teaching, while monitoring the student's response. If the difficulty persists despite this support, the student is referred for a comprehensive assessment. Referral is a significant decision, because it signals that the school has tried what it can and that this has not been enough. In the field of giftedness, this stage is usually called nomination . Teachers and families nominate students in whom they see indicators of giftedness, and those students are then assessed. search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.t: These words overlap in everyday use, but each has a specific meaning in the literature, and knowing the difference helps in reading reports and sources accurately: Table 1.2: The difference among testing, measurement, assessment and evaluation. Term Meaning Example Test An organized set of tasks or questions administered in a specified way An intelligence test, or a 20-word spelling test Measurement Expressing a characteristic in numbers according to rules Scored 14 out of 20, or has a standard score of 85 Assessment The complete process of gathering information from multiple sources in order to make a decision Tests, interviews, observation and records, ending in a decision Evaluation Making a judgment about the worth or adequacy of something; in some systems also used to mean the comprehensive assessment of a student Evaluating a program's effectiveness, or the comprehensive evaluation of a student's eligibility The key point here is that testing is a small part of assessment. Sound assessment combines tests with observations, interviews and a review of records and work samples, as we will see in the evidence-gathering framework in Section 1.7.

search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.t: Before we diagnose a disability, we must ask: What is disability in the first place? Where does the problem lie? How we answer these two questions is a stance with consequences, for it determines what we measure and where we look for solutions. There are three main models: The medical model The problem lies in the individual Disability is a defect in the individual's body or functions, to be diagnosed and treated or compensated for. The focus is on the impairment and its causes. In diagnosis: looking for symptoms, matching them against criteria, and determining severity. The social model The problem lies in the environment Disability arises from the barriers society places in front of those who differ: buildings a wheelchair cannot reach, curricula that ignore individual differences. The focus is on removing barriers (Oliver, 1990). In diagnosis: asking about the barriers in the student's environment and what needs to change around the student. The biopsychosocial model The problem lies in the interaction between the two Disability results from an interaction between the individual's health condition and the environmental and personal factors surrounding him or her (Engel, 1977). This model is the foundation of the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health issued by the World Health Organization (World Health Organization [WHO], 2001). In diagnosis: describing the impairment, what the student is able to do, and the environmental factors that hinder or help. It is often said that modern diagnosis follows the third model, but this claim is a generalization that needs qualifying. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision (DSM-5-TR), remains at its core a categorical classification belonging to the medical model: the criteria are either met or not met, even though the manual adds severity specifiers and levels of support that move it closer to graded description (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). The biopsychosocial model, by contrast, underlies the International Classification of Functioning specifically, a descriptive classification that addresses functioning, participation and environmental factors and leaves the diagnosis of conditions to the medical systems. There is also growing discussion in the literature of dimensional models that describe psychological difficulties along graded continua rather than in discrete categories, one of the best known being the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology ( HiTOP ). Good practice comes closest to combining the two logics: the assessor judges whether criteria are met using a categorical logic when the system requires it, and then describes the impact of the condition and its relationship to the environment using a biopsychosocial logic. When we say that a student with autism spectrum disorder “requires substantial support,” we are describing the student's relationship to the environment as well as what the student has. The same student may need less support in a calm, structured classroom and more in a crowded, changeable one.

search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.t: Diagnosis rests on classification systems that define categories and their criteria. The most important thing for a teacher to know is that there are two kinds of systems, medical and educational, and that each serves a different purpose. Table 1.3: Medical and educational classification systems and their purposes. System Issuing body Purpose Who uses it Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders ( DSM-5-TR ) American Psychiatric Association, 2022 Diagnosing mental and developmental disorders using detailed criteria Psychiatrists and psychologists International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision ( ICD-11 ) World Health Organization; adopted in 2019 and in force since January 1, 2022; its clinical descriptions and diagnostic requirements for mental and developmental disorders were published in 2024 Classifying all diseases and health conditions, including developmental ones, for diagnostic and statistical purposes Health systems around the world International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health ( ICF ) World Health Organization, 2001 Describing what a person can do and participate in, and the environmental factors at play, rather than diagnosing the condition Rehabilitation and service-planning teams Educational categories Each country's education legislation and regulations Determining who is entitled to special education services School teams and education departments Clinical diagnosis relies on one of the first two manuals (American Psychiatric Association, 2022; WHO, 2019, 2024). The two converge for most developmental categories, though they differ in naming and detail, differences taken up in the category chapters of Part Three. An example of an educational system: the US categories The US Individuals with Disabilities Education Act ( Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, IDEA ) was reauthorized in 2004 as the Individuals with Disabilities Education Improvement Act ( IDEIA ), though it is still known by its original acronym. The law specifies thirteen categories eligible for services: autism, deaf-blindness, deafness, emotional disturbance, hearing impairment, intellectual disability, multiple disabilities, orthopedic impairment, other health impairment, specific learning disability, speech or language impairment, traumatic brain injury (resulting from a blow or impact), and visual impairment including blindness. The law also permits a developmental delay category for children aged 3 to 9 (IDEA, 2004). Note three important points about this list: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder ( Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, ADHD ) is not a separate category. A student diagnosed with it usually qualifies for services under the category of “other health impairment.” In other words, medical diagnoses and educational categories do not always coincide. Saudi regulations depart from this arrangement, as we will see in the next section. Giftedness is absent. The law concerns disabilities, and gifted services in the United States are governed by separate legislation. This explains why a twice-exceptional student, that is, a gifted student who also has a disability or disorder, falls between two systems that are not coordinated with each other (Chapter 13 discusses this group in detail). The labels differ from those of the medical manual. “Emotional disturbance” is a broad educational category that encompasses conditions bearing different names in the medical manual. 1.5.1 The regulatory framework in Saudi Arabia In this section we present the Saudi education system in the same detail as the US example, since it is the framework within which the assessment procedures discussed in this book are carried out. Special education in Saudi Arabia is organized at two levels: general laws that establish the rights of persons with disabilities, and regulatory documents issued by the Ministry of Education that define the categories, eligibility criteria and assessment and diagnosis procedu

search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.t: An assessment that ends in a diagnosis changes the course of a student's life: the school the student attends, the curriculum the student learns, how others see the student, and how the student sees himself or herself. For this reason, legislation and professional standards have set out principles that protect students from error and injustice. Among the clearest formulations are those in the implementing regulations of US law governing evaluation procedures (34 C.F.R. §300.304). The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing treat fairness as a third foundation of testing alongside validity and reliability, devoting their third chapter to it (American Educational Research Association [AERA] et al., 2014). Table 1.6 sets these principles against the provisions of Saudi regulations. Table 1.6: Principles of fair assessment, what they mean in practice, and their counterparts in Saudi regulations. Principle What it means in practice Counterpart in Saudi regulations Multiple tools and strategies No single measure is used as the sole basis for any decision; a single score, however precise, is not enough on its own to support a judgment. “Not relying solely on the results of a single measure when determining a pupil's eligibility,” and using formal and informal methods (Rules, Article 80; Organizational Guide) Assessing all areas of suspected need If there is doubt about hearing, language or attention, each is assessed, rather than only the area for which the student was referred. A multidisciplinary team and information gathered from varied sources (Rules, Article 80) Appropriate language and mode The student is assessed in his or her native language or mode of communication; a deaf student is assessed in sign language if that is the student's language. We found no explicit provision in either document specifying the language or mode of assessment Freedom from bias Tools are chosen so that they do not disadvantage the student because of culture or background. Standardized tests that are “valid, reliable and suited to the child's environment” (Rules, Article 80) Measuring what is intended to be measured If a student has a motor disability, his or her intelligence is not measured with a test that depends on motor speed, lest the score fall because of the student's hand rather than ability. “Appropriate measures and clear instructions” (Rules, Article 80), with no detail on adapting administration for students with sensory and motor disabilities Validity of the tool and qualifications of the examiner The tool is used for the purpose for which its validity has been established, and it is administered by a trained person according to its instructions. Using “tools and measures approved by the Ministry of Education,” administered and interpreted “by qualified specialists” (Organizational Guide). We found no published text specifying the qualification levels required for each class of standardized psychological test Informed family consent The family knows what will happen and why, and consents in writing before the process begins. Written consent from the parent or guardian after formal notification; if no reply is received within fourteen days, this is deemed consent (Organizational Guide; the Regulations specify two weeks) Confidentiality Only those entitled to access the information may see it, and it is stored in a way that protects it. “Maintaining the confidentiality of all information” (Rules, Articles 76 and 80); the Personal Data Protection Law (1443 AH) classifies health data as sensitive data Sources: implementing regulations of US law (34 C.F.R. §300.304), Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (AERA et al., 2014), Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif] (1422 AH [Arabic]), and Ministry of Education (1436 AH-a [Arabic]). search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.s: 1.7 Sources of evidence: the RIOT/ICEL framework
search.t: How can we be sure that the evidence we have gathered is sufficient and varied? School psychology offers a simple, practical framework for this purpose, known by its acronym ( RIOT/ICEL ; Christ, 2008). The acronym is formed from the initial letters of its words: the first part ( RIOT ) covers the methods of gathering information ( Review, Interview, Observe, Test ), and the second part ( ICEL ) covers the domains ( Instruction, Curriculum, Environment, Learner ). The framework is a two-dimensional matrix: four methods of gathering information, applied across four domains in which the problem may lie. The four methods: review, interview, observation and testing. The four domains: instruction, curriculum, environment and the learner. The central idea of the framework is that the problem may lie outside the student: in the way he is taught, in a curriculum pitched above his level, or in a noisy environment. An assessment that looks at the student alone may diagnose a disability that does not exist. Table 1.7 presents the matrix with examples in each cell. Table 1.7: The RIOT/ICEL matrix, with examples in each cell. A balanced assessment fills cells in every row and every column rather than confining itself to the testing cell in the learner row. Review Review Interview Interview Observation Observe Testing Test Instruction Instruction Lesson plans and the teaching methods used so far Asking the teacher how the skill was presented Observing the clarity of explanation and the pace of teaching Trying a different teaching method and measuring the response to it Curriculum Curriculum Difficulty level of the textbook and the sequence of skills Asking the teacher about the prerequisites for the skill Observing whether the task matches the student's level Measuring text readability, or assessing prerequisite skills Environment Environment Attendance records, and changes of school and teacher Asking the family about circumstances at home Observing noise, lighting and where the student sits Classroom environment scales Learner Learner Medical reports, previous results and samples of the student's work Asking the student what he finds difficult Observing his behavior across different situations Ability and achievement tests and diagnostic scales For the teacher Most of the cells in this matrix are in your hands before they are in the specialist's. You are the one who knows how the student is taught, the level of the curriculum and the classroom environment, and you hold the student's daily work. When you attach this information to the referral, you give the team half the picture before it begins.

search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.t: No single specialist has all the knowledge needed to understand a student fully. Diagnosis is therefore the work of a team, which, depending on the case, may include the psychologist, the special education teacher, the classroom teacher, the speech-language pathologist, the physician, the occupational therapist, the audiologist, the social worker and the family. Teams differ in how they work together: Multidisciplinary Each specialist assesses alone and writes a separate report. Their recommendations may conflict without their ever meeting. Interdisciplinary Each specialist assesses within his or her own field; they then meet, share their findings and reach a joint decision and plan. Transdisciplinary The team assesses the child together in a single session, with one member working directly with the child under the guidance of the others. This model is common in early childhood. Figure 1.2: Three models of teamwork. The solid circle at the center represents the child, the hollow circles around it represent the specialists, and the lines represent communication: dashed between each specialist and the child alone, solid between specialists when they work together. The assessment team in Saudi regulations The Regulations assign assessment and diagnosis to a team made up of the relevant special education teacher, the behavioral training teacher (the psychologist), the child's guardian, and anyone whose participation the case requires (Article 81). Among the psychologist's duties they list “conducting assessment and diagnosis” using formal tools, such as standardized intelligence scales and adaptive behavior scales, and informal tools, such as interviews, observation and checklists (Articles 48 and 49) (Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif], 1422 AH [Arabic]). The Organizational Guide widens the team to include the school principal, the vice principal for student affairs, the special education teacher, the general education teacher, the student counselor or social worker, specialists according to the disability category, the physician or nurse where available, and the student's guardian “if possible” (Ministry of Education, 1436 AH-a [Arabic]). The phrase “if possible” is weaker than what the Regulations themselves establish when they make the guardian a member of the team, and weaker than what this book holds in the next section. The family as a partner in assessment and decision-making The family has known the student since birth, and in situations no one else sees. Its role in assessment goes well beyond answering questions: The holder of consent: Assessment does not begin without the family's informed consent, and the family has the right to ask questions and to object. A source of developmental history: When the child walked, when he began to talk, and what changed and when. A witness to behavior in a different setting: What the family sees at home may differ from what the teacher sees, and the difference is itself information. A partner in the decision and the plan: The family attends the results meeting, understands the findings and takes part in setting goals. The Regulations grant the family explicit rights in this regard: the guardian's permission must be obtained for diagnosis, for preparing the program and for approving any modification; the family is to be invited to take part in diagnosis, program planning and evaluation; their child's condition is to be explained to them “in understandable language”; and the student is to be rediagnosed at the family's request if they believe he has not been placed in the appropriate program (Article 76). The Regulations also require the family's participation in preparing, implementing, evaluating and monitoring the individualized education program (Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif], 1422 AH [Arabic]). For the teacher: When you talk to the family about your concern Begin with what the student does well; the family needs to know that you see their child as a whole person. Describe what

search.s: 1.9 The general pathway and its common errors
search.t: Detailed procedures vary across countries and categories, but most systems follow a broadly similar pathway: Observation and screening The teacher or the family notices indicators, or the student is flagged in screening results. Teacher, family, screening team Classroom support and documentation Instructional adjustments and additional support for a set period, with the response measured and documented. Teacher, supported by the school team Referral and consent If the response is insufficient, a referral is written with the evidence attached, and the family's consent is requested. Teacher, school administration, family Comprehensive assessment The team gathers evidence from multiple sources, using tools suited to each area of suspected need. Multidisciplinary team Decision meeting The team and the family discuss the results and determine whether the criteria are met and whether the student is eligible for services. Team, family Plan, monitoring and reevaluation The individualized education program ( Individualized Education Program, IEP ) is developed, progress is monitored, and the student is reevaluated periodically or as needed. Special education teacher, classroom teacher, family Some systems set binding timelines for these steps. In the US system, for example, the initial evaluation must be completed within sixty days of parental consent, unless the state sets a different timeline (IDEA, 2004). The purpose of such timelines is to ensure that a student does not wait for months without services or a decision. Table 1.8 sets each step against the provisions of the two systems. Table 1.8: Steps of the general pathway in the US system and their counterparts in Saudi regulations. Step In the US system (as an example) Counterpart in the Saudi system 1. Observation and screening The state is obliged to locate, identify and evaluate children with disabilities ( Child find ; 34 C.F.R. §300.111) A right to the “early detection of disability” (Law on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Article 9); for giftedness: the National Program for Gifted Identification, upon registration 2. Classroom support and documentation For learning disabilities, evidence of appropriate instruction and repeated measurement of progress is required, and the response to intervention model may be used (34 C.F.R. §300.307, §300.309) For learning disabilities, it must be established that general education services are inappropriate or of limited effectiveness, without specifying how this is to be established; the student may be placed under observation “for a full semester” where needed (Regulations, Article 80) 3. Referral and consent Informed written parental consent before the initial evaluation (34 C.F.R. §300.300) Written consent from the guardian after formal notification; no response within 14 days is treated as consent (Organizational Guide) 4. Comprehensive assessment Completed within sixty days of consent, unless the state sets a different timeline Carried out by the assessment team using tools approved by the Ministry, in seven steps that begin with notifying the guardian and end with the final report (Regulations, Article 82). We found no timeline in either document for completing the initial evaluation that corresponds to the sixty-day limit 5. Decision meeting A team that includes the parents determines eligibility, and the family receives a copy of the evaluation report (34 C.F.R. §300.306) The assessment team issues the final report; the guardian is a member of the team under the Regulations, and “if possible” under the Guide 6. Plan and reevaluation An individualized education program with specified components (34 C.F.R. §300.320); reevaluation at least once every three years, and not more than once a year unless the family and the agency agree (34 C.F.R. §300.303) An individualized education program covering present levels of performance, long-term and short-term goals written in measurable behavioral terms, services, and performance cri

search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.t: The argument we have developed in this chapter holds that assessment begins with the decision to be made and then selects its tool, and that each step in the pathway has its own question: screening sorts, identification gathers initial evidence and refers, diagnosis matches criteria, and eligibility determines the need for services. It follows that no step should be asked for what it cannot provide. A screening result does not establish a disability, a medical diagnosis does not automatically confer educational eligibility, and a teacher's opinion is the beginning of identification. It follows, too, that evidence should be gathered from multiple tools and sources, that instruction, curriculum and environment should be examined before a shortfall is attributed to the student, and that the family should be a partner in the decision as well as a source of information. Some of what this chapter has presented, however, is a matter of terminology or of judgment. Using “identification” for the stage before referral is a terminological choice we have adopted for this book; the meaning of the term differs between the field of giftedness and the field of disabilities; medical and educational categories do not always coincide; and combining criterion-based judgment with a description of functioning in context calls for professional judgment that no ready-made rule can supply. Deciding whether the evidence is sufficient to move from one step to the next remains a professional judgment, one that must be reasoned and that weighs the numbers, the documents and all the other evidence.

search.c: Chapter 1: Concepts of diagnosis and identification
search.t: Chapter summary Assessment is a means to a decision, and its first question is: What decision do we want to make? Screening sorts, identification gathers initial evidence and refers, diagnosis matches criteria, and eligibility determines the need for services. Using “identification” for the stage before referral is a terminological choice made for this book. A screening tool is judged by its sensitivity and its specificity together, and its negative predictive value tells us how confident we can be that we have not missed anyone. Medical diagnosis and educational eligibility are two different questions, and medical and educational categories do not always coincide. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual is categorical at its core, the biopsychosocial model underpins the International Classification of Functioning, and good practice combines criterion-based judgment with a description of functioning in context. In Saudi Arabia, diagnosis is governed by the Regulations for Special Education Institutes and Programs (1422 AH) and the Special Education Organizational Guide (1436–1437 AH); the Law on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (1445 AH) establishes the right to diagnosis and early detection; and the identification of gifted students follows a separate pathway. Fair assessment draws on multiple tools and sources, is conducted in the student's language, uses tools valid for their purpose, and rests on the family's informed consent. The RIOT/ICEL framework is a reminder that the problem may lie in instruction, curriculum or the environment, as well as in the student. Glossary of terms Screening A quick procedure applied to an entire group to determine who needs a more in-depth assessment. Identification In this book: the stage of gathering initial evidence and attempting support within the classroom, in preparation for a referral decision. In much of the literature, the term denotes the entire process of determination up to the decision; in the field of giftedness, it is a multi-criteria educational process for determining who needs gifted services, not a clinical diagnosis. Identification; detection A term that overlaps in the Arabic literature with “identification” and is generally used for the process of locating and identifying gifted students or students with disabilities, as in the “National Program for Gifted Identification” and the “early detection of disability.” Referral A formal request for a comprehensive assessment of the student, accompanied by the evidence and the family's consent. Nomination A proposal by a teacher, the family or the student himself that a student be assessed within a gifted identification program. Diagnosis A judgment that the criteria for a particular category apply to the student, based on a comprehensive assessment. Eligibility A decision on whether the student is entitled to special services, based on the diagnosis and its impact on his learning. Sensitivity The ability of a tool to capture those who actually have the problem; a property strongly required of screening tools. Specificity The ability of a tool to rule out those who do not have the problem. Negative predictive value The proportion of those with a negative result who are actually free of the problem; it is affected by the prevalence of the problem in the group. Informed consent The family's agreement after learning what will be done, why, and who will have access to the results. Diagnostic overshadowing Attributing new symptoms to a known disability, which leads to another condition being missed. Confirmation bias The assessor's tendency to see the evidence that supports a prior hypothesis and to overlook the evidence against it. Cut-off score The threshold that a scale or a system sets for making a decision. Multidisciplinary team A group of specialists from different fields who take part in assessing the student, each usually working alone. Interdisciplinary team A team in which each member assesses the student within his

2 Chapter 2 Measurement fundamentals What does a score of 78 mean? How does a percentile rank differ from a percentage? And why does the psychologist write two more numbers on either side of a score? In this chapter we provide the keys for reading assessment reports of every kind, and we show what a number can tell us and where its meaning stops. Scene from a team meeting Umm Majed sits in the school meeting with a six-page report in front of her. She reads: “Full-scale score 72, percentile rank 3, confidence interval 65 to 79.” She looks up and asks the teacher: “Does this mean my son passed with three percent? Does he have a disability or not?” The teacher hesitates. He knows the number is not a pass rate, but he does not know how to explain that, nor why the report lists two additional numbers around the score. We return to Umm Majed at the end of the chapter to give her two questions a precise answer. The concepts presented here recur throughout the category chapters, for they are the shared language in which every diagnostic report is written. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Classify a reported assessment result as norm-referenced or criterion-referenced, and justify the classification by the question the result answers. Convert a score among the common standard score metrics, and locate it on the normal curve and within its descriptive classification. Interpret a percentile rank correctly, and correct a statement that confuses it with a percentage or an age equivalent. Calculate the standard error of measurement, the confidence interval and the standard error of the difference, and use them to judge a score close to a cut-off or a difference between two scores. Calculate positive and negative predictive values from sensitivity, specificity and prevalence, and explain why they differ between universal screening and a referred group. Evaluate whether an instrument is appropriate for a particular student in light of the five sources of validity evidence, reliability, norms, language and fairness evidence. Identify the ethical or professional principle at stake in a described assessment situation, and propose a course of action consistent with it.

Assessment results reach teachers and families as numbers: a standard score, a percentile rank, a confidence interval and a descriptive classification. The percentile rank is the percentage of the student’s peers in the norming sample (the representative group from which the instrument’s norms were derived) who scored lower than the student did; a percentile rank of 84 means the student outperformed 84% of them. Each of these numbers carries a specific meaning and has limits it cannot exceed, and misreading it leads to a mistaken decision: a percentile rank taken as the proportion of correct answers, as Umm Majed understood it in the opening scene; a score treated as an exact figure free of error; or a firm decision made when the confidence interval straddles the cut-off. In most categories, the diagnostic judgment rests on where the student stands relative to peers, on how precisely that position is estimated, and on whether the instrument suits its purpose and the student to whom it was administered. We open the chapter by distinguishing norm-referenced from criterion-referenced measures (Section 2.1), then present the mean and standard deviation (Section 2.2), the normal curve, standard scores and their descriptive classifications (Section 2.3), and percentile ranks and their pitfalls (Section 2.4). We then take up reliability/precision and the standard error of measurement, together with the related matters of score differences, regression toward the mean and floor and ceiling effects (Section 2.5), followed by validity, sensitivity, specificity and fairness (Section 2.6), and then norms, standardization and test adaptation (Section 2.7). We apply all this to reading a realistic score table (Section 2.8), and close with ethics, professional responsibility and levels of qualification (Section 2.9).

Before we ask “How much did the student score?” we must ask “Compared with what?” A score on its own has no meaning. Eighty points may be excellent on a hard test and weak on an easy one. Measures are therefore divided into two main types according to what the score is compared with: Norm-referenced measures Norm-referenced Where does the student stand relative to peers? The student’s score is compared with the scores of a large group of same-age or same-grade peers, called the norming sample . The result tells us the student’s position among them: average, above average or below average. Examples: intelligence tests, adaptive behavior scales, and rating scales such as the Gilliam Autism Rating Scale, Third Edition ( Gilliam Autism Rating Scale, GARS-3 ). Criterion-referenced measures Criterion-referenced Has the student mastered the target skill? The student’s score is compared with a predetermined level of performance. The result tells us what the student can and cannot do, regardless of peers. Examples: “Reads 40 words per minute with 95% accuracy,” or “Adds two two-digit numbers with regrouping on 8 of 10 problems.” The two types complement each other. Diagnosis usually calls for norm-referenced measures, because its question is “Is the student’s performance unusually far from that of peers?” Instructional planning, by contrast, calls for criterion-referenced measures, because its question is “What skill should we teach next?” A single tool may combine both logics. One example is curriculum-based measurement , a set of brief, repeated probes used to track a student’s reading or mathematics week by week (defined and discussed in detail in Chapter 4). It serves as a general indicator of growth: its scores are interpreted normatively when compared with seasonal grade-level norms, such as fall, winter and spring percentile ranks, and at the same time against a specific growth goal set for the student. It thus draws on both frames of reference at once. An example of the difference Saad, a fourth grader, obtained a percentile rank of 50 on a standardized reading test, placing him exactly in the middle of his peers. This is norm-referenced information, and it does not point to a problem. On a criterion-referenced test, however, his teacher noticed that he could not distinguish between letters that share the same shape and differ only in their dots, such as ب (bāʾ), ت (tāʾ) and ث (thāʾ). The first test does not reveal this, yet it is precisely what the teacher needs to know in order to decide what to teach tomorrow.

search.s: 2.2 The mean and the standard deviation
search.t: Every standard score is built on two numbers: the mean ( Mean ), the center of the norming sample’s scores, and the standard deviation ( Standard deviation, SD ), the degree to which scores are spread around that center. A small standard deviation means people’s scores lie close together; a large one means they are widely dispersed. To make the idea of standard deviation concrete, imagine two classes of twenty students each, both with an average height of 140 centimeters. In the first class, heights range from 135 to 145; in the second, from 120 to 160. The mean is the same, but the spread differs. A student who is 150 centimeters tall would be considered very tall in the first class and fairly ordinary in the second. It is the standard deviation that tells us so. This gives us the rule on which diagnosis rests: we measure how far a student lies from the mean in standard deviations rather than in points. A distance of two standard deviations from the mean signifies the same thing on any test, however its scores are calculated.

search.s: 2.3 The normal curve and standard scores
search.t: When we measure a trait such as intelligence or height in a large number of people, the scores usually fall into a bell shape: most people cluster near the mean, and their numbers dwindle the further we move from it in either direction. This shape is the normal curve ( Normal curve ), and among its properties are fixed proportions that do not change: About 68% of people fall between one standard deviation below the mean and one standard deviation above it. About 95% fall between two standard deviations below the mean and two above it. Only about 2% fall more than two standard deviations below the mean, and roughly the same proportion more than two standard deviations above it. This last point is the origin of thresholds that recur throughout this book. The criterion of “two standard deviations below the mean” is used for intellectual disability, and “two standard deviations above the mean” appears in many definitions of giftedness. By this statistical criterion alone, then, each of the two groups represents about 2% of people at either end of the distribution. 34% 34% 14% 14% 2% 2% Mean −3 −2 −1 0 +1 +2 +3 — 55 70 85 100 115 130 145 Standard score (100, 15) 1 4 7 10 13 16 19 Scaled score (10, 3) 20 30 40 50 60 70 80 T-score (50, 10) 0.1 2 16 50 84 98 99.9 Percentile rank Figure 2.1: The normal curve, with the common score types aligned beneath it by position. Each column represents the same position expressed in different metrics: a full-scale score of 70 on an intelligence test is equivalent to a subtest score of 4 and to a T-score of 30, and all three mean two standard deviations below the mean. Types of standard scores Tests convert the raw score, the number of correct answers, into a standard score with a fixed mean and standard deviation. The benefit is that standard scores can be compared across ages and tests. The most widely used types are: Table 2.1: Common types of standard scores. Type Mean — Where you will encounter it z-score ( z ) 0 1 In calculations and research; it is the basis from which all other types are derived Standard score 100 15 Composite and index scores on intelligence and achievement tests and adaptive behavior scales Scaled score 10 3 Subtests of intelligence scales, and the subscales of the GARS-3 T-score ( T ) 50 10 Behavioral and emotional rating scales, including many measures of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder ( Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, ADHD ) To convert any score to another type, we first convert it to a z-score and then from the z-score to the desired type: z = (X − M) ÷ SD z-score = (student’s score − mean) ÷ standard deviation Worked example 1 Hind obtained a standard score of 82 on an intelligence test with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. 2 The z-score: (82 − 100) ÷ 15 = −1.2 , meaning she is one and one-fifth standard deviations below the mean. 3 Expressed as a T-score, it would be: 50 + (−1.2 × 10) = 38 . 4 Her percentile rank is about 12, meaning her performance exceeds that of about 12% of her peers in the norming sample. Watch the direction of the score On ability tests, a higher score means better performance. On many behavioral rating scales, however, a higher score means more problems. A T-score of 70 is excellent on a reading test and worrying on a hyperactivity scale. Always check the test manual or the report for what a high score means. Descriptive classifications Tests translate the standard score into a verbal description that is easy to understand. The percentile rank is, on the surface, the easiest score for families to understand, and it is also the one most prone to misunderstanding. It means the percentage of peers in the norming sample who scored lower than the student . A percentile rank of 30 means the student outperformed about 30% of his peers, and that about 70% of them outperformed him. The first pitfall: confusing it with percentage correct The percentile rank has nothing to do with the percentage of correct answers. A student who answered 80% of the questions may have a percentile rank of 20 if the test was easy and most of his peers answered more than that. This is the trap Umm Majed fell into when she thought her son had “passed with three percent.” The second pitfall: the distances between ranks are unequal Because most people cluster around the mean, moving a few percentile ranks near the mean takes only a small difference in performance, whereas moving the same number of ranks at the extremes takes a large one. Compare these two moves, each spanning a similar number of ranks: From rank 50 to rank 60 4 standard score points From rank 90 to rank 99 16 standard score points Figure 2.2: What each move is worth on a standard score scale with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. Ten ranks near the mean equal about 4 points, whereas nine ranks at the extreme equal about 16 points. For this reason, percentile ranks should not be subtracted from one another or averaged, nor used to measure a student’s progress. If a student moves from the 5th to the 10th percentile, his progress may be far greater than the two numbers suggest. The third pitfall: age and grade equivalents Age equivalents ( Age equivalent ) and grade equivalents ( Grade equivalent ) express performance in terms of an age or a school grade. A teacher may read in a report that “the student’s reading age equivalent is 7 years, 3 months,” while the student is actually ten, and conclude that he reads like a seven-year-old. That reading is inaccurate. An age equivalent means only that the student’s raw score equals the average raw score of children of that age; it does not mean that his skills or errors resemble theirs. These scores are also unevenly distributed, and they do not show whether the gap is large relative to the student’s peers. This is why the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing urge great caution in their use (AERA et al., 2014), and why standard scores and percentile ranks are preferred.

search.s: 2.5 Reliability/precision and the standard error of measurement
search.t: Reliability ( Reliability ) is the consistency of a measure’s results. If the test were given to the same student twice under similar conditions, would he obtain two similar scores? A scale that shows a different weight each time is useless, however accurate it may be on average. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing use the compound term “reliability/precision” ( Reliability/precision ) to cover traditional reliability coefficients as well as every other index of score precision, such as the standard error of measurement and the information function, which we present at the end of this section (AERA et al., 2014). Types of reliability Table 2.3: Types of reliability and the question each one answers. Type Question it answers How it is calculated Test–retest reliability Does the score remain stable over time? The test is given twice with a short interval between administrations, and the correlation between the two is calculated Internal consistency Do the test items measure the same thing? Calculated from the item intercorrelations in a single administration; the best known index is Cronbach’s alpha ( Cronbach's alpha ) Interrater reliability Do two different raters assign the same score? Two people rate the same student and their ratings are compared; this is especially important for observation and rating scales Alternate-forms reliability Do two forms of the test yield similar results? Two equivalent forms are administered, and the correlation between them is calculated Reliability is expressed as a coefficient ranging from zero to one. Salvia and colleagues (Salvia et al., 2017) proposed widely used benchmarks: at least 0.60 when scores are used to describe groups, at least 0.80 for screening decisions, and at least 0.90 for important decisions about an individual, such as diagnosis and classification. Reliable and valid The results are consistent and hit what is meant to be measured Reliable but not valid The results are consistent but measure something else Not reliable The results are scattered, so the measure cannot be valid Figure 2.3: The relationship between reliability and validity, illustrated with target shooting. Reliability is a prerequisite for validity, but it is not sufficient on its own. — No measure is perfectly reliable. A student’s score on any given day is affected by fatigue, attention, guessing and the conditions in the room. The score we obtain is therefore an estimate of the true score, the score the student would have obtained had he been measured without any error. The standard error of measurement ( Standard Error of Measurement, SEM ) is a number that tells us how much the student’s score would be expected to fluctuate if we measured him many times over: SEM = SD × √(1 − r) standard error of measurement = standard deviation × square root of (1 − reliability coefficient) From it we build a confidence interval ( Confidence interval ): a range of scores within which we can say, with a given degree of confidence, that the true score lies. For a 95% confidence interval, we multiply the standard error by approximately 1.96, then add the result to the score and subtract it from the score. Worked example: Majed’s score 1 Majed obtained a full-scale score of 72 on an intelligence test with a standard deviation of 15 and a reliability coefficient of 0.95. 2 The standard error of measurement: 15 × √(1 − 0.95) = 15 × 0.224 ≈ 3.4 3 The 95% confidence interval: 72 ± (1.96 × 3.4) = 72 ± 6.6 , that is, from about 65 to about 79. 4 The result: we can be 95% confident that Majed’s true score on this test lies between 65 and 79. This range straddles the cut-off score of 70 . Traditional cut-off score 70 Majed’s score 72 55 60 65 70 75 80 85 90 Figure 2.4: Majed’s score and the confidence interval around it. The point lies above the cut-off score, but the band extends to either side of it, so we cannot say on the strength of the number alone that he “exceeded” it or “fell short” of it. A cut-off s

If reliability asks, “Does the scale measure consistently?”, validity asks, “Does it actually measure what it is meant to measure? And are the decisions we base on its scores sound?” In the modern view, validity is a property of the interpretation of a scale’s scores for a particular purpose, and it changes with the purpose and with the person tested. A scale that is valid for screening three-year-olds may not be valid for diagnosing an adolescent. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing treat validity as a single, unified concept, sometimes called construct validity : the degree to which the evidence supports interpreting the score as representing the intended construct. The construct is what all the evidence, taken together, attests to. The Standards draw this evidence from five sources (AERA et al., 2014): Table 2.4: The five sources of validity evidence in the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, with examples from adapting scales for Arabic-speaking settings. Source of evidence Question Example Content Do the items cover the facets of the construct adequately, and do they suit the setting in which they are used? An autism spectrum disorder scale whose items cover the two core domains in the diagnostic manual: difficulties in social communication and interaction, and restricted, repetitive behaviors and interests. For the Arabic version, local experts review each item: does it describe a behavior one would expect to see in a Saudi home or school? Response processes Do test takers or raters actually engage the processes the construct assumes when they respond? Saudi children are asked to think aloud while solving the items of a reasoning test, or parents are asked what they understand by a statement on a rating scale. If it turns out that a child fails because he does not know a Standard Arabic word in the question, the item is measuring vocabulary, not reasoning Internal structure Do the items and dimensions relate to one another as the theory predicts? Factor analysis of the Arabic version: does it retain the structure of the original? A factor analysis of the Arabic version of the Childhood Autism Rating Scale arrived at a three-factor model of 14 items (Alotaibi & Alotaibi, 2021), and an Omani study of the Adaptive Behavior Assessment System (ABAS-3) supported a single general-factor model among children with intellectual disability (Emam et al., 2020) Relations to other variables Do scores correlate with what they are expected to correlate with, predict the criterion, and distinguish between groups? The Saudi version of the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Third Edition, correlated with the Saudi version of the Stanford-Binet at 0.81 (Ejbara, 2024). In a validation of the Arabic version of the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers across nine Arab countries, sensitivity reached 0.86 and specificity 0.80 (Seif Eldin et al., 2008) Consequences What are the effects, intended or unintended, of using the scores in decisions? Does using a scale for nomination to gifted programs lead to lower-than-expected representation of students from villages or of a particular group? (Chapter 14 returns to this question) The older division into “content validity,” “criterion validity” and “construct validity” still appears in many test manuals and Arabic textbooks. In that scheme, “criterion validity” corresponds to part of the fourth source, while “construct validity” corresponds to validity as a whole in the modern view. The second and third sources, however, are the most important questions we ask when evaluating an Arabic adaptation: Does the Arab child understand the item as intended? And has the adaptation retained the structure of the original? Sensitivity and specificity, and why the value of a positive result changes For screening and diagnostic tools, validity evidence based on relations to other variables is usually reported through two concepts: sensitivity ( Sensitivit

A standard score means “the student's position among his peers in the norming sample.” The norming sample ( Norm sample ) is the group to which the scale was administered to derive its norms. If the norming sample does not resemble the student, the score loses its meaning. We therefore ask three questions of any instrument before using it: Who is in the norming sample? Does it represent the children we are assessing in age, environment and language? A test normed on American children compares a Saudi child with American children rather than with peers in his own environment. When was it normed? Average performance on intelligence tests has risen across generations in many countries, a phenomenon known as the Flynn effect (Flynn, 1984). A meta-analysis, that is, a study that statistically combines the results of many studies, estimated it at about two to three standard-score points per decade (Trahan et al., 2014). The phenomenon, however, is neither universal nor constant in direction; a slowdown or even a reversal has been documented in some countries in recent decades (Bratsberg & Rogeberg, 2018). Where the effect exists, old norms inflate the scores of today's children, masking an existing disability at one end and swelling the number identified as gifted at the other. The practical lesson is the same in both cases: know the year in which the norms were collected, and treat scores near cut-off points with caution when the norms are old. In what language and culture? Translation alone is not enough. A question about “snow” or “Thanksgiving” is familiar to a child in one setting and strange to a child in another. From translation to standardization To simplify the path an instrument travels from one culture to another, this book distinguishes three levels. The division is the author's own teaching simplification, built on what international guidelines require (see the next box): Table 2.7: Three levels in transferring an instrument from one culture to another (the author's simplification). Level What happens What can be done with the scores Translation Items are rendered into Arabic literally or nearly so The original norms cannot properly be used to judge the child Test adaptation Items and examples are modified to suit the culture, with back-translation (translating the Arabic version back into the original language and comparing it with the original), expert review, item analysis, and verification of measurement invariance across the two versions and of the absence of differential item functioning (see 2.6.1) Better than translation, but the original norms remain unsuitable Local standardization The adapted version is administered to a representative sample of the local population, new norms are derived, and reliability and validity are studied in that population Standard scores become meaningful for children in that population For the specialist: What do the International Test Commission guidelines actually say? The second edition of the International Test Commission Guidelines for Translating and Adapting Tests consists of eighteen guidelines grouped into six categories. Unlike the transfer levels in our table, they follow the stages of the work (International Test Commission, 2017): Precondition: obtaining permission from the copyright holder, and verifying before starting that the construct being measured is meaningful in the new culture. Test development: translating and adapting the items with a team qualified in both languages and in the subject matter, and trying out the items on small samples. Confirmation: gathering empirical evidence of the equivalence of the two versions: measurement invariance, examination of differential item functioning, reliability, and validity in the new population. Administration: controlling administration instructions and conditions so as to reduce sources of bias in the new population.
