search.t: The following signs are warning signals. Their value lies in the teacher documenting them and discussing them with the school counselor or the support team, especially when they persist, appear in more than one situation, or represent a clear change from the student's previous state. Table 10.3: Signs that warrant attention, by school level. Stage Attention and activity Externalizing behavior Emotion (internalizing) Kindergarten and early grades Restless movement exceeding that of the classmates closest in age, great difficulty waiting for a turn, and repeated accidents caused by impulsivity Temper outbursts far more intense and prolonged than expected for the child's age, and repeated aggression toward peers Intense crying at separation that lasts for weeks, complete silence at school with normal speech at home, and recurrent morning physical complaints Upper elementary grades Assignments left unfinished despite understanding, repeated careless errors, and materials constantly lost Constant arguing with adults, refusal to follow instructions with more than one teacher, and lying or taking others' belongings Excessive fear of mistakes or of tests, avoidance of participation, withdrawal from play, and sadness or irritability lasting for weeks Middle and high school A sudden decline as the number of subjects grows, inability to plan projects and deadlines, and quiet inattention that had gone unnoticed before Unexcused absences, serious rule violations, aggression, associating with peers who break rules, and frequent intense irritability Increasing absences, falling grades, withdrawal from friends, changes in sleep or eating, and expressions of hopelessness or worthlessness (see also the warning box in 10.4)

search.t: 1 Documented observation Record the behavior with an operational definition, that is, a description that can be observed and counted, across different situations, together with what precedes and follows it. Consider the student's relative age within the class and any recent change in his or her life. 2 Sensory check, screening and classroom support Confirm that hearing and vision are intact as a precondition for any diagnostic instrument. Then conduct universal behavior screening that captures externalizing and internalizing problems together, or use a broad screening measure such as the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. Alongside these, make adjustments to the environment, instruction and behavior management, and monitor their effect. Persists despite support: referral 3 Ruling out other causes Ask about sleep and health, assess achievement to rule out a learning disability, and ask about family circumstances, recent changes and traumatic events. Formal referral begins with the parent's written consent. 4 Comprehensive multi-informant assessment Rating scales from the family and from two teachers where possible, and from the student if old enough; a developmental history interview; direct observation; and a functional behavioral assessment ( Functional Behavioral Assessment, FBA ) when the function the behavior serves needs to be understood. Are the criteria met in two settings, with impact, and with no better explanation? Yes Diagnosis, then the eligibility decision A licensed health professional issues the diagnosis, specifying presentation and severity, and the school's assessment team decides eligibility for services No No diagnosis for now Address the most likely cause, and monitor Figure 10.5: The decision pathway for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and behavioral and emotional disorders. Hearing and vision screening comes in the second step, before any diagnostic instrument, and the third step deliberately precedes the comprehensive assessment, because inattention and difficult behavior have many possible causes. Universal behavior screening Schools usually wait for a student to catch the teacher's eye, which means that a student who disturbs no one may never be seen at all. For this reason, schools that operate a multi-tiered system of supports are turning to universal behavior screening ( Universal behavior screening ): the teacher rates every student in the class, referred or not, with a brief tool two or three times a year, as is done for reading. Table 10.4 presents three well-known examples. Table 10.4: Examples of universal behavior screening systems in schools. System Method What it captures Student Risk Screening Scale ( Student Risk Screening Scale, SRSS ) and its extended version for internalizing problems ( SRSS-IE ) The teacher rates every student on a single list of a few items using a short scale, in one sitting for the whole class The original version targets externalizing problems; the extended version adds items for internalizing problems Behavioral and Emotional Screening System ( Behavioral and Emotional Screening System, BESS ) Brief teacher, parent and student forms, part of the Behavior Assessment System for Children family (Reynolds & Kamphaus, 2015) An overall risk level (normal, elevated or extremely elevated) covering both externalizing and internalizing problems Systematic Screening for Behavior Disorders ( Systematic Screening for Behavior Disorders, SSBD ) Successive gates: the teacher ranks students on externalizing and internalizing lists, then rates the highest-ranked students with more detailed checklists; in the original version, direct observation in the classroom and on the playground follows Both kinds together; it was designed from the outset so that internalizing problems would not be missed These systems are useful only under two conditions. search.t: Broadband screening Captures externalizing and internalizing problems together and highlights strengths. SDQ Rating scales Measure disorder symptoms or a broad range of problems across multiple informants. Vanderbilt · Conners 4 · ASEBA · RCADS Computerized measures Computer-based attention tasks, used only as a supplement. CPT The profiles follow a single template: the idea behind the tool, its actual format, a scene from its administration, a table of its key information, how its results are interpreted, and finally its limitations. Where we have not verified a figure in the technical manual itself, we write “in the technical manual” or “in published studies,” and we have not carried over figures from secondary sources; examiners should read these values from their original sources before relying on the tool (see Chapter 2). This book does not reproduce the items of any instrument, and the drawings of forms are meant only to illustrate the layout of the page. For the specialist: Why do informants disagree? A well-known meta-analysis pooled the results of dozens of studies on informant agreement about children’s behavioral and emotional problems. The mean correlation was about 0.60 between informants who see the child in the same setting, such as two parents; about 0.28 between informants who see the child in different settings, such as a parent and a teacher; and about 0.22 between children’s self-ratings and the ratings of others (Achenbach et al., 1987). A later, extensive review concluded that this discrepancy is information in its own right, and that averaging it away squanders that information: it tells us where the behavior appears and with whom, and it reveals problems that only the child can see (De Los Reyes et al., 2015). The practical rule is this: for externalizing problems, teachers and parents are strong sources; for internalizing problems, especially in adolescents, the student’s self-report is essential, because anxiety and sadness may go unnoticed by anyone else. SDQ Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire Broadband screening The idea A brief tool completed by someone who knows the student. Within minutes it screens for the most prominent behavioral and emotional problems while also measuring a positive domain, which makes it suitable for screening in both schools and clinics (Goodman, 1997). What it looks like A single page of 25 statements, divided equally among five subscales: emotional problems, conduct problems, hyperactivity/inattention, peer relationship problems, and prosocial behavior. For each statement, the respondent chooses one of three options: “Not true,” “Somewhat true,” or “Certainly true.” There are parent and teacher forms, a self-report form from age 11, and an optional supplement asking about the impact of the difficulties on the student’s life. 0 1 2 1 2 3 4 5 6 … 1 2 3 1 Details of the student and the respondent, with brief instructions: answer based on the student’s behavior over the past six months. 2 Twenty-five statements in which the five scales alternate, each followed by three boxes scored 0, 1 and 2, with reverse scoring for the positively worded statements. 3 Impact supplement: Do the difficulties affect home life, schoolwork and relationships? search.s: 10.9 When is a judgment made? Four cases
search.t: Case 1: Faisal, 7 years 8 months Combined presentation, moderate severity Background: He is the student in the first scene. His teacher documented his behavior for two weeks and tried seating him near her desk, breaking tasks into smaller parts and a reinforcement system; he improved slightly, then slipped back. His age is roughly in the middle of his class. His mother says he “hasn’t sat still since he started walking,” and that his kindergarten teachers complained about the same thing. Mother’s rating Teacher’s rating Inattention symptoms present 7 of 9 8 of 9 Hyperactivity symptoms present 8 of 9 7 of 9 Impaired performance In relationships with siblings In reading and relationships Anxiety and depression items Low Low Figure 10.8: Hypothetical summary of the mother’s and teacher’s Vanderbilt ratings. The picture is consistent across home and school and exceeds the six-symptom criterion on both lists. The team added that hearing and vision screening was normal, his sleep was regular, and an achievement test showed a mild weakness in reading consistent with his inattention rather than with a difficulty in phonological awareness. Direct classroom observation recorded him out of his seat in 60% of intervals using partial-interval recording (see Chapter 4), compared with 15% for two classmates observed for comparison. A ✓ Both lists 6+ B ✓ Since kindergarten C ✓ Home and school D ✓ Clear impact E ✓ No better explanation Decision: The physician diagnosed Faisal with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, combined presentation, of moderate severity: his symptom count exceeds the required threshold by one or two symptoms on each list, and his impairment is clear at home and at school without reaching a level that disrupts most aspects of his day (see Table 10.1). A classroom support plan, behavior management training for the family and monitoring of his reading skills are recommended. What evidence could change the decision? If his reading weakness persisted after his attention in class improved, an assessment for a co-occurring learning disability would be warranted. And if kindergarten records showed that what his mother described had not been noticed there, Criterion B would need firmer confirmation before the diagnosis is settled. Case 2: Haya, 11 years Anxiety explains the picture Background: She is the student in the second scene. Her teacher requested an assessment for a possible predominantly inattentive presentation. But the specialist asked about timing and learned that Haya had performed well until the end of fifth grade, that her father had gone abroad for work the previous summer, and that every evening she asks her mother whether he is all right. These are the main questions to ask before reaching a judgment: Table 10.14: Differential diagnosis of ADHD and behavioral and emotional disorders. Possible cause Similarity Distinctive features Relative age and immaturity Restlessness and weak self-control Behavior is consistent with that of the peers closest in age, as in Saud’s case Anxiety Daydreaming, fidgeting and difficulty concentrating Daydreaming due to preoccupation with worries, and an onset linked to an event, as in Haya’s case Depression Poor concentration and unfinished tasks, and irritability that may be read as defiance Sadness or irritability, loss of interest in things previously enjoyed, and a clear change from previous functioning, as in Lamia’s case Oppositional defiant disorder Refusing instructions and not completing tasks The refusal is directed at the person making the request rather than at the task, and it appears even with short, easy tasks. It frequently co-occurs with ADHD — Temper outbursts and irritability Severe, recurrent outbursts, persistently irritable mood between outbursts, and onset before age ten Learning disability Avoiding tasks and not completing them Inattention appears only in the difficult subject, while the student attends well in others. The two may co-occur Hearing or visual impairment Does not respond or follow along Improves when the sensory impairment is treated, which is why sensory screening precedes any diagnostic tool Insufficient sleep or sleep problems Fatigue, daydreaming and quick temper A history of late or interrupted sleep, or snoring Trauma and family stress Hypervigilance, emotional reactivity and poor concentration A history of difficult events, after which behavior may change noticeably Giftedness with an unsuitable curriculum Boredom, daydreaming and interrupting Usually improves with enrichment and tasks matched to the student’s level. But the disappearance of the behavior during a stimulating activity does not rule out the disorder (see the box in 10.1), and the two may co-occur Autism spectrum disorder Social difficulties and impulsivity The social difficulty lies in reading social cues, not in impulsivity alone; both diagnoses may be given together Co-occurring condition The conditions in Table 10.14 are not always alternatives; many of them co-occur in the same student. Oppositional defiance frequently accompanies ADHD, anxiety and depression often occur together in adolescents, and published reviews report that a substantial proportion of students with learning disabilities also have ADHD, with estimates varying according to samples and criteria (DuPaul et al., 2013). Knowing that two disorders can co-occur is only a first step; each combination then calls for an assessment procedure that keeps one condition from masking or inflating the other: With learning disabilities: Achievement is measured with standardized tools in every ADHD assessment, and the team checks whether inattention appears across all subjects or only in the area of weakness. If treatment for attention begins, academic skills are measured again afterward. With oppositional defiance: Ask about symptoms in situations that involve no demands and no authority, such as free play or watching a program; inattention that appears there cannot be explained by defiance. With anxiety and depression: Establish when each began, and ask the student directly using a measure of internalizing problems, because poor concentration is a shared symptom that will be counted twice unless care is taken. With autism spectrum disorder: Read the attention and impulsivity items on rating scales with caution, because some may be elevated for reasons related to autism itself, such as not responding to one’s name or absorption in a special interest; rely on observation across varied situations (see Chapter 9). search.t: In the Saudi context: Who diagnoses, and who decides eligibility? The Special Education Organizational Guide lists “attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorders” and “behavioral and emotional disorders” as two separate special education categories (Ministry of Education, 1436 AH [Arabic]). The earlier Disability Welfare Law had counted “behavioral and emotional disorders” among disabilities (Disability Welfare Law, 1421 AH [Arabic]); it was later replaced by the Law on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which defines a person with a disability as someone with a “long-term disorder or impairment” in functions that include “psychological” functions (Law on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, 1445 AH [Arabic]). Table 10.15 compares this regulatory framework with the two diagnostic manuals and with U.S. law. Table 10.15: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and behavioral and emotional disorders in the diagnostic manuals, US law and Saudi regulations. Element DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 US law (IDEA) Saudi regulations Category Separate diagnoses: attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorder, anxiety, depression and others No separate category for ADHD, which is usually served under “other health impairment”; the “emotional disturbance” category covers emotional and behavioral conditions Two separate categories: “attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorders” and “behavioral and emotional disorders” (Organizational Guide) Definition and criteria Detailed criteria specifying the number of symptoms, duration and age in DSM-5-TR; a description of features without a set number in ICD-11 Five characteristics, over a long period of time and to a marked degree, adversely affecting educational performance; includes schizophrenia and excludes social maladjustment alone For eligibility: “Hyperactivity, attention deficit or both, requiring intervention according to an accredited report.” We found no detailed criteria in the Guide for emotional disorders, nor any counterpart to the exclusion of social maladjustment Who decides A qualified clinician, according to each country’s licensing rules A team of qualified professionals together with the parents Assessment and diagnosis team: the school principal, the vice principal for student affairs, the special education teacher, the general education teacher, the school counselor, specialists relevant to the category, a physician where available, and the parent or guardian where possible. An “accredited report” is required, without naming who issues it Instruments A comprehensive clinical evaluation, supported by rating scales from multiple sources Multi-instrument evaluation; no single procedure may be relied upon “Tools and measures approved by the Ministry of Education,” “not relying solely on the results of a single scale,” administered and interpreted “by qualified specialists.” We found no published list of these instruments Consent and reevaluation Not applicable Parental consent, and reevaluation at least every three years Written consent from the guardian after notification, with no response within 14 days treated as consent; rediagnosis no earlier than 6 months and no later than 18 months after the initial diagnosis Who issues the diagnosis? We found no published text that specifies precisely who is authorized to diagnose attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or emotional disorders in Saudi Arabia. search.c: Chapter 10: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Behavioral and Emotional Disorders
search.t: The central argument we have sought to set out in this chapter is that judgment in these categories goes beyond the mere presence of a behavior: it turns on the number of symptoms, when they first appeared, the range of settings in which they show themselves and their effect on functioning, and on the absence of a more likely explanation. It follows that assessment begins with sensory checks and universal screening, rests on rating scales from multiple informants, compares the student with the peers closest in age, treats the student’s own report as essential for internalizing problems, and keeps computerized tests in a merely supplementary role. It also follows that the clinical diagnosis, made by a licensed health professional, must be kept distinct from the eligibility decision, made by the assessment team. Some of the chapter’s questions, however, remain contested or unsettled. The exclusion of social maladjustment alone from the emotional disturbance category in US law is a matter of debate; the ICD-11 does not require a set number of symptoms as the DSM does; and Saudi regulations treat emotional disturbance as a separate category without published detailed criteria, leaving it to the team to state the criteria on which it based its judgment.

search.c: Chapter 10: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Behavioral and Emotional Disorders
search.t: Chapter summary Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is diagnosed on the basis of at least six symptoms in one or both lists, several of which appeared before age 12; several symptoms are present in two settings, they interfere with functioning, and no other disorder better explains them. The diagnosis specifies the presentation and the severity, and the ICD-11 does not require a set number of symptoms. A learning disability is not among the exclusionary criteria, and autism has not been an exclusion since the fifth edition of the DSM. The youngest students in a class are more likely to be misdiagnosed, according to studies from more than one country, so the student should be compared with the peers closest in age. The quiet presentation and internalizing problems are often overlooked, particularly in girls and adolescents. Oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorder, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, anxiety, depression and posttraumatic stress disorder each have distinct criteria, and in children and adolescents they take particular forms, such as irritable rather than sad mood in depression. The emotional disturbance category in US law requires a long period of time, a marked degree and an educational impact; it includes schizophrenia and excludes social maladjustment alone, an exclusion that remains a matter of debate. Saudi regulations treat the category as separate, without published detailed criteria. Assessment begins with sensory checks and universal screening and rests on rating scales from multiple informants; the student’s own report is essential for internalizing problems. Computerized tests serve only as a supplement. Clinical diagnosis falls within the remit of a licensed health professional, and the eligibility decision within that of the assessment team. Glossary of terms Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) A neurodevelopmental disorder marked by a persistent pattern of inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, or both. Executive functions Capacities that direct behavior toward a goal, such as planning, working memory and self-control. Presentation The current picture of symptoms: predominantly inattentive presentation, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation, or combined presentation. In partial remission A specifier used when full criteria were previously met but have not been fully met over the past six months, while impairment in functioning persists. Relative age effect The greater likelihood that the youngest students in a class will be diagnosed because they are compared with older classmates. Externalizing problems Problems directed toward others, such as aggression, defiance and rule-breaking. Internalizing problems Problems directed inward, such as anxiety, sadness, withdrawal and somatic complaints. Oppositional defiant disorder A persistent pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentativeness, defiance and vindictiveness. Conduct disorder A repetitive and persistent pattern of violating the rights of others or major age-appropriate social norms or rules. Limited prosocial emotions A specifier for conduct disorder describing lack of remorse, lack of empathy, unconcern about performance and shallow affect. Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder Severe, recurrent temper outbursts with persistently irritable mood between them, beginning before age 10. Emotional disturbance An educational category in US law for students whose emotional or behavioral characteristics impede their learning over a long period of time and to a marked degree. Social maladjustment A term left undefined in US regulations; students so described are excluded from the emotional disturbance category unless they are also found to have an emotional disturbance. Universal behavior screening Periodically rating every student in a class with a brief instrument to find those who need support or evaluation, including students who have not been referred. search.s: Chapter 11: Sensory and multiple disabilities and communication disorders
search.t: 11 Chapter 11 Sensory and multiple disabilities and communication disorders In these categories, much of the diagnostic work falls to equipment and medical specialists, from the audiometer and the letter chart to the device that measures pressure in the middle ear. Yet the educational question remains the team’s to answer: what does this number mean for the student’s learning? And how do we assess the student in a way that reaches past the disability to the ability behind it? This chapter takes up these questions and dwells on the hardest of them, which arises when several disabilities converge in a single child, nearly every standardized instrument becomes unusable, and careful functional assessment is all that remains. Three messages to the counseling office The second-grade teacher: “Khalid daydreams a lot, and he only follows instructions if I repeat them. He often asks the boy next to him what I said. The odd thing is that in some lessons he is fully present, and in others it’s as if he’s in another world. Should we refer him for an ADHD evaluation?” The first-grade teacher: “Rahaf holds the book very close, tires quickly when reading, and confuses letters that look alike.” The kindergarten teacher: “Abdulrahman is six, and he says ‘galam’ (گلم) instead of ‘qalam’ (قلم, pen) and ‘tamaka’ (تمكة) instead of ‘samaka’ (سمكة, fish). Does he have an articulation disorder?” The three messages raise questions that this chapter sets out to answer. Could what looks like inattention be a hearing loss that face-to-face conversation with the child fails to reveal? How do we assess vision in a way that serves learning? And how do we tell a child’s dialect apart from a disorder in his speech? We then move on to harder questions that the messages did not raise: How do we assess the ability of a deaf student who communicates in sign language? And how can a judgment be reached about a child who cannot see, cannot speak and cannot hold a pencil? Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Read an audiogram, determining the degree and type of loss by comparing air conduction with bone conduction, and infer which speech sounds the child is missing. Classify results for distance visual acuity and visual field according to the international classification and the Saudi regulations, and specify what functional vision assessment and learning media assessment add to the medical report. Identify, for each communication disorder, its distinguishing feature, the specialist who assesses it and an appropriate assessment procedure. Apply the criteria for developmental language disorder to a child’s data, and distinguish it from dialectal difference and second-language learning. Select instruments for assessing the ability of a student who is deaf, blind or has a motor impairment, and determine in a given scenario whether an accommodation invalidates norm-based interpretation of the score. Plan a functional assessment for a child with multiple disabilities or deafblindness for whom standardized instruments are unsuitable. Judge whether the evidence in a new case is sufficient to warrant a judgment, and justify that judgment through the steps of the decision pathway, including ruling out sensory impairment before assigning any other category.

search.c: Chapter 11: Sensory and multiple disabilities and communication disorders
search.t: In sensory disabilities and communication disorders, equipment and medical specialists carry a large share of the diagnosis. Yet the importance of these categories extends well beyond their own borders, because weak hearing, vision or language can mimic any other category. A student who follows instructions only when they are repeated, as in one of the messages at the start of the chapter, may be referred for an attention evaluation when the root of the problem lies in his hearing. The educational question remains the team’s to answer: what does the medical number mean for the student’s learning? And how can the student be assessed in a way that reaches past the disability to the ability behind it, especially when disabilities converge and standardized instruments are, more often than not, unusable? We open the chapter by explaining why these categories matter for all the others (Section 11.1), then present hearing impairment (Section 11.2) and visual impairment (Section 11.3), from measurement to functional assessment. Next we address communication disorders and the assessment of need for augmentative and alternative communication (Section 11.4), developmental language disorder and how it presents in Arabic (Section 11.5), and the difference between difference and disorder (Section 11.6), followed by multiple disabilities, deafblindness, physical and health impairments, and brain injury (Section 11.7). We then turn to warning signs and decision pathways (Section 11.8), instrument profiles (Section 11.9), four cases (Section 11.10), and differential diagnosis and co-occurrence (Section 11.11), and we close with the Saudi and Arab context (Section 11.12).

search.c: Chapter 11: Sensory and multiple disabilities and communication disorders
search.s: 11.1 Why do these categories matter for every category?
search.t: Hearing and vision screening appears in the decision pathway of almost every category in special education. The reason is that a hearing or vision impairment can resemble any other category: it may look like inattention, as we will see in Khalid’s case in this chapter, or like a learning disability, or autism, or even intellectual disability if the student is assessed with instruments that do not suit his senses. Sensory disabilities are therefore the gateway of exclusion in every other diagnosis: ruling out hearing and vision impairment is a step that precedes any diagnostic instrument, and we do not judge a child’s ability until we are sure that he hears and sees what we present to him. This chapter brings together three groups of categories joined by a single feature: the disability lies in the very channels of reception and expression on which assessment instruments depend. Hearing and visual impairments affect what reaches the child; communication disorders affect what comes out of the child; and multiple and physical disabilities affect both, as well as the ability to point, grasp and write. In all of these cases, the first question in assessment becomes: does the instrument measure what it was designed to measure in this child, or does it measure the disability? Common misconceptions “The child passed newborn hearing screening, so his hearing is fine.” Hearing loss may emerge after birth, may be acquired, after meningitis for example, or may be a fluctuating conductive loss that comes and goes with ear infections. A screening result is a snapshot of a single day. “A hearing aid restores normal hearing.” A hearing aid amplifies sound but does not fully restore its clarity, and its benefit is weaker in noise and at a distance. “Glasses solve vision problems.” Glasses correct refractive errors; they do not repair retinal disease, cerebral visual impairment or a restricted visual field. “Sign language is simplified gesture.” Sign languages are complete natural languages with their own vocabulary and grammar, and they differ from one country to another. “A child who does not speak does not understand.” The absence of speech may be motor or sensory in origin, and many of these children understand far more than they are able to express.

search.c: Chapter 11: Sensory and multiple disabilities and communication disorders
search.t: The audiogram The audiologist measures the softest sound the child can hear at different frequencies, from low-pitched to high-pitched sounds, in each ear separately, and plots the results on a chart called an audiogram ( Audiogram ). The horizontal axis represents frequency in hertz, from low on the left to high on the right. The vertical axis represents sound intensity in decibels, with louder sounds toward the bottom. The lower the marks fall, the louder a sound the child needs in order to hear, and thus the more severe the hearing loss. Hearing is measured in two ways. In air conduction ( Air conduction ), sound is delivered through headphones and travels through the outer and middle ear to the inner ear. In bone conduction ( Bone conduction ), a small vibrator is placed behind the ear, and sound reaches the inner ear through the bones of the skull, bypassing the outer and middle ear. Comparing the two is what reveals where the problem lies: if air conduction is reduced while bone conduction is intact, the problem lies in the pathway of sound to the inner ear; if both are reduced, the problem lies in the inner ear or the nerve, as in the left ear in Figure 11.1. Speech banana 250 500 1000 2000 4000 8000 Frequency (Hz) 0 20 40 60 80 100 Intensity (dB) Normal Mild Average Severe and profound O Right: air X Left: air < ] Bone conduction Figure 11.1: A hypothetical audiogram for Khalid. The right-ear marks (circles) fall between 5 and 15 dB, indicating normal hearing. The left-ear marks (× symbols) slope from 45 dB at the low frequencies to 70 dB at the high frequencies, averaging about 60 dB across the main speech frequencies, which indicates a moderate-to-severe loss. The left-ear bone-conduction marks (], measured with the right ear masked by noise so that it could not respond in its place) lie close to the air-conduction marks, with no gap between them: a unilateral sensorineural loss. Most of the shaded area labeled “Speech banana” lies above the left-ear marks, so Khalid can barely hear speech in that ear and relies on his right ear alone. Had the bone-conduction marks been normal, with a gap between them and the air-conduction marks, the loss would have been conductive. The shaded area labeled “Speech banana” is the range in which the sounds of ordinary speech fall. Any speech sound that lies above the child’s marks, that is, softer than them, goes unheard. This explains why some children hear “that someone is talking” without understanding the words: they hear the loud, low-pitched sounds such as vowels, but miss many of the soft, high-pitched sounds such as /s/, /f/ and /θ/. Degrees and types of hearing loss Degree is usually determined by the average of the thresholds at the main speech frequencies in each ear. Score Approximate range (dB) What the child may miss without a hearing aid Slight 16–25 Some faint and distant speech; tires in noise Mild 26–40 Much of faint or distant speech, and high-pitched consonant sounds Average 41–55 Most speech at normal conversational level Moderately severe 56–70 Nearly all ordinary speech; needs a hearing aid and language intervention Severe 71–90 Does not hear speech, even loud speech, without amplification Profound 91 or more May perceive some loud sounds as vibration; relies on vision or on a cochlear implant Classifications differ across sources, and the differences are substantial. search.t: Visual acuity Visual acuity ( Visual acuity ) is the sharpness of vision. It is measured with a chart of letters or symbols of decreasing size and expressed as a fraction. A value of 6/6 means that the person sees at six meters what a person with normal vision sees at six meters. A value of 6/60 means that the person must come as close as six meters to see what a person with normal vision sees from sixty meters. In systems that use feet instead of meters, 6/6 is written as 20/20. With young children and those who do not know letters, charts with simple symbols are used, such as LEA symbols, a circle, a square, an apple and a house, or four-letter charts ( HOTV ) on which the child points to the matching letter on a card in front of him without having to name it. This is distance acuity . Near acuity ( Near acuity ) is measured at reading distance and is not always equal to distance acuity: some children see the board but tire when reading a book, and others the reverse. Nor does acuity reveal contrast sensitivity ( Contrast sensitivity ), the ability to distinguish an object from its background when their colors are similar, such as gray print on white paper or a stair step the same color as the floor. A student’s acuity may be acceptable on a black-on-white chart, yet he stumbles over a faded photocopied worksheet. E 6/60 F P 6/36 T O Z 6/24 L P E D 6/18 P E C F D 6/12 E D F C Z P 6/9 F E L O P Z D 6/6 Normal or near-normal 6/12 or better Mild impairment Worse than 6/12 to 6/18 Moderate impairment Worse than 6/18 to 6/60 Severe impairment Worse than 6/60 to 3/60 Blindness Worse than 3/60, or a visual field no greater than 10 degrees in radius around the point of fixation Figure 11.2: An illustration of a visual acuity chart, with the categories of distance vision impairment in the International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision (ICD-11) (World Health Organization, 2019). Acuity is measured in the better eye with correction. A person whose visual field in the better eye is restricted to 10 degrees or less is also classified as blind, whatever their acuity. This differs from the Saudi regulations, under which a student is considered educationally blind if acuity is below 6/60 or the visual field is narrower than 20 degrees (see 11.12). Visual field The visual field ( Visual field ) is the area a person can see without moving the eyes. Visual acuity may be good at the center of vision while the field is restricted, so the student sees what is directly in front of him clearly, as if looking through a tube, but misses what lies to either side. Such a student may read the small letters on the chart yet bump into classmates in the hallway and fail to see the whole board. Normal field Sees the whole scene, out to both sides Restricted field Sees only the center and misses what lies to either side Figure 11.3: One scene viewed with two visual fields. Acuity alone does not reveal a restricted field, which is why each is measured. Functional vision assessment, learning media assessment, and orientation and mobility The ophthalmologist or optometrist provides acuity, field and the medical diagnosis. The educational assessments are carried out by the teacher of students with visual impairments and other specialists: Functional vision assessment ( Functional vision assessment ): shows how the student actually uses vision in the classroom, the hallways and the playground: what print size the student reads comfortably, from what distance the board is visible, what lighting and contrast suit the student, and how long the student can sustain visual work before tiring. Learning media assessment ( Learning media assessment ): determines the most suitable medium for the student to learn reading and writing: regular print with magnification devices, large print, braille, a combination of media, or auditory media. search.t: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision ( DSM-5-TR ), classifies communication disorders into several types (American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2022). Under its implementing regulations, the U.S. Individuals with Disabilities Education Act ( IDEA ) adds voice disorders to the category of “speech or language impairment”; these do not appear in the diagnostic manual because they are not neurodevelopmental disorders (U.S. Department of Education, 2006, 34 CFR §300.8(c)(11)). All of these disorders are assessed by the speech-language pathologist: Table 11.3: Types of communication disorders and their distinguishing features. Disorder Distinctive features Example Language disorder Persistent difficulty in acquiring and using language, in vocabulary, sentence structure or connected discourse, in comprehension or expression (see 11.5) A six-year-old who speaks in two-word sentences and does not understand questions beginning with “why” Speech sound disorder Persistent difficulty producing speech sounds that is inappropriate for the child’s age and interferes with the intelligibility of speech A five-year-old who substitutes so many sounds that only his family can understand him Childhood-onset fluency disorder Repetitions or prolongations of sounds and syllables, or blocks before words, that interfere with communication; commonly known as stuttering “B-b-b-baba,” or a long silent block before a word Social (pragmatic) communication disorder ( Social [pragmatic] communication disorder ) Difficulty using language in social situations, without restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior, which is what distinguishes it from autism spectrum disorder Does not know when to start or end a conversation and does not grasp hints Voice disorders Deviation in voice quality, pitch, loudness or resonance from what suits the child’s age and sex, such as persistent hoarseness or the excessive nasality that accompanies cleft palate A student whose voice has been hoarse for months and gives out by the end of the school day In assessment, the speech-language pathologist uses standardized language tests such as the Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals, Fifth Edition ( CELF-5 ) (Wiig et al., 2013), presented in the third profile in 11.9. The pathologist also uses picture-based articulation tests in which the child names pictures covering the sounds of the language in their various positions in the word: initial, medial and final. A language sample ( Language sample analysis ) drawn from the child’s natural speech is analyzed, yielding measures such as mean length of utterance. For stuttering, the percentage of stuttered syllables in a speech sample is calculated, and a standardized instrument may be used to rate severity, such as the Stuttering Severity Instrument, Fourth Edition ( SSI-4 ) (Riley, 2009). For voice disorders, voice therapy begins only after an ear, nose and throat physician has examined the larynx, because persistent hoarseness may have an organic cause that requires medical treatment. Comparison with ICD-11 The International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision ( ICD-11 ), was adopted in 2019 and came into effect on 1 January 2022. It places speech and language disorders among the neurodevelopmental disorders under the heading “developmental speech or language disorders,” distinguishing developmental speech sound disorder , developmental speech fluency disorder and developmental language disorder ( Developmental language disorder ). The most important difference from the American manual is that pragmatic impairment in ICD-11 is a subtype of developmental language disorder, “with impairment of mainly pragmatic language,” alongside other subtypes, including one that affects both receptive and expressive language and one that affects mainly expressive language. The classification states explicitly that the language in question may be spoken or signed (World Health Organ

search.c: Chapter 11: Sensory and multiple disabilities and communication disorders
search.t: Children whose language was delayed for no apparent reason used to be described in many ways: “language delay,” “developmental aphasia” and “specific language impairment” ( Specific language impairment ). The last of these usually required the child’s language to be clearly below his nonverbal intelligence. An international panel of specialists then came together in a consensus study known as CATALISE and settled on a unified term: developmental language disorder ( Developmental language disorder, DLD ) (Bishop et al., 2017). The international classification (ICD-11) has adopted the same term. What has changed? Language disorder or developmental language disorder? “Language disorder” is used for any child with a language difficulty that is likely to persist beyond early childhood and that affects communication or learning. If the difficulty is associated with a known condition, such as sensorineural hearing loss, autism, intellectual disability or a genetic syndrome, the term is “language disorder associated with….” The term “developmental language disorder” is reserved for children whose difficulty is not associated with any of these conditions (Bishop et al., 2017). A discrepancy with nonverbal intelligence is not required. A child whose nonverbal intelligence is in the low average range, above the level of intellectual disability, can be diagnosed with developmental language disorder. A British population study found that about 7% of children at school entry have the disorder, and that children with low nonverbal intelligence did not differ from others in the severity or impact of their language difficulties (Norbury et al., 2016). Requiring a discrepancy had denied children services without justification. Co-occurrence does not rule out the diagnosis. The presence of ADHD, dyslexia or developmental coordination disorder does not preclude a diagnosis of developmental language disorder. How does it present in Arabic? Describing this disorder in Arabic requires more than translating what is known about it in English. Arabic is a derivational language rich in morphology, and difficulty in it surfaces in places specific to the language. Table 11.4 presents areas that the speech-language pathologist would do well to examine in the child’s language sample and in structured tasks, judging them against the standard of the child’s own dialect. Table 11.4: Areas to examine in a child’s Arabic when developmental language disorder is suspected. Area What is observed Example prepared by the author Morphological patterns Difficulty deriving words from their roots according to their patterns, and reliance on a single form that the child repeats Says “الرجل الذي يكتب” (“the man who writes”) and does not use “الكاتب” (“the writer”) at an age when his peers use it Plural forms Overgeneralizing the sound masculine or feminine plural to words that take a broken plural in his dialect, and continuing to do so after peers have moved past it “كتابات” instead of “كتب” (“books”), and “ولدين” (“two boys,” dual) for more than two Attached pronouns Omitting or confusing them, or using the noun in place of the pronoun “أعطى أحمد الكرة أحمد” (“Ahmad gave the ball to Ahmad”) instead of “أعطاه الكرة” (“he gave him the ball”) Agreement Failure of the verb or adjective to agree with its subject or the noun it modifies in gender and number “البنت راح” (“the girl went,” with a masculine verb), “الأولاد يلعب” (“the boys plays”) Connected discourse Short, disjointed stories, few connectives, and difficulty retelling a story heard in its correct sequence Retells a five-event story in two unconnected sentences Comprehension Difficulty understanding long sentences, passive constructions and complex questions, sometimes masked by reliance on context Carries out the first of two instructions and leaves the second The dilemma of diglossia The Arab child speaks a dialect at home and encounters Modern Standard Arabic at school and in books, and the examiner’s or the tes

search.t: Among the most important things a teacher should know is that a child who speaks in his own dialect does not have a disorder. Children learn to talk from their families and pronounce words as the people around them do. A child who says “گلم” (galam, “pen”) in a community where everyone pronounces the qaf as a g is speaking entirely correctly by the standard of his dialect. A disorder, by contrast, is measured as a departure from the pattern of the child’s own dialect. Among the patterns that warrant evaluation is the replacement of fricatives ( Fricatives ), sounds produced with a continuous stream of turbulent air, such as s, sh and z, with stops ( Stops ), sounds in which the airflow is blocked and then released in a single burst, such as t and d. This substitution is called stopping ( Stopping ). Dialectal difference: not a disorder قلم → گلم (qalam → galam, “pen”) Pronouncing the qaf as a g is a feature of many dialects across the Arabian Peninsula. The child learns Modern Standard Arabic at school, and his pronunciation is not treated. A pattern that warrants evaluation سمكة → تمكة (samaka → tamaka, “fish”) Replacing a fricative such as s with a stop such as t is a pattern that fades with development. Because the child’s dialect does not pronounce s as t, its persistence across an entire class of sounds, together with poor speech intelligibility, warrants evaluation. Figure 11.4: A child’s pronunciation is judged by the standard of his dialect and community. The same rule applies to a student learning Arabic as a second language. His errors in sentence structure may simply be a natural stage in learning a new language. To tell the two apart, we ask about his first language: does he speak it with fluency appropriate for his age? A genuine language disorder appears in both languages, whereas difficulty learning a second language appears in the new language alone. Here dynamic assessment , presented in Chapter 5, is useful: the child is taught a new language skill during the assessment session itself, and the examiner observes how quickly he learns it. A child who learns quickly once taught is most likely showing limited experience with the language, whereas one who learns very slowly despite instruction warrants a more in-depth evaluation.

search.s: 11.7 Multiple disabilities, deafblindness, physical and health impairments, and brain injury
search.t: In these categories, standardized instruments recede to the margins, because most of them assume a child who can see, hear, point, hold a pencil and sit still for a full hour. Functional assessment, repeated observation in natural settings and curriculum-based measurement become the primary sources of evidence. Table 11.5 presents the definitions of these categories in U.S. law and the focus of assessment in each. Saudi regulations specify corresponding categories, which are presented in Section 11.12. Table 11.5: Categories of multiple, physical and health impairments and brain injury in U.S. law, and the focus of assessment in each. Category Definition in U.S. law (abridged) Focus of assessment Deafblindness ( Deaf-blindness ) Concomitant hearing and visual impairments, the combination of which causes such severe communication and other developmental and educational needs that they cannot be accommodated in programs designed solely for deaf children or solely for blind children Communication: how the child receives and expresses information, and a joint functional assessment of his remaining hearing and vision Multiple disabilities Concomitant impairments, such as intellectual disability with blindness or with an orthopedic impairment, the combination of which causes such severe educational needs that they cannot be accommodated in a program designed for one of the impairments alone. Does not include deafblindness Functional skills in daily routines, communication, and the means of access to learning Orthopedic impairment A severe orthopedic impairment that adversely affects educational performance, including impairments caused by a congenital anomaly, by disease, or by other causes such as cerebral palsy and amputation Access: seating, writing and mobility, and adapting assessment instruments so that motor impairment is not measured in place of the intended ability Other health impairment Limited strength, vitality or alertness due to chronic or acute health problems, such as asthma, diabetes, epilepsy, heart conditions, sickle cell anemia, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, that adversely affects educational performance The effect of the condition and its treatment on attention, energy and attendance, and distinguishing between instruction the student has missed and what he is unable to do Traumatic brain injury An acquired injury to the brain caused by an external physical force, resulting in functional or psychosocial impairment that adversely affects educational performance. Does not include congenital or degenerative injuries or those induced by birth trauma Comparison with the student’s level before the injury, and tracking rapid change in the first months Source: IDEA (2004) and its implementing regulations (U.S. Department of Education, 2006, 34 CFR §300.8(c)). Assessing the child with deafblindness A child with deafblindness is seldom both totally deaf and totally blind; most of these children have residual hearing, residual vision, or both. Assessment therefore begins with a joint functional assessment of hearing and vision : what the child sees, at what distance and in what lighting; what he hears and under what conditions; and how he uses the two senses together. This assessment is carried out over several days in familiar settings, because the child’s responses are affected by fatigue, medication and location. Next comes the communication assessment , the centerpiece of the entire evaluation. Many of these children are at the pre-symbolic communication stage: they communicate through body movements, changes in facial expression, crying, and taking an adult’s hand and guiding it, before words, signs or pictures have developed. The assessment asks: does the child act intentionally to influence others? Does he use real objects as symbols, such as holding a spoon to ask for food? Does he understand tactile communication ( Tactile communication ), such as signs made with his hand resting on the signer’s h

search.t: Warning signs Teachers and families are the first to notice. Table 11.7 brings together signs that call for referral to a specialist; their value lies in raising the alert. Any one of them warrants a hearing or vision examination, regardless of the result of earlier screening. Table 11.7: Warning signs in hearing, vision and communication. Area Signs at home or in class Refer to Hearing Often asks for things to be repeated; watches classmates to know what to do; understands better when he can see the speaker’s face; turns up the television; mispronounces and misspells high-pitched sounds; has recurrent ear infections; or performs inconsistently from one week to the next An audiologist, and an ear, nose and throat specialist when an infection is suspected Vision Holds the book close to his face; tilts his head; closes one eye; rubs his eyes; bumps into objects or stumbles on stairs; tires quickly when reading; copies from the board with many errors; or one eye appears to turn An ophthalmologist, then a teacher of students with visual impairments for a functional assessment Language Does not combine two words into a phrase by age two; at school age speaks in shorter, simpler sentences than his peers; does not understand complex instructions; or cannot recount what happened to him in order A speech-language pathologist, after a hearing examination Speech, fluency and voice Speech is unintelligible to people outside the family after age four; stutters with facial tension or avoids speaking; or hoarseness persists for weeks A speech-language pathologist, and an ear, nose and throat specialist for hoarseness At any age Loss of words or skills the child had already acquired Urgent referral to a physician For the teacher: three observations in class Change the channel and note the difference: Give the student a spoken instruction while you stand behind him, then a similar instruction while he can see your face, then a written instruction. If he carries out the instruction clearly better when he sees your face or reads it, hearing should be checked before attention. Record when and where: If you find yourself saying “sometimes he hears and sometimes he doesn’t,” write down the days, where the speaker was in relation to the student, and the noise level. Fluctuation linked to colds, and a difference between one side of the student and the other, are two patterns an audiologist knows well. Enlarge the print once: Make an enlarged copy of a page from the student’s textbook, and compare his errors and fatigue on the two pages. If his errors on similar-looking letters disappear, the root of the problem lies in vision, and his reading itself is most likely sound. The value of these observations is that they turn a general complaint into information the specialist can use; the diagnosis itself remains the specialist’s responsibility. Decision pathways Figures 11.5, 11.6 and 11.7 present the decision pathway for each of the three main categories. A single principle runs through them: medical or audiological measurement identifies the impairment, educational assessment determines its impact, and the educational category is assigned only when an impact on learning has been established. In the pathway for communication disorders, a hearing examination comes at the second step as a prerequisite for any language instrument. 1 Screening or observation Newborn or school screening, or one of the signs in Table 11.7. Did not pass, or a sign appeared 2 Diagnostic audiological evaluation Pure-tone audiometry by air and bone conduction, tympanometry and speech discrimination, or brainstem measures for children who cannot respond. Determines the degree, type and ear. 3 Medical referral In conductive loss, the cause is treated first and hearing is retested after treatment. In sensorineural loss, hearing aids or a cochlear implant are determined. Loss persists after treatment 4 Educational assessment Functional hearing in the classroom, language in the child’

search.t: The three profiles present core procedures in these categories: audiometry, functional vision assessment together with learning media assessment, and a comprehensive language test. The first two are professional procedures without published norms, so some fields in their tables differ from those in the test profiles. Where we were unable to verify a figure in the technical manual itself, we have written “in the technical manual.” This book does not publish the items of any test; the examples were prepared by the author. PTA · OAE · ABR Audiometry: pure tones, tympanometry and objective measures Hearing impairment The idea Pure-tone audiometry ( Pure-tone audiometry, PTA ) determines the softest sound the child can hear at each frequency, by air and bone conduction, and thus yields the degree and type of loss. Tympanometry shows whether the eardrum moves normally, and so indicates fluid behind it. Otoacoustic emissions and the auditory brainstem response, for their part, are objective measures that require no response from the child; they are used with newborns and with children who cannot respond. What it looks like A sound-treated booth, an audiometer, headphones, and a bone-conduction vibrator. The response method changes with age: an older infant is rewarded with a lighted toy when he turns toward the sound, a preschooler drops a block into a basket each time he hears a sound, and an older child raises his hand or presses a button. In tympanometry, a small probe is placed at the entrance of the ear canal for a few seconds. A scene from administration The audiologist tells a six-year-old: “Every time you hear the beep, even if it’s very soft, put the bead in the box.” She begins with a clearly audible tone at 1000 Hz, then lowers it by 10 dB each time he responds and raises it by 5 dB each time he does not, until she reaches the softest sound he responds to on most trials. She notices that the child has begun dropping the bead whenever she looks at him, responding to her glance rather than to the sound, so she varies the timing of the presentations to keep him from guessing. Table 11.8: Profile of pure-tone audiometry, tympanometry and objective measures. Purpose To determine the presence, degree, type and ear of hearing loss, and to monitor it Ages Objective measures from birth; behavioral testing with age-appropriate methods from about 6 months, and by the conventional method from about age 5 Edition and year A standard clinical procedure governed by professional guidelines (ASHA, 1997) Publisher Not applicable Qualification level A licensed audiologist; school screening is conducted by trained personnel under professional supervision Time About half an hour to an hour for a full evaluation; longer with young children Score types Thresholds in decibels for each frequency and ear, the pure-tone average, the word recognition percentage, and the tympanogram type (normal; flat, usually indicating fluid; or shifted toward negative pressure) Cutoff scores 20 dB for screening; degrees of loss according to the adopted classification (Tables 11.1 and 11.2); educational eligibility limits according to the regulations (see 11.12) Reliability Thresholds typically vary within 5 dB between two successive tests; reliability is lower with young children and when the child cooperates poorly Classification accuracy High for determining degree and type in a cooperative child; a single test does not detect fluctuating loss Year of norm collection Not applicable; the child is compared with reference thresholds for normal hearing Arabic version Pure-tone testing requires no language. Speech discrimination testing, however, requires equivalent Arabic word lists; at the time of writing we had not verified any recent, published, standardized Saudi lists, so the lists used and their source should be ascertained How are the results interpreted? search.s: 11.10 When is a judgment made? Four cases
search.t: Case 1: Khalid, age 7 Hearing loss in one ear: no judgment about attention for now The story: Khalid is the student in the first letter. His second-grade teacher noticed that he drifted off during lessons, followed spoken instructions only after they were repeated, and watched his classmates to copy them, and that he was “present” in some lessons and “absent” in others. The teacher suspected an attention problem. When the specialist requested teacher ratings, she noticed that the complaints were strongest from the Arabic teacher, who explains while standing by the window to Khalid’s left, and weakest from the mathematics teacher, who stands at the board to his right, writes a great deal and explains with visual examples. In a quiet one-to-one session, with the specialist seated facing him, his attention was good and his questions were to the point. His mother reported that he turns his head when spoken to, always holds the phone to his right ear, and cannot tell where someone is calling him from in the market. Khalid had passed newborn hearing screening and had never been screened at school. The team therefore postponed the attention assessment and requested hearing screening first. Table 11.12: Evidence in Khalid’s case. Source Result School screening Passed in the right ear; heard none of the tones in the left ear, including on retest Audiological evaluation As in Figure 11.1: the right ear is normal, and the left shows a moderate-to-severe sensorineural loss. Tympanograms are normal in both ears, so there is no fluid. Speech discrimination in noise is clearly weaker when speech comes from his left side Ear, nose and throat physician No medically treatable cause. The loss most likely developed after birth, since he passed newborn screening. Annual testing is requested, because some unilateral losses change over time Classroom observation He sits near the window, with the air conditioner on his right and the Arabic teacher on his left. He often turns to the classmate beside him after spoken instructions Attention ratings High from the Arabic teacher, low from the mathematics teacher, and few concerns at home Speech-language pathologist (brief screening) His vocabulary and sentence structure are age-appropriate. His spelling errors cluster in soft, high-pitched sounds such as s, f and th Decision: No judgment of ADHD is made for now. Nor does Khalid meet the “hard of hearing” criterion in the Saudi regulations, because that criterion is measured in the better ear , and his right ear is normal. Still, the loss is permanent and its effect in the classroom is evident. It is worth noting here that the US legal definition of hearing impairment requires only an effect on learning, without stipulating a degree or both ears (U.S. Department of Education, 2006, 34 CFR §300.8(c)(5)). The team recommends, immediately and without waiting for any decision, that he sit at the front of the classroom with his right ear toward the teacher and away from sources of noise, that he be able to see the speaker’s face, that important instructions be written down, and that his understanding be checked by asking him what he has been asked to do rather than “Do you understand?” The audiologist will weigh the benefit of a wireless hearing system ( Remote microphone system ) that carries the teacher’s voice to his good ear. His attention will then be reconsidered after several months of these accommodations: if symptoms of inattention persist in two settings under adequate listening conditions, the team will proceed with an evaluation (see Chapter 10). The lesson of the case: What looked like inattention had an auditory explanation. Khalid does not follow instructions because he does not hear them in full when they come from his left or through noise, and he copies his classmates to find out what is expected. The clue that alerted the team was the way his performance varied with where the speaker stood and how material was presented. A child who “hears we

search.t: Similar conditions Sensory disabilities and communication disorders resemble many categories, and many categories resemble them. Table 11.16 brings together the conditions that recur most often in referrals, and the evidence that distinguishes them. Table 11.16: Differential diagnosis in sensory disabilities and communication disorders. What it looks like What it may be Distinguishing evidence Inattention Hearing loss, including fluctuating and unilateral loss Performance improves when the student can see the speaker’s face or the instruction is written, and fluctuates with bouts of ear infection. Hearing is tested before any attention measure Difficulty in reading or spelling Low vision or hearing loss Visual errors disappear when print is enlarged; auditory errors concentrate on the sounds the child cannot hear Autism spectrum disorder Hearing loss, deafblindness or developmental language disorder Intact nonverbal communication and a desire to interact, with improvement once the sensory barrier is removed. Restricted and repetitive patterns are absent in developmental language disorder Intellectual disability Sensory or motor disability, language deprivation, developmental language disorder or brain injury Performance on a tool suited to the functioning channel, adaptive behavior, nonverbal ability and pre-injury performance Central auditory processing disorder Inattention, developmental language disorder or undetected hearing loss Full audiological evaluation, followed by assessment of language and attention, before this explanation is accepted (see 11.2) Language disorder Dialectal difference or second-language learning Judgment against the standard of the child’s dialect, assessment of the child’s other language, and dynamic assessment Communication disorder (does not speak at school) Selective mutism Speaks fluently at home, as family recordings confirm. The diagnostic manual classifies it among the anxiety disorders Low vision originating in the eye Cerebral visual impairment The eye examination is normal or does not explain the impairment, with distinctive patterns on functional assessment Co-occurring condition Many causes of deafness and blindness, such as extremely preterm birth, certain infections before and after birth, and genetic syndromes, also affect the brain, so other disabilities occur alongside the sensory disability in the same child. Surveys report that a considerable proportion of deaf and hard-of-hearing children have an additional disability, and that visual impairment is common among children with cerebral palsy and multiple disabilities, although estimates vary with samples and definitions. Developmental language disorder, for its part, frequently co-occurs with dyslexia, ADHD and developmental coordination disorder. Each combination carries its own guidance for assessment: Sensory disability with suspected intellectual disability: A judgment of intellectual disability requires both a tool suited to the functioning channel and adaptive behavior that supports it; where this is not possible, the judgment is deferred, as in Salman’s case. Hearing impairment with a suspected learning disability: Evidence is sought from outside the second language, such as difficulty in sign language itself, or in arithmetic despite full access to instruction, as in Mashael’s case. Sensory disability with suspected autism: The sensory loss is addressed first, with a hearing aid, glasses or accommodations, and the social symptoms are then reconsidered. Any autism measure used with a deaf or blind child is interpreted with great caution, because its items assume intact hearing and vision. Developmental language disorder with reading difficulty: Listening comprehension and decoding are each measured separately; if both are weak, the two problems co-occur. search.s: 11.12 In the Saudi and Arab context
search.t: In the Saudi context: How are this chapter’s categories defined? The Special Education Organizational Guide adopts eleven categories, six of which concern this chapter: hearing impairment, visual impairment, language and speech disorders, multiple impairments, physical and health impairments, and deafblindness (Ministry of Education, 1436 AH [Arabic]). The Regulations for Special Education Institutes and Programs set the levels of hearing and vision on which admission is based (Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif], 1422 AH [Arabic]). Table 11.17 compares these regulations with the two diagnostic classifications and with US law. Table 11.17: This chapter’s categories in the diagnostic classifications, US law and the Saudi regulations. Category DSM-5-TR, ICD-11 and the World Health Organization US law (IDEA) Saudi regulations Hearing impairment Not a disorder in the diagnostic manual. The World Health Organization grades severity by the four-frequency average in the better ear, with loss beginning at 20 decibels Two categories: deafness, when the child cannot process linguistic information through hearing even with amplification; and hearing impairment, whether permanent or fluctuating. No numbers are given, and an effect on educational performance is required Deaf: a loss of 70 decibels or more; hard of hearing: 35 to 69 decibels; in the better ear after the use of hearing aids, as reported by an accredited specialist body. Admission to their programs requires an IQ of no less than 75 on the Wechsler scale or 73 on the Stanford-Binet (the Regulations, Article 4) Visual impairment Categories of acuity in the better eye; blindness is worse than 3/60, or a field no more than 10 degrees in radius An impairment in vision that, even with correction, affects educational performance, including partial sight and blindness. No numbers are given Blind: acuity below 6/60 in the better eye after correction, or a visual field of less than 20 degrees; low vision: 6/24 to 6/60 (the Regulations; the Organizational Guide) Communication disorders Four disorders in DSM-5-TR; in ICD-11, developmental language disorder, with pragmatic impairment as one of its subtypes Speech or language impairment: stuttering, impaired articulation, a language impairment or a voice impairment A category of “language and speech disorders.” In the sources we were able to verify, we found no published eligibility criteria for it Multiple, physical and health impairments, and brain injury No umbrella category; each condition is diagnosed on its own, and ICD-11 allows a “provisional” category of intellectual disability when assessment is not feasible Five separate categories: deaf-blindness, multiple disabilities, orthopedic impairment, other health impairment and traumatic brain injury Three categories: multiple impairments, deafblindness, and physical and health impairments. There is no separate category for brain injury. We have not verified the text of their definitions and detailed criteria Who decides The audiologist and ophthalmologist for measurement, and the speech-language pathologist for communication A team of qualified professionals together with the parents The school assessment team, after the guardian’s written consent, together with a report from the specialist body for hearing and vision (the Organizational Guide) Reevaluation Depending on the condition At least every three years, unless the parents and the agency agree otherwise The diagnosis is repeated no sooner than 6 months and no later than 18 months after the initial diagnosis, and thereafter as needed (the Organizational Guide) Two points emerge from the table. First, the Saudi regulations classify a student as educationally blind within wider limits than the international classification: a student with an acuity of 4/60 has “severe low vision” under the international classification but is “blind” under the regulations. This makes educational sense, since students in this range usually need the me

search.c: Chapter 11: Sensory and multiple disabilities and communication disorders
search.t: The central argument we have sought to develop in this chapter is that the number produced by a device or a medical examination is where educational judgment begins, not where it ends. The audiogram and vision measurements establish the degree and type of loss, but what this means for the student’s learning calls for functional assessment and learning media assessment, and a deaf student’s language development is measured in the student’s stronger language. It follows that hearing and vision screening should precede any diagnostic tool; that the team should watch for forms that are easily missed, such as fluctuating and unilateral loss and auditory neuropathy; that neither dialect nor second-language learning should be treated as a disorder; and that the report should name the classification it has adopted for degrees of hearing and vision. The hardest judgments we have discussed remain those in multiple disabilities and deafblindness, where standardized tools usually fall away. Judgment then rests on repeated functional and communicative assessment in natural settings, and no degree of intellectual disability is assigned when it cannot be validly measured. The line between an accommodation that preserves the norms and one that invalidates them remains a matter of judgment in each case: what changes the mode of access usually preserves them, and what changes the construct invalidates them, in which case the result is reported descriptively.

search.c: Chapter 11: Sensory and multiple disabilities and communication disorders
search.t: Chapter summary Hearing and vision screening is the gateway of exclusion in every diagnosis and precedes any diagnostic tool, because impairment in either can resemble any other category. The audiogram shows the softest sound a child hears at each frequency, and comparing air and bone conduction determines the type of loss. Fluctuating and unilateral loss and auditory neuropathy are forms the team can easily miss. Classifications of degrees of hearing and vision differ across sources, and between the international classification and the Saudi regulations, so the report names the classification it has adopted. Vision is measured through distance and near acuity, visual field and contrast sensitivity, complemented by functional vision assessment, learning media assessment, orientation and mobility, and the areas of the expanded core curriculum. Communication disorders are of five types, including voice disorders, and are assessed by the speech-language pathologist after hearing has been tested. Developmental language disorder does not require a discrepancy with nonverbal intelligence. Dialect is not a disorder, second-language learning is not a language disorder, and a deaf student’s language development is measured in the student’s stronger language. In multiple disabilities and deafblindness, standardized tools usually fall away, so judgment rests on repeated functional and communicative assessment in natural settings, and no degree of intellectual disability is assigned when it cannot be validly measured. An accommodation that changes the mode of access usually preserves the norms; one that changes the construct invalidates them, and the result is then reported descriptively. Glossary of terms Audiogram A chart showing the softest sound a person hears at different frequencies in each ear. Decibel The unit for measuring sound intensity; the higher the value, the louder the sound. Bone conduction Transmission of sound to the inner ear through the bones of the skull, bypassing the outer and middle ear. Conductive hearing loss Loss arising in the outer or middle ear, shown by a gap between air and bone conduction; it may be temporary or fluctuating. Sensorineural hearing loss Loss arising in the inner ear or the auditory nerve, usually permanent. Auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder A disorder in which the inner ear functions but the signal is not transmitted to the brain in an orderly way, so speech understanding is poorer than the audiogram would predict. Tympanometry A measurement of eardrum movement; a flat tracing usually indicates fluid behind the eardrum. Saudi Sign Language A complete natural language used by deaf people in the Kingdom, with its own vocabulary and grammar. Language deprivation A child’s reaching an advanced age without a fluent language, spoken or signed, because full access to a language was never provided. Visual acuity Clarity of sight, expressed as a fraction such as 6/6 and measured at distance and near. Contrast sensitivity The ability to distinguish an object from its background when their colors are close. Visual field The area a person can see without moving the eyes. Functional vision assessment An assessment of how a student actually uses vision in learning situations and daily life. Learning media assessment An assessment that determines the most suitable medium for a student with low vision or blindness to learn reading and writing. Expanded core curriculum Skills that a student with visual impairment needs to be taught explicitly, in nine areas, including braille, orientation and mobility, and independent living. Cerebral visual impairment Impairment in the brain’s processing of what the eye sees, with the eye itself intact or nearly so. Developmental language disorder A persistent language difficulty with functional impact, not associated with a known condition such as hearing loss, autism or intellectual disability, and not requiring a discrepancy with nonverbal intelligence.
