12 Chapter 12 Giftedness Where the inquiry into disability categories turns to what impedes learning, the inquiry into giftedness turns to what lies beyond what the classroom offers. And because giftedness does not force itself on our attention as disability does, the greatest danger in identifying it is overlooking a gifted student whom no one noticed, a more serious error than misidentifying one. Scene from the teachers’ room The fourth-grade teachers were asked to nominate students for the gifted program. Each teacher nominated her highest-scoring students: the organized ones who raise their hands and hand in their homework on time. None of them nominated Jana, because she “daydreams a lot, and her spelling grades are average,” even though her teacher the previous year had thought she might be gifted. But the science teacher remembered that two months earlier, in an open-ended project, Jana had designed an experiment to test which types of soil hold water the longest, and had recorded her results in a table that nobody had asked her for. Is Jana gifted? Are the nominated students gifted? Perhaps, and perhaps not: high grades and good conduct are not giftedness, and daydreaming and average grades do not rule it out. In this chapter, we set out how to answer that question with evidence rather than impressions. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Compare four models of giftedness (Renzulli, Gagné, Subotnik and colleagues, and Pfeiffer) in terms of what each looks for, its tools, its threshold, and whom it may miss. Determine, in a given identification program, which features are consistent with the principles of fair identification and which violate them, and propose a modification for each violation. Design opportunities to display giftedness that precede nomination, and determine, in a given situation, how their absence affects teacher nomination. Interpret the results of ability and creative thinking measures for a gifted student, including the difference between the General Ability Index and the Cognitive Proficiency Index, the ceiling effect, and the results of above-level testing. Apply the admission criteria in Saudi regulations and the result of the Mawhiba measure to a given student, and critique them in light of the principles of identification. Judge whether the evidence in a new case suffices for a determination of giftedness and the choice of service, justify that judgment, and distinguish the gifted student from the high achiever and from the student with a disorder.

Identifying gifted learners differs from diagnosing disability both in the direction of the question and in the nature of the costliest error. The inquiry into disability categories is directed at what impedes learning; the inquiry into giftedness is directed at what exceeds what the classroom provides. Because giftedness does not catch a teacher’s attention the way disability does, the greater risk is that a gifted student will be missed, whether because he or she was never given an opportunity to show ability or because the student did not fit the picture of the organized, high-scoring pupil, as happened to Jana in the opening scene. Who is found and who is missed depends on the definition of giftedness adopted, on the instruments and their ceilings, and on the admission rules. We open the chapter by defining giftedness and its models (Section 12.1), then present the principles of identification and the construction of local norms (Section 12.2), followed by nomination, the opportunity to display, and nomination and observation tools (Section 12.3). We then take up ability measures and their limits, the ceiling effect, and above-level testing (Section 12.4), followed by creativity, achievement, and performance (Section 12.5), instrument profiles (Section 12.6), and identification in the Saudi context and the decision pathway (Section 12.7). We apply all of this to three cases (Section 12.8) and close with what resembles giftedness and what conceals it (Section 12.9). Identification, not diagnosis: what sets the concept apart in giftedness In the field of gifted education, the term identification ( Identification ) denotes a comprehensive educational process whose purpose is to determine which students need enrichment or acceleration services beyond what the regular classroom offers. Giftedness is not a disorder whose symptoms are sought out; it is high potential or performance for which we seek the service that will develop it. The process therefore starts from the program’s definition of giftedness and from the services it provides: the instrument is chosen according to the type of service, multiple criteria are used instead of a single score, and the student is compared with local norms that take into account the opportunities he or she has had (NAGC, 2019b; Pfeiffer, 2015). Its outcome is a decision to place the student in a program, open to review, unlike a permanent classification that follows the student, because giftedness develops and emerges at different times (Lohman & Korb, 2006). Its most common error is omission : missing the student who was never nominated in the first place, which happens more often than placing a student who does not need the program (Card & Giuliano, 2016). With disabilities, by contrast, identification is bound up with determining eligibility for special education services: the questions are whether the student has a disability in one of the specified categories and whether it affects his or her learning to a degree that calls for those services. In many categories, such as autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, this runs alongside a clinical diagnosis made against the criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (American Psychiatric Association, 2022) or the International Classification of Diseases ( ICD ), issued by a qualified professional and sometimes the basis for treatment outside school. The question in disability is “What impedes this student’s learning, and does he or she qualify for services?”; in giftedness it is “What does this student need that the classroom does not provide?” For this reason, we prefer the term “identification” for giftedness and use “diagnosis” when we are speaking of a disorder, as when distinguishing giftedness from conditions that resemble it in Section 12.9.

Definitions of giftedness abound, and no single agreed definition unites them. This multiplicity has practical consequences, because the definition a program adopts determines whom it looks for and with which tools. A program that defines giftedness as a high IQ will administer an intelligence test; one that defines it as creativity will look for creative products; and one that defines it as excellence in a particular domain will measure that domain. The most prominent conceptions follow. Giftedness as high general intellectual ability The scientific study of the gifted began with Lewis Terman, who launched his longitudinal study of gifted children in the 1920s and defined the gifted child by a very high score on an intelligence test: an IQ of roughly 135–140 or above on the Stanford–Binet for most of his sample, that is, approximately the top 1% (Terman, 1925). General intellectual ability remains part of most definitions, but relying on it alone has been criticized for overlooking giftedness in specific domains, creativity, and motivation. Renzulli’s Three-Ring Conception In his Three-Ring Conception, Joseph Renzulli proposed that gifted behavior emerges when three traits come together: above-average (though not necessarily exceptional) ability, task commitment, and creativity (Renzulli, 1978). What matters in this model is that it speaks of gifted behavior that appears in certain situations, rather than a fixed trait that a student either has or lacks. Environment and learning opportunities Above-average Mean Task commitment Creativity Behavior Gifted Figure 12.1: The Three-Ring Conception. Gifted behavior emerges where ability, commitment, and creativity intersect, surrounded by an environment that either provides or withholds opportunities for it to appear. Renzulli distinguishes between two kinds of giftedness. The first is schoolhouse giftedness ( Schoolhouse giftedness ), proficiency in learning lessons and taking tests, which ability and achievement tests detect well. The second is creative-productive giftedness ( Creative-productive giftedness ), the capacity to produce original ideas and products for a real audience, which tests alone do not reveal (Renzulli, 1986). This distinction bears directly on identification. In the Schoolwide Enrichment Model associated with the theory, a talent pool ( Talent pool ) of roughly 15–20% of students is formed, instead of selecting a small number by a cutoff score, by combining ability and achievement scores with teacher ratings. Students who display gifted behavior during enrichment activities may then move to a higher level of service, even if they were not in the pool to begin with (Renzulli & Reis, 2014). This is what the phrase “above-average, though not necessarily exceptional, ability” means. Gagné’s model: from gifts to talents In his Differentiated Model of Giftedness and Talent ( Differentiated Model of Giftedness and Talent, DMGT ), François Gagné distinguishes between two words often used as though they meant the same thing: gifts ( Gifts ), high natural abilities not yet refined, and talents ( Talents ), mastered skills in a particular field that have developed from those gifts through learning and practice. Gagné later revised his model in a second version (DMGT 2.0), changing three things that bear directly on identification (Gagné, 2009, 2013). First , gifts now span six domains: intellectual, creative, social, perceptual, muscular, and motor control. Intellectual ability is thus one domain among six, and a student may be gifted in a domain that an intelligence test does not measure at all. Second , the developmental process became a separate component with three dimensions: the activities the student gains access to, along with their content and format; the investment he or she makes in time, effort, and money; and progress, with its stages, pace, and turning points. The process is surrounded by intrapersonal catalysts, such as physical and mental traits and goal

Most of the literature and professional standards agree on a set of principles for fair identification, among them those set out in the Pre-K–Grade 12 Gifted Programming Standards issued by the same association (NAGC, 2019b): Table 12.3: Principles of fair identification of gifted learners and what they mean in practice. Principle What it means in practice Aligning identification with services Instruments are chosen according to what the program will provide. A mathematics acceleration program, for example, needs a measure of mathematical ability specifically. Multiple sources The decision rests on evidence from ability, achievement, observation, and performance taken together, rather than on a single score. Universal screening All students at a given grade level are assessed, rather than waiting for nominations, because nomination misses many. A study in a large U.S. school district found that moving from nomination to universal screening markedly increased the representation of students from low-income and minority families in gifted programs (Card & Giuliano, 2016). Fair instruments Instruments that do not disadvantage a student because of language, background, or disability, including nonverbal tests within their limits (see Section 12.4) and local norms ( Local norms ), that is, comparing the student with peers in the same school or district rather than with the national norming sample alone. Ongoing identification Doors remain open across grade levels, because giftedness develops and emerges at different times. A longitudinal study that followed elementary students found that a large proportion of those who exceeded a high cutoff in one year no longer did so two or three years later, while others crossed it later on (Lohman & Korb, 2006). A label assigned once and never reviewed errs in both directions. How are local norms constructed? The idea behind local norms is simple: we ask where the student stands among those who have had similar opportunities to learn, rather than among a national sample that includes far wealthier schools. Peters and colleagues found that computing norms at the school level increases the representation of underrepresented groups in gifted programs (Peters et al., 2019). Applying them, however, requires decisions made in advance and announced openly, which the following box summarizes. Six questions before using local norms Who is the reference group? Students in the same grade who share the same opportunities to learn: the school, or a group of similarly situated schools within the education directorate, such as its rural schools. Schools with very different opportunities should not be pooled into one group, as this reintroduces the very problem local norms were meant to solve. What is the minimum size? There is no agreed figure, but the upper ranks require large numbers. In a class of 20 students, the “top 5%” is a single student. A percentile rank is the percentage of the student’s peers in the reference group or norming sample who scored lower than the student; a percentile rank of 84 means the student outperformed 84% of them. In a class of this size, a percentile rank of 95 does not distinguish the first student from the second, and a change in one or two answers is enough to change the judgment. If the group numbers only in the tens, it is better to enlarge it or to combine years. School or directorate? School norms come closer to the question “Who needs more than his or her class provides?”, while directorate norms are more statistically stable. A common compromise is to compute norms for a group of similarly situated schools, or for the school with several years combined. Should data be pooled across years? Yes, when classes are small, provided that the instrument and administration conditions remain constant and that the report says so. What are their limits? The label does not transfer between schools: a student identified in one school might not be identified in another. The absolute

search.s: 12.3 Nomination and the opportunity to display
search.t: Teacher nomination remains the most widespread route into identification. It has its uses, since the teacher sees the student over a long period and in many situations. But it has well-known limits: teachers tend to nominate high-scoring, well-behaved students who fit the image of the “good student,” and to overlook those who are quiet, those who differ linguistically or culturally, and those whose ability is masked by a difficulty. Nomination may even be influenced by the teacher as well as by the student: a large U.S. study found that the likelihood of a student being identified as gifted varied with the background of the student’s teacher, even when students’ test scores were equal (Grissom & Redding, 2016). In Saudi Arabia, Alfaiz examined the accuracy of parent and teacher nomination in identifying gifted students (Alfaiz, 2026), a question on which local practitioners will need to follow the evidence. The opportunity to display In his research on the visibility of gifted students for nomination, the author of this book proposes a framework he calls the opportunity to display ( Opportunity to display ), which locates a reason for the shortcomings of nomination deeper than teacher bias: a teacher cannot see what the classroom gives the student no opportunity to show . A classroom built on memorization and short answers does not reveal a student’s ability to solve an open-ended problem, pose an original question, or build a project. Many nomination checklists ask about behaviors, such as curiosity, unusual questions, and original thinking, that appear only in activities that allow for them. When such activities are absent, what might be called the teacher’s inference load increases: the teacher is forced to infer giftedness from indirect signs such as grades and good conduct, and so falls back on nominating high achievers. The framework is close to well-established ideas in the literature; what it adds is to make opportunity a first step in the identification pathway, where it had been a circumstance mentioned when interpreting results. An instrument such as the Teacher’s Observation of Potential in Students links observation to providing rich learning activities over several weeks (Coleman et al., 2010). Local norms compare the student with those who have had similar opportunities (Peters et al., 2019). And Pfeiffer’s “potential to excel” lens concerns students who have not yet had the opportunities (Pfeiffer, 2015). What is new here is the question that comes before all of them: did the classroom offer anything to observe in the first place? What this means in practice Before we ask teachers to nominate, we need to give students opportunities to show what they can do: open-ended activities, problems without a single solution, and independent projects, even if only for a few weeks. Observation and nomination come afterward. In Jana’s scene at the start of the chapter, no one noticed her ability until the open-ended science project gave her an opportunity to display it. For the teacher: indicators worth noticing These are situations to watch for and record; when you see them, note the date and context, without waiting for grades: Grasps a new idea after a brief presentation and grows restless when it is repeated. Asks questions that go beyond the lesson, or connects two subjects no one else has connected. Reaches a solution by a route other than the one taught, and can explain that route. Holds a deep, sustained interest in a topic outside the curriculum and knows more about it than would be expected at his or her age. Uses vocabulary or reasoning beyond his or her years, or understands complex humor before peers do. Produces outside school what does not show up in it: a project, a program, drawings, or writing. Shows clear improvement in performance and behavior when given a harder task. If you notice these indicators in a student whose grades are average or whose behavior is disruptive, that is all the more reason to reco

Group and individual tests In universal screening, group ability tests are typically administered to an entire class, on paper or online, such as the Cognitive Abilities Test ( CogAT ), which measures verbal, quantitative, and nonverbal reasoning, and the Naglieri Nonverbal Ability Test, Third Edition ( NNAT3 ), which relies on figural matrices and is therefore little affected by language. Students who exceed the screening cutoff , the score above which a student is referred for more in-depth assessment, are then evaluated with an individual intelligence test such as the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children or the Stanford–Binet (Chapter 3 presents these instruments in detail, and the Cognitive Abilities Test profile appears in Section 12.6). Limits of nonverbal tests Nonverbal tests are often presented as the answer to fairness for linguistically diverse students and those from less advantaged settings. There is some truth in this, but the literature points to three limits (Lohman, 2005). First , nonverbal reasoning predicts academic achievement less well than verbal and quantitative reasoning do, and academic programs need students who will succeed in their subject matter. Second , such tests sometimes narrow group differences, though their effect on this is weaker than commonly assumed. Third , relying on them alone may exclude students who genuinely excel in verbal or quantitative reasoning, since their performance on matrices and figures is not necessarily exceptional. The alternative this literature proposes is to keep the nonverbal test within a battery that includes verbal and quantitative reasoning, and then to compare the student with those who have had similar opportunities, that is, against local norms. The General Ability Index and the Cognitive Proficiency Index On the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fifth Edition ( WISC-V ), the Full Scale IQ ( Full Scale IQ, FSIQ ) is influenced by the Working Memory and Processing Speed indexes (Chapter 3 defines these indexes). Many gifted students, particularly twice-exceptional learners, perform noticeably lower on these two indexes than on reasoning and comprehension. Two composite scores are therefore derived from the scale to separate the two sides. The first is the General Ability Index ( General Ability Index, GAI ), built from five subtests in verbal comprehension, visual-spatial processing, and fluid reasoning: Similarities, Vocabulary, Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, and Figure Weights. The second is the Cognitive Proficiency Index ( Cognitive Proficiency Index, CPI ), built from four subtests in working memory and processing speed: Digit Span, Picture Span, Coding, and Symbol Search. The former describes what the student can reason through; the latter describes how efficiently he or she processes information quickly and accurately (Kaufman et al., 2016). The difference between the two indexes is read like any difference between two scores: Is it statistically significant, that is, too large to be attributed to measurement error? And how rare is it in the norming sample? (See Chapter 2.) A student with a General Ability Index of 132 and a Cognitive Proficiency Index of 104 shows a 28-point gap. Such a difference merits interpretation if it proves to be both significant and rare, as established by statistical computation rather than by the visual impression of a jagged profile. The National Association for Gifted Children recommends using the General Ability Index in identifying gifted students and not requiring the Full Scale IQ when a student’s profile is uneven (NAGC, 2018). When a student reaches the ceiling of several subtests, answering the last items or most of them, the Full Scale IQ and the General Ability Index can no longer capture the student’s ability, because the score cannot go beyond the highest value in the norm tables. For this reason, the publishers of some scales, including the Wechsler, have issued extended norms ( Extended norms )

Measuring creative thinking Among the best-known instruments for measuring creative thinking are the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking ( Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, TTCT ), whose profile appears in Section 12.6. They come in a verbal form and a figural form. In the figural form, the student is given incomplete or repeated shapes and asked to complete them as meaningful drawings and to give each drawing a title. The responses are then scored on several dimensions, among them fluency ( Fluency ), the number of ideas; flexibility ( Flexibility ), the variety of their categories; originality ( Originality ), their rarity relative to other people’s responses; and elaboration ( Elaboration ), how much the student adds to the basic idea (Kim, 2006). Table Umbrella Setting sun Turtle Open seashell Space station landing F Fluency: six ideas. X Flexibility: furniture, weather, nature, animals, and science fiction: five categories. O Originality: “space station landing” and “open seashell” are rarer than “umbrella” and “table.” E Elaboration: sparse in most drawings, greater in the sun and the space station. Figure 12.4: An illustrative activity designed by the author in the style of repeated-figures tasks; it is not taken from any published test. A hypothetical student completed a semicircle in six ways, and alongside the drawings is a reading of the responses on the four dimensions. Creativity tests have important limitations. They measure divergent thinking ( Divergent thinking ), the production of many and varied ideas, which is only one facet of creativity. Performance on them is sensitive to the instructions and to the student’s mood on the day of testing, and their reliability is lower than that of intelligence tests. Their predictive validity, that is, their capacity to predict creative achievement in adulthood, remains contested: some longitudinal studies have found a relationship between their scores and creative achievement decades later, while critics consider the relationship modest and inconsistent across studies (Kim, 2006). For this reason they serve as a supplementary source, alongside assessment of the student’s actual creative products over time. For evaluating the product itself, a well-known method is the Consensual Assessment Technique ( Consensual Assessment Technique ), proposed by Teresa Amabile (Amabile, 1982). Its premise is that the creativity of a product is defined by the judgment of those who know the field: the product, whether a story, a drawing, or a design, is presented to several judges with expertise in the field, each of whom rates its creativity independently of the others, and their agreement is then examined. If they agree to an acceptable degree, the mean of their ratings is taken as a measure of the product’s creativity. This method comes closest to what “performance before a panel” means in the arts, writing, and design, provided that the judges are experts in the field and that they rate independently before any discussion. Achievement and performance Very high achievement in a domain signals a talent already realized in it. It is measured with achievement tests, preferably supplemented by above-level testing to overcome the ceiling effect, as discussed earlier. Performance, for its part, is measured through authentic performance tasks, that is, tasks resembling what specialists in the field actually do, and through portfolios that collect samples of the student’s work over time. In some domains, such as the arts, sports, and leadership, performance before an expert panel is the primary source of evidence, because paper-and-pencil tests do not capture it.

The following profiles present four instruments that represent the main types of evidence used in identifying gifted learners: a group ability test for screening, a teacher rating scale, a test of creative thinking, and the above-level testing procedure. The profile of the Mawhiba test appears in Section 12.7, together with the regulatory context in which it is used. None of the profiles reproduces items from any published test. CogAT Cognitive Abilities Test, Form 7 Group ability test The idea Students learn at school through three symbol systems: words, numbers, and shapes and pictures. This test was therefore designed to measure reasoning within each system separately rather than to yield a single IQ. The aim is to identify the student’s ability profile so that suitable instruction or programming can be chosen (Lohman, 2011). What it looks like Three batteries, each with three subtests. Verbal battery: verbal or picture analogies, sentence completion, and classification. Quantitative battery: number analogies, number puzzles, and number series. Nonverbal battery: figure matrices, paper folding, and figure classification. At the early levels, from kindergarten to second grade, items are presented as pictures and directions are read aloud, so the student does not need to read. The test is administered on paper or online to a whole class. A scene from administration At a private international school that teaches in English, the administration decides to conduct universal screening of its third graders. Teachers administer the three batteries over two consecutive mornings. The profile of one student, whose first language is Arabic, reads as follows: Quantitative 131, Nonverbal 128, Verbal 112. The school summarizes the profile with a code such as “9B (V-)”: the number is the median stanine, the letter describes the extent of variation across the batteries, and the parenthesis identifies the relatively low battery. The school psychologist asks: is the lower verbal score a weakness in verbal reasoning, or an effect of learning in a second language? She decides to compare him with peers who are also learning in a second language before reaching any judgment. Table 12.5: Profile of the Cognitive Abilities Test. Purpose Measurement of verbal, quantitative, and nonverbal reasoning for universal screening and instructional planning Ages Kindergarten through Grade 12, in grade-based levels Edition and year Form 7, 2011 Publisher Riverside Qualification level Administered in class by the teacher under standardized directions; results interpreted by a trained professional Time The manual specifies the time for each battery by level; the three batteries are administered in one or more sessions Score types Standard age score with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 16 (not 15); percentile ranks and stanines based on age and grade norms; a composite score; and an ability profile summarizing level and pattern Cutoff scores Set by each program according to its service Reliability High for the composite according to the technical manual, and lower for individual batteries Classification accuracy Not applicable in the diagnostic sense. What matters is its predictive validity for achievement, which is stronger for the verbal and quantitative batteries than for the nonverbal battery Year of norm collection U.S. norms; consult the publisher for the norm year used in scoring Arabic version At the time of writing we know of no published standardized Arabic version How are the results interpreted? Interpretation begins with pattern before level: are the three batteries close together or divergent? Scores are then chosen to fit the service. A mathematics acceleration program looks first at the quantitative and nonverbal scores, and a language program looks at the verbal score. Note that the standard age score has a standard deviation of 16, so a score of 130 on it is not equivalent to 130 on a Wechsler scale. Its limits Its items and norms are i

search.s: 12.7 Identification in the Saudi context and the decision pathway
search.t: The National Program for Gifted Identification began in 2011 as an annual project run in partnership by the King Abdulaziz and His Companions Foundation for Giftedness and Creativity (Mawhiba), the Ministry of Education, and the National Center for Assessment, initially targeting students in the third and sixth grades of elementary school and the third grade of intermediate school (Ministry of Education, 1437 AH [Arabic]). Today it targets students from the third grade of elementary school through the first grade of secondary school, that is, grades 3 to 10, with its main instrument, the Mawhiba Multiple Cognitive Abilities Test (King Abdulaziz and His Companions Foundation for Giftedness and Creativity, n.d. [Arabic]). Alongside it are the Ministry of Education’s school-based gifted programs, which have their own criteria. A recent review offers a comprehensive picture of gifted education and its programs in the Kingdom (Alfaiz et al., 2022). The box below sets out what the published documents stipulate on identification specifically. In the Saudi context: identification criteria in the published documents Table 12.9: Criteria for identifying gifted learners in the published Saudi documents we were able to review. Document What it stipulates Reading it with the chapter’s tools Regulations for Special Education Institutes and Programs (Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif], 1422 AH [Arabic], Article 8) A student is admitted if any one of the following conditions is met: high academic achievement over two semesters (97%, by our reading of the printed copy) together with an IQ of at least 115 on a standardized test; an IQ of at least 125 on the Wechsler scale or 127 on the Stanford–Binet; outstanding skills and abilities attested by the student’s teachers and peers; or creative or innovative thinking An “or” rule: one criterion suffices. The cutoff of 115 corresponds to roughly the top 16% and requires achievement alongside it; the cutoff of 125 corresponds to roughly the top 5%. The difference between 125 and 127 is explained by the standard deviation of 16 in older editions of the Stanford–Binet. The rule specifies neither an instrument nor a score for creativity Special Education Organizational Guide (Ministry of Education, 1436 AH [Arabic]) Does not list the gifted among its categories Regulation of giftedness moved to the gifted program guides, so it is no longer housed in a single document with disabilities Guide to Gifted Classes (Ministry of Education, n.d. [Arabic]) Students are nominated from among those classified in the national gifted identification project. If places remain unfilled, they are completed using the Ministry’s four criteria: a cognitive abilities measure, personal traits, academic achievement, and creative output, provided the student meets at least two criteria, one of which must be the cognitive abilities measure with a score of no less than 120 A compound rule: at least two criteria, with ability as a necessary condition. The cutoff of 120 corresponds to roughly the top 10%, approximately Gagné’s threshold Organizational and Procedural Guide for the School Program for Gifted Girls (Ministry of Education, 1437 AH [Arabic]) Admission for the top 5% of the national project’s results, from fourth grade of elementary school to second grade of secondary school The percentage is computed only among those who sat the test, since registration is optional National Program for Gifted Identification (King Abdulaziz and His Companions Foundation for Giftedness and Creativity, n.d. [Arabic]) The Mawhiba Multiple Cognitive Abilities Test, with optional registration; results are announced through the Mawhiba website We found neither the score scale nor the cutoff score in any official source. A peer-reviewed study reported an operational cutoff of 1540 (Almulhim, Aljughaiman, & Alfaiz, 2026) Three observations arise from these documents. First, the older regulations treated the criteria as alternatives, any one of whi

search.s: 12.8 When is the judgment made? Three cases
search.t: Case 1: Jana, age 10 General giftedness with a strength in science The rest of the opening scene: Jana is a fourth grader whom her teachers did not nominate because she daydreams a lot and her spelling grades are average. After the science teacher mentioned her soil project, she proposed to the school that all the girls in the grade be offered open-ended activities for two weeks, after which the teachers would complete a structured observation checklist. Jana stood out in curiosity, reasoning, and inquiry. The school then encouraged all the students’ families to register for the Mawhiba test, and her family registered her at the first level. The figures in the table are hypothetical, for illustration. Table 12.12: Evidence in Jana’s case. Source Result What it means Observation checklist after the open-ended activities High in curiosity, reasoning, and inquiry; average in self-discipline and organization Gifted behaviors that emerged once the opportunity was provided Mawhiba Multiple Cognitive Abilities Test 97th percentile among applicants from her grade; her strongest domain was scientific and mechanical reasoning High reasoning relative only to those who sat the test nationally Seventh-grade science test, administered to her in fourth grade 72nd percentile on seventh-grade norms At least three years ahead of her grade in science Spelling Standard score of 98 (average) Not inconsistent with giftedness, and does not call for further assessment at this point Decision: Jana is identified as gifted, with a particular strength in science, and is placed in a science enrichment program with acceleration in science. Her daydreaming is not settled for now. Eight to twelve weeks after she joins the program, she is observed systematically in a regular lesson and in one that offers suitable challenge, and the question is asked: does the daydreaming diminish when she meets a challenge? Yet this is a supporting question, not a decisive one . The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision ( DSM-5-TR ), states that signs of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder may be minimal or absent when the child is receiving frequent rewards for appropriate behavior, is under close supervision, is in a novel setting, or is engaged in especially interesting activities (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). If the daydreaming persists across more than one setting and visibly affects her organization and performance at home and at school, an assessment for the disorder or for anxiety is completed as a possible case of twice-exceptionality, not as an alternative to giftedness (Chapters 10 and 13 take up this distinction in detail). What evidence could change the decision? If her performance in the advanced science course falls short of what the above-level test result suggests, the team would revisit the amount of acceleration and the starting point. If the daydreaming persists at home and at school after she has found challenge, with effects on her organization and performance, an assessment for possible twice-exceptionality would be added to the giftedness decision. Case 2: Mishari, age 11 Local norms bring him into view The story: Mishari is a fifth grader at a small school in a remote village. There are 18 students in his class, the school has a basic laboratory, and there is no regular enrichment activity. His score on the group ability test fell below the national admission cutoff for one of the programs. Yet he is the top student in his school by a wide margin, and from parts of old devices he has built a robotic arm that moves on simple commands, which he taught himself to program from online videos. The figures in the table are hypothetical, for illustration. Table 12.13: Evidence in Mishari’s case. search.s: 12.9 What can be mistaken for giftedness, and what can hide it
search.t: Table 12.15: Situations in which giftedness may be wrongly suspected or hidden, and how the team handles them. Situation What happens How we handle it The high achiever High marks earned through effort and discipline, with above-average but not exceptional ability Needs challenge in the subjects where he or she excels, which may suffice without a general gifted program, as in Dana’s case The gifted underachiever Very high ability with average or low achievement, owing to boredom or to emotional or environmental factors Detected through ability measures, since achievement conceals it; needs support for motivation alongside challenge Giftedness that resembles a disorder Boredom, daydreaming, repeated questions, and intense sensitivity may be misread as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or an emotional disorder (Webb et al., 2005) The student is observed systematically in an ordinary lesson and in one that offers suitable challenge, and a supporting question is asked: does the behavior diminish when the student is challenged? Its disappearance does not rule out the disorder, since symptoms may lessen during interesting or novel activities, under close supervision, or with frequent rewards (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). It is therefore combined with a developmental history, ratings from more than one informant across more than one setting, and evidence of functional impact at home and at school Giftedness with a disability (twice-exceptional learners) The disability masks the giftedness, the giftedness masks the disability, or each masks the other so that the student appears average A comprehensive assessment that looks for strengths and weaknesses together and compares the General Ability Index with the Cognitive Proficiency Index rather than relying on the full-scale score alone. A Saudi study estimated that about 5.9% of a sample of 6,875 students in four private schools in Riyadh may belong to this group (Almulhim, Aljughaiman, Alnaim, et al., 2026) (Chapter 13 treats it in detail) The gifted student who is linguistically diverse or from a low-opportunity environment Lower scores on verbal tests and on national norms Local norms, performance assessment, and a nonverbal test within a battery that includes verbal and quantitative reasoning (Lohman, 2005), as in Mishari’s case

The central argument of this chapter is that the definition of giftedness determines the tools of identification, and that every definition and every admission rule determines, at the same time, who may be missed. It follows that teacher nomination should not be relied on alone, since it is limited by teachers’ biases and by the opportunities to display that the classroom affords; that universal screening and local norms should widen access, with due attention to their conditions; that a nonverbal test should form part of a broader battery; and that above-level testing should be used when the ceiling limits what we can read of a student’s ability. Creativity tests serve as a complement, alongside the evaluation of real products. Some questions in the chapter nonetheless remain contested, and the evidence on others has yet to be published. The predictive validity of creativity tests is disputed. The Mawhiba test is a national instrument developed in Arabic, but registration is optional, and its score scale and technical evidence are unpublished. Saudi documents use different IQ thresholds (115, 120, and 125) with different combination rules. Distinguishing giftedness from a disorder remains a judgment that no single question can settle: the disappearance of a behavior under challenge is a supporting clue that needs others alongside it. And identification extends beyond the question “Is the student gifted?” to the service that suits the domain and level of the student’s giftedness.

Chapter summary The definition of giftedness determines the tools of identification; contemporary definitions encompass both potential and achievement and take the environment into account. Each of the four models has those it may miss. Gagné distinguishes natural gifts from developed talents and sets a threshold at the top 10%, with five levels that help in reading admission rules. Teacher nomination is limited by teachers’ biases and by the opportunities the classroom affords for giftedness to be displayed. Universal screening and local norms widen access; local norms carry conditions on the size of the reference group and limits on how far the label transfers. A nonverbal test is part of a broader battery. The General Ability Index is useful with uneven profiles, and its difference from the Cognitive Proficiency Index is read in terms of significance and rarity. Above-level testing solves the ceiling problem and sets the starting point for acceleration. Creativity tests measure divergent thinking; their predictive validity is disputed, and they are used as a complement alongside the evaluation of real products. The Mawhiba test is a national instrument developed in Arabic, but registration is optional and its score scale and technical evidence are unpublished; Saudi documents use different IQ thresholds (115, 120, and 125) with different combination rules. In distinguishing giftedness from a disorder, the disappearance of a behavior under challenge is a supporting question that needs further evidence. The most important question after “Is the student gifted?” is “What service suits the domain and level of the student’s giftedness?” Glossary of terms Gift High natural ability not yet refined through learning and practice. Talent A mastered skill in a specific field, developed from gifts through learning and practice. Opportunity to display The situations a learning environment offers the student in which to display his or her abilities. Universal screening Assessing all students at a given grade level rather than relying on nomination. Ceiling effect A test’s inability to discriminate among high-performing students because it contains too few difficult items. Above-level testing Administering a test designed for older students to an able student in order to gauge how far ahead he or she is. General Ability Index General Ability Index, GAI A composite score measuring reasoning and comprehension without working memory or processing speed. Cognitive Proficiency Index, CPI A composite score drawn from working memory and processing speed subtests, compared with the General Ability Index to describe an uneven profile. Talent pool A broad group of students, about 15–20%, offered enrichment services in Renzulli’s model, with flexible entry for those who display gifted behavior. Excellence gaps Differences between groups in the proportions of students who reach advanced levels of performance. Consensual Assessment Technique Evaluating a product’s creativity through independent ratings by judges familiar with the field, then examining their agreement. DT→PI A model used in talent search programs that pinpoints what a student does not yet know of an advanced course, teaches only that material, and then tests the student at the end of the course. Divergent thinking The capacity to generate many varied and original ideas for a single problem. Three-Ring Conception Renzulli’s conception of gifted behavior as the intersection of above-average ability, task commitment, and creativity. Local norms Comparing a student’s performance with that of peers in the same school or area rather than with the national norming sample alone. Creative-productive giftedness The capacity to produce original ideas and products for a real audience; Renzulli contrasts it with schoolhouse giftedness, that is, skill at learning lessons and taking tests.
