13 Chapter 13 Twice-exceptional learners A student who is gifted and has a disability at the same time: the phrase may sound contradictory to anyone who sees giftedness and disability as opposite poles. Yet reality shows them coexisting in a single student, each concealing the other, so that the student falls between two systems, neither of which sees him fully as he is. Scene from a meeting that never took place Imagine two meetings at the same intermediate school in the same week. In the first, the gifted program team reviews the list of students whose performance has slipped and proposes withdrawing Yasser from the program: “He didn’t hand in his research project report, and his written test scores aren’t what you’d expect from a student in the program.” In the second, the learning disabilities team discusses the list of struggling students, and Yasser’s name never comes up: “He reads well, his Arabic grades are average, and he doesn’t need services.” The two teams never met. Had they done so, they would have seen a student who solves math problems taught in secondary school and explains the idea behind his project orally with a fluency that astonishes his teachers, then spends a full hour writing a single paragraph about it, riddled with errors. Yasser is fourteen, in the third year of intermediate school (ninth grade), and has been in the gifted program since fourth grade. His teacher in the program noticed that the gap between what he says and what he writes widens year after year: he avoids writing reports, asks to present his project orally, and his papers are full of spelling errors no one would expect from a student at his grade level. In this chapter we show why his difficulty was nearly overlooked and how to build an assessment that captures both sides at once, and then we return to his full case in Section 13.8. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Define twice-exceptional learners using the two reference definitions, and identify the difference between them. Classify a student in a given description into one of the three groups, and explain how each of his two sides masks the other. Identify what each of the usual identification models misses, and compare the arguments for normative comparison and intra-individual comparison. Design an assessment protocol that opens both the giftedness and the disability tracks together for a given student, and justify each of its components. Interpret an uneven cognitive profile using the difference between the General Ability Index and the Cognitive Proficiency Index, and explain why no judgment can rest on it alone. Determine, in a given case, which of three possibilities is most likely—giftedness only, giftedness with a disorder, or a disorder only—and state the deciding evidence. Judge whether the evidence in a new case suffices for a determination, and justify that judgment.

In twice-exceptional learners, giftedness and disability coexist, each concealing the other, so that their performance often appears average and catches the attention of neither the gifted team nor the special education team. Their cases therefore fall into the zone where the usual models break down: a student may be proposed for withdrawal from the gifted program because the disability has lowered his performance, and excluded from learning disabilities services because his giftedness has lifted his achievement to the average range—just as the opening scene portrays through two meetings that never converged. Judgment in such cases requires applying the criteria for each side separately, reading the uneven profile systematically, and knowing when a discrepancy counts as evidence and when it does not. We open the chapter by defining twice-exceptional learners and locating them within the book’s chapters (Section 13.1), then present masking and the three groups (Section 13.2), the reasons the usual models fail these students (Section 13.3), and the debate over identification criteria (Section 13.4). We then take up the assessment protocol, the reading of an uneven cognitive profile, and the adaptation of identification tools for learners with sensory and physical disabilities (Section 13.5), followed by the decision pathway that opens both tracks together (Section 13.6) and the three possibilities in differential diagnosis (Section 13.7). We apply all of this to four cases (Section 13.8) and close with the Saudi and Arab context (Section 13.9).

Twice-exceptional ( Twice-exceptional, 2e ) learners are students who show potential for high performance or creative productivity in one or more domains and who, at the same time, have one or more disabilities under recognized eligibility criteria (Reis et al., 2014). The literature stresses that the combination of the two exceptionalities produces a unique situation that is more than the sum of the two conditions: giftedness changes how the disability presents, the disability changes how the giftedness presents, and the student needs instruction that attends to both sides at once (Baldwin et al., 2015). Two definitions are widely cited in the literature, and they serve different functions: Two reference definitions The operational definition (Reis et al., 2014) It specifies who counts as twice-exceptional: a student who shows potential for high achievement or creative productivity in one or more domains and who has one or more disabilities according to recognized eligibility criteria, such as learning disabilities, speech and language disorders, emotional and behavioral disorders, physical disabilities, autism spectrum disorder, and health impairments such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. By tying the category to existing criteria, the definition is easy to apply in schools. The community of practice consensus definition (2014; in Baldwin et al., 2015) It describes how the two exceptionalities interact and what the student needs: exceptional ability may dominate the disability, may conceal it, or may itself be concealed by it. These students need specialized identification methods that take the interaction between the two sides into account; dual differentiated instruction that develops their talents while meeting their learning needs; concurrent services that include the social and emotional domain; and teachers prepared to work with them. The first, then, is a definition for eligibility , answering the question “Is this student one of them?”; the second is a definition for practice , answering the question “What does that mean for how we assess and teach him?” The assessment team needs both: the first in order to decide, and the second in order to know where to look and why the usual tools fall short. Their number is not precisely known, because definitions and identification methods vary widely across studies and because many of these students are never identified at all (Foley Nicpon et al., 2011). Among recent studies, one examined the cognitive and achievement characteristics of students from a U.S. national sample who were identified as potentially twice-exceptional (Maddocks, 2020). In the Kingdom, an exploratory study of 6,875 students in grades 2 through 12 at four private schools in Riyadh estimated that about 5.9% of them may be twice-exceptional: 23.6% showed a discrepancy of more than 1.5 standard deviations between their performance in two subjects, and 24.5% of these then appeared possibly gifted (Almulhim et al., 2026). This is a preliminary estimate based on indicators of discrepancy in achievement, and it would need individual diagnostic assessment to confirm. It does not estimate the prevalence of the group in Saudi schools, but it does signal that the group may be less rare than is commonly assumed. Recent literature favors planning for these students that begins with their talents and interests rather than their deficits, an approach known as the strength-based, talent-focused approach (Baum et al., 2014). The examples in this chapter include Yasser, gifted in mathematics with a writing difficulty; Joud, linguistically gifted with autism spectrum disorder; and Faris, gifted in mathematics with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Set against them is Muhannad, a gifted student some of whose characteristics resemble a disorder. Twice-exceptional learners across the chapters of this book This chapter stands on its own, but twice-exceptional learners also appear in the chapters on specific

How does each side mask the other? One way to picture it is as two forces pulling the student’s performance in opposite directions: giftedness lifts it, and the disability drags it down. What the teacher sees in the grades is the net result of this tug-of-war, and it may well be an average performance that draws no one’s attention. What his ability alone predicts 130 What the difficulty alone predicts 75 What the teacher sees in the grades 98 60 85 100 115 140 Figure 13.1: A hypothetical example of masking. The gray band is the average range, 85 to 115. High ability compensates for the difficulty, and the difficulty pulls performance down to a level that looks ordinary. The gifted team does not notice him because his performance is not high, and the learning disabilities team does not notice him because it is not low. The figure is a conceptual representation : the three numbers illustrate the direction of the pull between the two sides and are not meant to be added to or subtracted from one another. The three groups Because of this masking, twice-exceptional learners appear in schools in three groups (Brody & Mills, 1997; Baum & Owen, 2004): Gifted, with the disability overlooked Visible giftedness Visible disability Identified as gifted, with his difficulties explained away as laziness, lack of interest, or “gifted eccentricity.” He stumbles whenever demands increase and may be withdrawn from the program because his performance has declined. The risk: he is blamed for what he cannot control Disabled, with the giftedness overlooked Visible giftedness Visible disability Diagnosed with a disability and receiving services that focus on his weaknesses. No one sees his high abilities, so he is offered no challenge; he may grow bored, and his performance then looks even worse. The risk: his giftedness goes to waste Neither side identified Visible giftedness Visible disability The hardest group to identify, and in the view of many researchers the largest. The student looks average and may be struggling in silence with double the effort and a frustration no one understands. The risk: he is not seen at all Figure 13.2: The three groups of twice-exceptional learners in schools. Faded bars represent a side that is present but invisible to those around the student; bar lengths are illustrative only. The claim that the third group is the largest is a common hypothesis in the literature (Baum & Owen, 2004) that still awaits proof, since by their very nature we have no prevalence data on students who go unidentified. Yasser, in the scene that opens this chapter, belongs to the first group: he is in the gifted program, and his writing difficulty is invisible to anyone who hears him speak—so much so that he was nearly withdrawn from the program over the reports he never handed in. Had he never been nominated for the program in the first place, he would have belonged to the third group.

search.s: 13.3 Why do the usual models fail them?
search.t: To identify learning disabilities and giftedness, schools rely on familiar models, among them response to intervention, which treats a student’s failure to improve with instruction of graduated intensity as an indicator of difficulty; the criteria for specific learning disorder in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision ( DSM-5-TR ), which require the skill to be clearly below what is expected for the student’s age (APA, 2022); and the admission criteria of gifted programs. When we examine these models, we find that each of them may miss the twice-exceptional student (Chapter 6 discusses identification models in detail). Researchers warned early on that relying on the response to intervention model alone may hide these students, because its screening looks for those who fall below their peers (Crepeau-Hobson & Bianco, 2011): Table 13.2: The usual identification models, what each requires, and why each may miss the twice-exceptional student. Model What it requires Why it may miss him — Performance below peers that does not improve with intervention His performance is at the level of his peers or slightly above, so he never shows up in screening Diagnostic manual criteria for specific learning disorder A skill clearly below what is expected for age His skill is in the low-average range, above the threshold for clearly low performance for his age Gifted program criteria A high score on the Full Scale IQ or in achievement The Full Scale IQ is pulled down by working memory and processing speed, and achievement is pulled down by the difficulty The “and” rule across criteria Exceeding the threshold on every criterion He exceeds the threshold in ability but falls short of it in achievement, and so is excluded Teacher nomination Behavior that matches the image of a gifted student The teacher sees frustration, avoidance, and slowness, and the giftedness is hidden from view

The most important scholarly debate in this area turns on a single question: what do we compare the student’s performance against? Normative comparison Is the student’s performance below that of his same-age peers? This is what the diagnostic manual’s criteria require. Proponents of this comparison argue that a student who reads in the average range does not suffer a functional impairment that would justify a diagnosis, and that diagnosing everyone with a gap between their abilities would expand the category without justification and turn “relative weakness” into a disability (Lovett & Lewandowski, 2006). Intra-individual comparison Is the student’s performance clearly below what his abilities predict? Proponents of this comparison argue that a student whose ability lies in the top 1% of his peers, and who reads at an average level only with double the effort, does indeed have a real difficulty with real consequences, even if he is not below his peers. In their view, requiring normatively low performance denies these students understanding and support (Assouline et al., 2010). Figure 13.3: The two lenses in the debate over identifying twice-exceptional learners. One study compared different methods of identifying gifted students with learning disabilities within a single sample and found that the methods differed considerably in how many students they identified and in which students, with limited agreement among them (Maddocks, 2018). In other words, who counts as twice-exceptional depends in part on the criterion we choose. A balanced practical position The gap between ability and achievement is not sufficient on its own, since everyone has uneven abilities. Nor is normatively low performance sufficient on its own, because it misses these students. The position toward which good practice leans is to base judgment on the gap together with converging evidence: a history of early difficulty in the same skill; processing indicators that explain it, such as weak phonological awareness in reading or weak orthographic knowledge in writing; a genuine functional impact , such as double effort, avoidance, or exhaustion; the persistence of the difficulty despite appropriate instruction targeting it; and a skill that actually lies in the low-average range or near the threshold, not merely below the student’s other abilities.

search.s: 13.5 Assessment: the protocol and the uneven profile
search.t: Reading an uneven cognitive profile Many twice-exceptional learners show a recurring pattern on intelligence scales such as the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fifth Edition ( WISC-V ): very high reasoning and verbal comprehension, alongside clearly lower working memory and processing speed. These two indexes enter into the calculation of the Full Scale IQ and pull it down. For this reason, identifying giftedness in these students relies on the General Ability Index ( General Ability Index, GAI ), which is calculated without these two indexes (NAGC, 2018). Chapter 12 (Section 12.4) explained this index, the ceiling effect, and above-level testing in detail. What this chapter adds is that the index has a counterpart that completes it: the Cognitive Proficiency Index ( Cognitive Proficiency Index, CPI ), calculated from the working memory and processing speed subtests—that is, from the efficiency with which the student processes information, independent of his reasoning ability. Comparing the two indexes is the systematic way to describe an uneven profile, rather than looking at the graph and judging by eye (Kaufman et al., 2016). Two questions are asked, in order: Is the difference statistically significant? That is, is it larger than measurement error alone would produce? This is settled by consulting the tables in the manual. Is it rare? Many statistically significant differences are common in the norm sample, and their presence signals nothing unusual. We therefore look at the proportion of the norm sample who showed a difference of this size, that is, the base rate. When a student reaches the ceiling on several subtests, ordinary scores do not reveal the full extent of his ability. Extended norms have been published for the WISC-V Full Scale IQ and General Ability Index that allow scores above the ceiling of the standard norms; the publisher should be consulted on the conditions for their use. But the uneven profile as a whole, however wide its gap, is not diagnostic : it appears in many gifted students with no disability whatsoever, and it is not sufficient on its own for any judgment. Fluid reasoning 134 Visual spatial 130 Verbal comprehension 128 Working memory 100 Processing speed 88 General Ability Index 135 Cognitive Proficiency Index 92 Difference between the two indexes 43 Full Scale IQ 122 70 85 100 115 130 150 Figure 13.4: A hypothetical profile for Yasser on the WISC-V indexes. The gray band is the average range, 85 to 115, that is, one standard deviation on either side of the mean, as in the book’s other graphs. (The test manual applies the label “average” only to the range 90 to 109 in its descriptive classification.) The difference between the General Ability Index and the Cognitive Proficiency Index is 43 points, a difference whose significance and rarity are checked in the manual’s tables before it is interpreted. The Full Scale IQ of 122 falls short of the cut-off score in many gifted programs, whereas the General Ability Index of 135 exceeds it. Principles of assessment Two lenses in one assessment: The assessment involves both someone who knows giftedness and someone who knows disability, or else an assessor who brings both kinds of expertise. Two questions are asked about the student together: What are his abilities? And what is holding him back? Start with strength: What the student excels at is measured with high-ceiling tools, such as above-level testing, performance tasks, and authentic products, rather than grade-level tools on which he reaches the highest possible score and which therefore cannot reveal how far his ability extends (see Chapter 12, Section 12.4). Measure skill by time and effort: Many twice-exceptional learners arrive at the correct answer eventually. Performance is therefore measured once under time limits and once untimed, and the assessor observes the effort the student expends and the compensatory strategies he relies on. Developmental and educational history: When did

search.s: 13.6 The decision pathway: opening both tracks together
search.t: In the chapters on specific categories, the decision pathway runs along a single line, from initial indicators to matching against the criteria of one category. With a student suspected of being twice-exceptional, however, the most common error is to open one track and close the other prematurely: the student is admitted to the gifted program and no one asks about his difficulty, or he is diagnosed with a disability and no one asks about his giftedness. For this reason, after the second step the pathway branches into two lenses that work together and then converge in a single reading of the profile before the decision. 1 Indicators from either side A nomination for giftedness, a referral for a difficulty, a gifted student declining as demands rise, or a striking gap between oral and written work. 2 Senses and learning opportunities A recent hearing and vision screening, and a review of attendance and of the instruction the student has received, before any tool is used. Both tracks open together 3 Two lenses at once The strength lens: the General Ability Index, an above-level test, and a product or performance task. The difficulty lens: skills timed and untimed, processing indicators, ratings from multiple informants, and observation in an ordinary lesson and in a challenging one. 4 Reading the profile as a whole The difference between the General Ability Index and the Cognitive Proficiency Index, with its significance and rarity; developmental and educational history; functional impact at school and at home; and response to the instruction provided. 5 Matching against each side’s criteria separately The program’s giftedness criteria, applied to an index that the difficulty does not depress, and the disorder criteria in the diagnostic manual and the applicable regulations. Neither side’s criterion is lowered because the other side’s is met. Which side’s criteria are met? Giftedness alone Giftedness only Gifted services, with monitoring of behavior after appropriate placement Both sides Giftedness with a disorder Dual services: challenge in the area of strength, and support and accommodations in the area of difficulty The disorder alone Disorder only Services for the disorder, while nurturing the student’s relative strengths and interests If the evidence is insufficient for any judgment: place the student in a setting suited to his ability, repeat structured observation after a set period, and close neither track. Figure 13.5: The decision pathway for a student suspected of being twice-exceptional. After sensory screening, the assessment branches into two lenses that work together; the criteria for each side are applied separately; and the pathway ends in one of three decisions, or in appropriate placement followed by renewed evidence gathering. The crucial point in the fifth step is that the team must not “go easy” on one side’s criteria because the other side’s are met. Giftedness does not prove a disorder, and a disorder does not rule out giftedness. What changes for the twice-exceptional student is the evidence accepted for each criterion, while the criterion itself stays fixed: the General Ability Index is used in place of the Full Scale IQ for the giftedness criterion, and for the difficulty criterion the skill is read under time limits and in terms of the effort expended.

When a student shows signs suggestive of both giftedness and a disorder, the team faces three possibilities, all of them plausible. It may be giftedness only, some of whose characteristics resemble a disorder when the student finds nothing suited to him (Webb et al., 2005). It may be giftedness with a disorder, which is twice-exceptionality. Or it may be a disorder only, with a relative strength in one part of the profile that does not rise to the level of giftedness. Error is possible in all three directions, and every error has its cost. Table 13.5: The three possibilities in differential diagnosis, what favors each, and what is not sufficient on its own. Possibility What favors it Not sufficient on its own The cost of error Giftedness only , resembling a disorder The concern centers on low-challenge situations and diminishes clearly after weeks of appropriate placement. There is no functional impact outside these situations, no developmental history of difficulty, and basic skills are intact on standardized, timed measurement The behavior disappearing during a favored or novel activity; this also happens with the disorder If the disorder is in fact present, the student is denied understanding and support and is blamed for what he cannot control Giftedness with a disorder (twice-exceptionality) Evidence of high ability from more than one source, such as the General Ability Index, above-level testing, and products, together with the disorder criteria being met: early history, a processing indicator or a behavioral pattern in two settings, functional impact, and persistence despite appropriate instruction or appropriate placement The gap between indexes; it is common among gifted students with no disability at all If the disorder is not present, the student is labeled with a diagnosis he does not need and may be given treatment he has no need for Disorder only , with a relative strength The disorder criteria are met, and the strength is a relative strength within the student’s own profile that does not clearly exceed his peers, or broad knowledge confined to a narrow interest without high-level reasoning in that domain An extensive memory for facts on a favorite topic, early mechanical reading without matching comprehension, or a single high index amid average ones If giftedness is present, it goes to waste, and the student receives services that focus on his weaknesses alone Caution: “What happens when he finds challenge?” is a helpful question, not a decisive one Comparing a student’s behavior in an ordinary lesson with his behavior in a lesson that offers genuine challenge is a useful comparison, but it does not settle the matter by itself. The diagnostic manual states that signs of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder may be minimal or absent when the child is receiving frequent rewards for appropriate behavior, is under close supervision, is in a novel setting, or is engaged in especially interesting activities (APA, 2022). A student’s ability to concentrate for hours on an activity he loves therefore does not rule out the disorder. What tips the balance toward one possibility or the other is the convergence of evidence: ratings from two settings, developmental history, functional impact at school and at home, and what remains of the behavior after weeks of appropriate placement. These carry more weight than an hour in a club he loves.

search.s: 13.8 When is a judgment warranted? Four cases
search.t: The four cases that follow cover the three possibilities set out in the previous section. In three of them, the criteria for both sides are met through different kinds of evidence: a writing difficulty, autism, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. In one, Muhannad’s case (Case 2), the evidence is not yet sufficient for any judgment about a disorder. Case 1: Yasser, age 14, ninth grade (third year of intermediate school) Giftedness with a writing difficulty The story: Yasser, whose scene opened this chapter, has been in the gifted program since fourth grade and trains with his school’s team for mathematics competitions. At the start of ninth grade, his program teacher referred him after he failed to submit the report for his research project, even though his oral presentation of the idea had astonished the judging panel. His family reported that he had been slow to learn letter formation and spelling in first and second grade, and that he “used to write words the way he said them”; they were told he would improve with time. The gap then widened in intermediate school, as reports and essay answers multiplied, and his older brother began writing down what Yasser dictated to him. What the two-lens assessment added: Table 13.6: Evidence in Yasser’s case through the two lenses. Lens Evidence What it means Senses Hearing and vision screening this year: normal No sensory explanation for the difficulty Giftedness General Ability Index 135, Cognitive Proficiency Index 92 and Full Scale IQ 122, as shown in Figure 13.4. The difference between the two indexes is statistically significant and rare according to the manual’s tables Very high ability, which the full-scale score underestimates Giftedness A mathematics test designed for twelfth-grade students: percentile rank 70 among students in that grade Realized mathematical talent three years ahead of his grade Reading Reading a fully vowelized text and an unvowelized text at grade level: accuracy 98% and 96%, fluency in the average range, and reading comprehension 118 Reading is intact in both conditions, so the difficulty must be sought beyond decoding Difficulty Standardized achievement test in writing: spelling 77, writing fluency 80, and written expression 84 At or below one standard deviation under the mean, and far below his ability Difficulty Analysis of spelling errors across three samples: most involve the hamza; tāʾ marbūṭa, open tāʾ and hāʾ; and letters of similar shape distinguished only by their dots, such as writing “ج” for “ح” or dropping dots; as well as spelling words as they are pronounced in his dialect A consistent weakness in orthographic and morphological knowledge that recurs in a clear pattern Difficulty Copying from a ready, legible text at a speed close to his peers’. Free handwritten composition, however, yielded forty-five words in ten minutes, in short, loosely connected sentences. When he wrote on the same topic using a keyboard, his text grew slightly longer but the spelling errors remained; when he spoke about it orally, his presentation was organized and rich The difficulty is linguistic, orthographic and organizational, not motor Fine motor Screening by an occupational therapist: average Developmental coordination disorder unlikely Intervention Twelve weeks in eighth grade of explicit instruction in spelling rules and the hamza in a small group: errors decreased on the trained words, but the gains did not transfer to his free writing Persistence of the difficulty despite targeted instruction Emotion He says, “My thoughts are faster than my hand,” and “I’m stupid in Arabic,” and he grows tense before essay tests An effect on self-concept and anxiety tied to writing A ✓ Persistent despite 12 weeks of intervention B ✓ Spelling 77 and written expression 84, with supporting evidence C ✓ Began in the early grades and intensified as demands increased D ✓ Intact senses, high ability, regular instruction, and intact motor skills How did the team read the e

search.s: 13.9 In the Saudi and Arab context
search.t: In the Saudi context: Can a student receive both gifted program services and learning disabilities services? The short answer: We found no published regulatory text that explicitly permits a student to combine a gifted program with a special education service, nor any text that prohibits it. The Special Education Organizational Guide lists eleven disability categories and does not address the gifted (Ministry of Education, 1436 AH [Arabic]). The gifted program guides we reviewed regulate nomination and admission and make no mention of students with disabilities (Ministry of Education, n.d., 1437 AH [Arabic]). In practice, then, the matter is left to the judgment of teams in schools and education directorates. Even so, the texts contain provisions that open the door rather than close it. The Regulations for Special Education Institutes and Programs defined both “superior ability and giftedness” and “learning disabilities” in a single document, set separate admission requirements for each, and did not make giftedness a reason to exclude a learning disability. Moreover, the admission requirement for learning disabilities in the Regulations is “a clear discrepancy between the student’s level of ability and level of academic achievement” in areas that include writing. This is the logic of intra-individual comparison, which suits twice-exceptional learners better than comparison with peers, although the Regulations do not specify a figure for this discrepancy (Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif], 1422 AH [Arabic]). Gifted classes, for their part, require meeting two or more criteria, one of which is a cognitive abilities test with a score of no less than 120 (Ministry of Education, n.d. [Arabic]), and the guide does not specify whether this refers to the full-scale score or to an index that the difficulty does not depress. Nor may the group be rare, as the preliminary estimate in Section 13.1 suggests (Almulhim et al., 2026). Saudi researchers have studied the experiences of teachers in the Hail region with these students (Alsamiri & Alsamani, 2023), teachers’ professional development needs for identifying them in inclusive schools (Alsamiri & Alsamani, 2026), and the barriers that elementary school teachers see to identifying and supporting them (Alsamani et al., 2026). Table 13.10: Twice-exceptionality in the diagnostic manuals, US law and Saudi regulations. Element DSM-5-TR US Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) Saudi regulations Is giftedness a category? No; the manual is designed for classifying disorders No; giftedness falls outside the law’s categories and is regulated by the states Yes; it was defined in the 1422 AH Regulations and is governed by the gifted program guides Does giftedness preclude a diagnosis of a disorder? No. The learning disorder criterion compares the student with age expectations, with leeway up to one standard deviation if other evidence supports it No. Eligibility requires both a disability and a need for special education No text prohibits it. The learning disabilities requirement is a discrepancy between ability and achievement, with no specified figure Is combining the two services explicitly provided for? Not applicable No explicit federal provision, and the law does not prohibit it We found no text that permits or prohibits it A question for reflection: If Yasser’s case came before your school tomorrow, who would request his evaluation: the gifted team or the learning disabilities team? And who has the authority to decide that he receives both services at once?

The central argument of this chapter is that twice-exceptional learners are identified through a multi-instrument protocol that opens the giftedness and disability tracks together and applies the criteria for each separately. It follows that response to intervention, normative criteria or the “and” rule cannot be expected to identify these students; that the difference between the General Ability Index and the Cognitive Proficiency Index should be read as a systematic description of an uneven profile, one that precedes any diagnosis and requires further evidence; and that early history and home–school discrepancies deserve particular weight, especially for gifted autistic girls, who may camouflage their traits for years. In every case, the team faces three possibilities: giftedness only, giftedness with a disorder, or a disorder only. Debate continues over the basis for judgment: normative comparison or intra-individual comparison. The balanced position presented in this chapter combines the discrepancy with history, processing indicators, functional impact and persistence despite appropriate instruction, but it remains a matter of professional judgment that has not yet settled into a rule. Two further questions also remain open: the claim that students in whom neither side has been detected form the largest group is a common hypothesis that awaits proof, and no published Saudi regulatory text has been found that either permits or prohibits combining a gifted program with learning disabilities services.

Chapter summary Twice-exceptional learners are gifted and also have a disability. The operational definition specifies who they are, while the consensus definition describes the interaction between the two sides and what these students need. Mutual masking makes their performance look average, so they appear in three groups. The claim that students in whom neither side has been detected form the largest group is a common hypothesis that has yet to be proven. The usual models, such as response to intervention, normative criteria and the “and” rule, may miss them. The debate centers on normative versus intra-individual comparison; the balanced position combines the discrepancy with history, processing indicators, functional impact and persistence despite appropriate instruction. Twice-exceptional learners are identified through a multi-instrument protocol that opens both tracks together and applies the criteria for each side separately. The difference between the General Ability Index and the Cognitive Proficiency Index describes an uneven profile systematically, but it does not diagnose on its own. The team faces three possibilities: giftedness only, giftedness with a disorder, or a disorder only. The question “What happens when the student finds the right challenge?” is a supporting one, to be weighed with other evidence, because symptoms of a disorder may be absent during a preferred activity. Gifted autistic girls may camouflage their traits for years, so early history and home–school discrepancies are given particular weight. We found no published Saudi regulatory text that either permits or prohibits combining a gifted program with learning disabilities services. Glossary of terms Twice-exceptional Twice-exceptional (2e) A student who has high performance potential in one or more domains and, at the same time, one or more disabilities. Masking Giftedness compensating for the disability and the disability depressing the giftedness, so that performance appears average. Normative comparison Comparing a student’s performance with that of same-age peers. Intra-individual comparison Comparing a student’s performance in one domain with the student’s abilities in other domains. Compensatory strategies Methods a student uses to overcome a difficulty, such as memorization or reliance on context, which may conceal it. Dual differentiation Instruction that provides challenge in areas of strength and support in areas of difficulty at the same time. Cognitive Proficiency Index Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI) A Wechsler index calculated from the working memory and processing speed subtests and compared with the General Ability Index to describe an uneven profile. Assessment protocol A set of instruments and procedures planned in advance, each answering a specific question in the assessment. Camouflaging An autistic person’s concealment of their traits by observing and imitating others and memorizing ready-made phrases, at an exhausting cost in effort. Dysgraphia A term used for a difficulty with handwriting or a difficulty with spelling and written expression; its counterpart in the diagnostic manual is specific learning disorder with impairment in written expression. Review questions A specialist wrote in a report: “The student is twice-exceptional because he exceeds the gifted program criteria and has a diagnosis of autism.” Which of the two reference definitions does this judgment rest on? And what does the other definition add to what the report should recommend? (Objective 1) A fifth-grade student in the gifted program has seen her grades decline in reading-heavy subjects, and her teacher attributes this to her being “busy with competitions.” In which of the three groups in Figure 13.2 would you tentatively place her? And what might each side be concealing in the other? (Objective 2) A student has a General Ability Index of 128 and reading fluency of 90, and has received no intervention because he never showed up in screening in t

14 Chapter 14 Fairness in diagnosis A student can be wronged in diagnosis without anyone intending it: a hard-of-hearing child comes close to an autism spectrum disorder diagnosis because no one checked his hearing; another student is nearly diagnosed with intellectual disability because he was tested in a language he has not mastered; and the youngest child in the class has activity that is perfectly expected for his age read as a disorder. In this chapter we move from the individual case to a broader question: how can we tell whether the diagnostic system as a whole is fair, and whether its fairness reaches beyond the single student? Scene from an end-of-year report A special education supervisor in an education directorate reviewed the referral records of the schools in her charge. Three things caught her eye. Boys were referred for behavior roughly four times as often as girls. Students who were not native speakers of Arabic made up twice as large a share of learning disabilities referrals as of the school population. And the schools in remote villages had not referred a single student to the gifted program in three years. She asked herself: do these numbers reflect real differences among students, or do they reflect the way we ourselves work? The fair answer is that both may be true at once. Our aim in this chapter is to show how to tell the two apart. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Calculate the risk index and risk ratio from a school’s data, and explain the limits of the risk ratio when numbers are small. Identify, in a given scenario, the point at which bias entered the diagnostic pathway, and propose a step to limit it. Calculate the representation index and the minimum fair representation in a gifted program, and propose two steps to raise the representation of an underrepresented group. Distinguish, in the description of a student learning in a second language, between conversational fluency and academic proficiency, and specify the evidence needed before referral. Critique the interpretation of a score pattern with the Culture-Language Interpretive Matrix in light of studies that have examined its validity. Name the cognitive bias at work in a given assessment scenario, and propose a strategy to reduce it. Judge whether the evidence is sufficient for a fair decision in a new case, and justify that judgment.

A student can suffer injustice in diagnosis without anyone meaning it to happen, when his hearing goes unchecked, when he is tested in a language he has not mastered, or when activity expected for his age is read as a disorder. Yet fairness is not tested in the individual case alone. Patterns of referral and diagnosis across the schools of an entire education directorate, like those the supervisor noticed in the opening scene, may reveal that certain groups are referred more often, or less often, than others. Judging the fairness of a diagnostic system requires distinguishing disparities in rates from actual bias, knowing the points through which bias enters, and knowing the tools that expose it. We open the chapter by defining what fairness in diagnosis means (Section 14.1), then turn to disproportionality, the ways it is measured and what happens when numbers are small (Section 14.2), and the points through which bias enters, along with its sources within the instrument (Section 14.3). We then address fairness in gifted identification, the representation index and the fair minimum (Section 14.4), followed by language and culture, the Culture-Language Interpretive Matrix and what studies say about its validity (Section 14.5), and assessor biases (Section 14.6). We offer a fairness checklist (Section 14.7) and close with three cases and a school audit (Section 14.8).

Fairness in diagnosis does not mean that every group should appear in special education or gifted programs in equal proportions. Some differences are real: attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, for example, genuinely is more prevalent among boys. Fairness means, rather, that every student has the same chance of being identified if he needs services, and that no student is misdiagnosed because of something unrelated to need: his language, his sex, his family’s poverty, the location of his school, or the expectations of the person assessing him. The “Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing” devote their third chapter to fairness in testing, defining it as the extent to which score interpretations are equally valid for all individuals and groups to whom the instrument is administered. They approach it from four angles: fair treatment of examinees during administration, freedom of measurement from bias, access to the construct the test measures without obstacles unrelated to it, such as the language of the instructions or the format of presentation, and the validity of the interpretation of an individual’s own score (AERA et al., 2014). Diagnostic error runs in two directions, and each carries a cost: Overdiagnosis A student who does not need services is diagnosed: he may be separated from his peers, expectations of him drop, he carries a label that does not fit him, and resources are diverted from those who need them. Underdiagnosis A student who needs services goes unidentified: he struggles for years without understanding or support, is blamed for what lies beyond his control, and loses time when intervention would have done the most good.

search.s: 14.2 Disproportionality and how it is measured
search.t: Disproportionality is present when the share of a group in a diagnostic category or program differs markedly from its expected share. It is measured with two simple indicators: Risk index: the proportion of a group’s members who have been diagnosed or referred, out of the group’s total number. Risk ratio: the risk index of one group divided by the risk index of a comparison group. A value of 1 indicates proportionate representation; a value above 1 indicates overrepresentation, and a value below 1 underrepresentation. U.S. regulations use the risk ratio to determine significant disproportionality at the state and district levels (U.S. Department of Education, 2024). Worked example: behavior referrals in one school 1 The school has 400 boys and 380 girls. Thirty-six boys and 8 girls were referred for behavior. 2 Risk index for boys: 36 ÷ 400 = 9%; for girls: 8 ÷ 380 ≈ 2.1%. 3 Risk ratio for boys compared with girls: 9 ÷ 2.1 ≈ 4.3. 4 In other words, a boy is more than four times as likely as a girl to be referred for behavior. 5 Caution: the figure of 4.3 rests on only 8 girls. Had two more girls been referred (10 girls), the risk ratio would be about 3.4; had two fewer been referred (6 girls), it would be about 5.7. A change of two referrals moves the ratio anywhere between “three times” and “nearly six times.” Boys: 9 in every 100 Risk index 9% Girls: 2 in every 100 Risk index about 2% Figure 14.1: The risk index made visible. Each grid has one hundred dots, each dot representing a student; the shaded dots are those referred for behavior. The risk ratio here is about 4.3. The number raises a question; it does not answer it A high risk ratio does not, on its own, prove bias. Behavior problems may genuinely be more common among boys. The right questions are these: is the difference larger than studies of real differences would lead us to expect? Are boys referred for behaviors that are overlooked in girls? And are internalizing problems in girls, such as anxiety, withdrawal and sadness, missed because they do not disrupt the classroom the way overt behavior does? The literature holds a genuine debate on this point: one large study found that some groups were less likely to be diagnosed than expected once other factors were controlled (Morgan et al., 2015), while other researchers criticized it on the grounds that the method of control itself may conceal bias (Skiba et al., 2016). The lesson is that the numbers mark the beginning of an inquiry and an invitation to complete it. When numbers are small The risk ratio is a fraction whose denominator is the risk index of the comparison group. When only a few members of that group have been referred, the denominator becomes fragile, and a change of one or two cases is enough to make the result jump, as the caution in the previous example showed. When the number is zero, the division cannot be performed at all. For this reason, a risk ratio in a small school, or in a rare category, should be read only alongside the raw counts on which it rests. More useful than a single year’s ratio is to pool data across several years and look at the trend over time. For the specialist: how do U.S. regulations deal with the instability of the ratio? Section §300.647 of the implementing regulations of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) governs how “significant disproportionality” is calculated, and it addresses the problem of small numbers with three tools. The first is a minimum cell size, meaning the number of group members diagnosed or referred, together with a minimum group size ( Minimum n-size ), meaning the group’s total membership. The ratio is not calculated unless both thresholds are met, and the regulation regards a threshold of no more than 10 for the cell and 30 for the group as presumptively reasonable. The second is the alternate risk ratio: when the comparison group in the district falls below these thresholds, the group’s risk index is compared with the risk index of

Many people assume that bias in diagnosis comes from the test. But the test is only one of four points along the way, and bias can enter at any of them: 1 Referral Whom the teacher notices and whom he does not. The disruptive student is referred, the quiet one is forgotten, and the culturally different student has his behavior misread. 2 Instrument Items familiar to one culture and not another, norms that do not represent the student, a language he has not mastered, and a test unsuited to his senses. 3 Interpretation Reading the score without regard to language and opportunity, and looking for what confirms the first hypothesis. 4 Decision A combination rule that excludes particular groups, services not available in every region, and pressure to find the student a placement. Figure 14.2: Four points at which bias enters the diagnostic pathway. A fair instrument alone does not guarantee a fair system. Sources of bias in the instrument Table 14.1: Sources of bias in the instrument and ways of detecting it. Type What it means Example Content bias Items that assume knowledge or experience not equally available to all students A question about snow or a train put to a child who has never seen either, or about vocabulary specific to one region Norm bias A norming sample that does not represent the student Comparing a Saudi student with American norms, or a rural student with urban-only norms Language bias A test that measures ability through a language the student has not mastered A student whose first language is not Arabic is tested on vocabulary and verbal comprehension in Arabic, and his verbal ability score drops because of his weak Arabic Predictive bias The same score predicts different performance in two groups. It is examined statistically by comparing the regression lines in the two groups: the slope of each and its intercept with the axis A test that predicts the success of urban students in a program better than it predicts the success of village students Situational bias Testing conditions affect one group more than others An unfamiliar examiner in a formal setting with a child unused to dealing with strangers Differential item functioning and measurement noninvariance An item on which two groups perform differently even though they are equal in the trait being measured, or an instrument that does not measure the same construct in the same way in the two groups An item on a verbal reasoning scale that is harder for students from one region because it contains a word common in another dialect, even though students from the two regions with equal total scores should perform equally on it The last row of the table differs from the others: rather than describing a type of bias, it describes two standard methods for detecting it . The first is differential item functioning ( Differential item functioning, DIF ). The idea is to compare students from two groups who are equal in ability , rather than comparing the two groups as wholes. If an item is harder for one group even though its members are equal in ability, then for that group the item is measuring something else as well, such as cultural knowledge or a local word. A difference between the two groups’ mean scores on an item does not by itself indicate bias, since it may reflect a real difference in the trait. The second is measurement invariance ( Measurement invariance ), which asks at the level of the whole instrument: is the factor structure the same in both groups? Are the items related to the factors with the same strength? Does the same score signify the same level of the trait? If invariance does not hold, comparing the two groups’ means is not warranted, nor is applying a single cutoff score to both (AERA et al., 2014). The practical question for the practitioner is whether the manual of the instrument he uses reports the results of these analyses for the groups with whom he uses it, such as boys and girls, different regions, and speakers of languages other than

The examples in the preceding sections all concern overrepresentation, where a group appears in special education more often than it should. In gifted programs, the best-known problem runs the other way: underrepresentation . Students from low-income families, from remote schools, and those learning in a second language are usually fewer in these programs than their share of the student body. Nor does the matter stop at the test. Groups differ in the proportions who reach advanced levels of performance in the first place, differences known as excellence gaps ( Excellence gaps ), and these gaps reflect, in large part, differences in opportunity more than in potential (Plucker & Peters, 2016). A program that admits only those who have already reached advanced performance inherits these gaps, then widens them by serving those who were already ahead. The representation index and the fair minimum The risk index and risk ratio apply here as well, but the gifted education literature often relies on two indicators that are easier to read: Representation index ( Representation index ): the group’s share among program students divided by its share among students at the same grade level. A result of 1 means proportionate representation; anything below it means underrepresentation. Equity formula ( Equity formula ), proposed by Donna Ford: it accepts that the two percentages may differ somewhat, since perfect correspondence is unrealistic, but it places a ceiling on the difference. The minimum acceptable representation of a group in the program is its share among students minus 20% of that share, that is, its share among students × 0.8 . Anything below that counts as underrepresentation that calls for review (Ford, 2013). The 20% margin is a practical convention. It spares the program from chasing small differences while obliging it to account for large ones. Worked example: a gifted program in an education directorate 1 Grades three through six in an education directorate enroll 4,000 students, 1,200 of them (30%) in village schools. The gifted program has 200 students, 20 of them (10%) from village schools. 2 Representation index for village students: 10 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.33. Their representation in the program is thus about one third of their share of the student body. 3 Fair minimum under Ford’s formula: 30% × 0.8 = 24%, that is, at least 48 of the 200 students. The shortfall is 28 students. 4 In risk ratio terms: the risk index for village students is 20 ÷ 1,200 ≈ 1.7%, for urban students 180 ÷ 2,800 ≈ 6.4%, and the risk ratio ≈ 0.26. A village student, in other words, is about one quarter as likely as an urban student to be identified as gifted. 5 The next question is “Where are they falling out?” before “How many should we add?” Did nomination or registration reach them? Were they given the test? Did they pass it and then fail to enroll because the program was too far away? Each point calls for a different remedy. Among directorate students In the gifted program 30% 10% Fair minimum 24% 0 10% 20% 30% 40% Share of village school students Figure 14.3: Share of village school students among the directorate’s students and in the gifted program, in the worked example. The dashed line marks the fair minimum under Ford’s formula (30% × 0.8 = 24%). Anything below it, like the second bar, is underrepresentation that calls for review. Where does the shortfall come from? Studies indicate that the shortfall accumulates at points close to those in Figure 14.2, with one more point added after the decision: the service itself. Nomination: when the door to a program is teacher nomination or a family request, who walks through it reflects the teacher’s judgment and the family’s awareness as much as the student’s ability. A large U.S. study found that the likelihood of a student being identified as gifted varied with the background of his teacher, even when students’ test achievement was equal (Grissom & Redding, 2016). In Saudi Arabia, Alfaiz examined the a

The language of conversation and the language of learning One of the most common sources of misdiagnosis is confusing second language learning with disability. Jim Cummins distinguished between two levels of language proficiency: basic interpersonal communicative skills ( Basic Interpersonal Communicative Skills, BICS ), the language of everyday talk and the playground, in which a second language learner reaches fluency close to that of peers in about two years ; and cognitive academic language proficiency ( Cognitive Academic Language Proficiency, CALP ), the language of textbooks, abstract concepts and lengthy instructions, which takes roughly five to seven years to reach the level of native speakers (Cummins, 1981). Basic interpersonal communicative skills About 2 years Cognitive academic language proficiency 5–7 years 0 2 4 6 8 Figure 14.4: Approximate time, in years, that a second language learner needs to approach native-speaking peers, after Cummins (Cummins, 1981). Conversational fluency comes in about two years; academic proficiency between the fifth and seventh year. A student who speaks Arabic fluently at recess after two years may need several more years before he can learn in it as effectively as his classmates. The danger is that a teacher sees a student chatting fluently in Arabic with classmates, then stumbling in reading and science, and concludes that he has a learning disability, when in fact he has not yet attained academic language proficiency. Saudi schools enroll many students from expatriate families whose first language is not Arabic, and these students most closely resemble those on whom the framework was built. These figures have limits that readers should know before using them. First, they are drawn from data on immigrant children learning English in Canada, and they do not carry over unchanged to another language or another education system. Second, it is often suggested that an Arab student who speaks a colloquial dialect encounters in Modern Standard Arabic something akin to a second academic language, since it departs from his dialect in vocabulary and structure. The analogy is reasonable, but it is an inference awaiting research, and it does not justify applying Cummins’s timeframes to that student. Third, the distinction between the two levels has itself drawn theoretical criticism: among other things, that it reduces language proficiency to two poles, and that it can be used to explain a student’s difficulties as a deficit in him rather than in his instruction. Cummins has addressed these criticisms, presenting the distinction as a tool for understanding the difference between fluency and learning, with approximate timeframes (Cummins, 2008). The practical conclusion nonetheless stands: fluency in conversation is not evidence of command of the language of learning . — How can we tell whether the low scores of a linguistically diverse student reflect his ability or his language? Flanagan and colleagues (Flanagan et al., 2013) proposed a method called the Culture-Language Interpretive Matrix (C-LIM). The idea is to classify subtests along two dimensions: how much cultural content they carry, and how much language they demand. The student’s scores are then placed in the cells of the matrix, and the scores in each cell are compared with an expected range for a student whose linguistic and cultural difference from the norming sample is similar to his. A highly different student, such as a recent arrival, is expected to show steeper drops in the high-loading cells than a student who has spent years in schools taught in that language. If scores decline steadily as cultural and linguistic loading increases, and fall within the range expected for such a student , language and culture likely explain the decline. If they fall below the expected range, however, language alone is not a sufficient explanation, and another cause should be sought. The criterion, then, is the size of the graded decline relat

Assessors are human, and the mind sometimes falls back on mental shortcuts in judgment that lead to predictable errors. These errors have long been studied in medicine, where many diagnostic errors were found to stem from the way clinicians think more than from gaps in their knowledge (Croskerry, 2003). The most prominent in our field are the following: Table 14.2: Common assessor biases and how to reduce them. Bias How it shows Example What reduces it Anchoring The first idea governs everything that follows A teacher notices that a student does not turn when his name is called, assumes autism from the outset, and never asks for a hearing check Writing at least three alternative hypotheses before the assessment Confirmation bias Seeking what supports the hypothesis and overlooking what contradicts it Dismissing a parent’s rating because it differs from what the team expected, instead of asking why the two differ Deliberately searching for evidence that contradicts the hypothesis Diagnostic overshadowing Attributing every symptom to a known diagnosis Anxiety in a student with intellectual disability is explained away as “part of his disability” Asking: does the known diagnosis actually explain this symptom? Halo effect, and its negative counterpart, the horn effect One salient trait colors judgment of everything else: a positive one raises it, a negative one lowers it Nominating well-behaved high achievers for giftedness while overlooking a gifted girl who asks endless questions and keeps untidy notebooks Observation tools with specific items, more than one rater, and judging work without knowing whose it is Availability bias Judging by whatever comes most readily to mind A teacher who attended a course on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder begins to see it in every highly active student Returning to the written criteria instead of relying on impressions For the teacher: five minutes before you refer or nominate You are the first point in Figure 14.2, which is why bias either begins with you or ends with you. Before you sign a referral or nomination form, ask yourself: What specific behavior did I see? How often? In which lesson? Write it down as it happened, before any interpretation. If another student in the class had done the same thing, would I refer him? And if this student were a girl rather than a boy, or the reverse, or came from a different family? Who in my class has never once crossed my mind? The quiet student, the newcomer, the one who has not yet mastered Arabic may need referral or nomination more than those who caught my attention. Did I give the student a chance to show what he can do, through an open-ended task or in a form other than writing, before judging him?

These are questions for the team to ask before any diagnostic decision, arranged according to the points in Figure 14.2: Referral Did the student receive sound instruction and adequate support before referral? And was this documented? Referral Was the student’s behavior compared with that of peers of the same age and background? Instrument Were hearing and vision checked? Instrument Was the instrument normed on a sample resembling the student in language and environment? And when was it normed? Instrument Was it administered in the student’s stronger language or through his means of communication? Did he need a nonverbal instrument? Instrument Does the instrument’s manual present evidence that its items are free of differential functioning, and of measurement invariance, for the group to which the student belongs? Interpretation Was the pattern of scores considered alongside their level? Were confidence intervals taken into account? Interpretation Did the team write alternative hypotheses and look for evidence against its first hypothesis? Interpretation Was information gathered from home and school, and was any conflict between them understood? Decision Is the decision rule made public, and does it avoid excluding any particular group without justification? Decision At the program level: are representation rates reviewed every year using raw counts and compared with the fair minimum? Decision Did the family take part in the decision and understand it?

search.s: 14.8 Three cases and a school audit
search.t: Case one: Zain, age 10 Most likely a second language effect The story: Zain arrived with his family two and a half years ago; his first language is Urdu. He speaks Arabic fluently with his classmates but is struggling in reading, science and social studies. His teacher referred him on suspicion of a learning disability. Table 14.3: Evidence in Zain’s case. Source Result What it means Length of time learning Arabic Two and a half years Conversational language mastered; academic language most likely not yet fully developed Direct measure of academic Arabic He read a passage from his grade’s science textbook, answered comprehension questions and defined subject vocabulary. His performance fell clearly below that of his Arabic-speaking classmates and close to that of two classmates who had been learning Arabic for the same length of time His difficulties are within what is expected for someone with his exposure to Arabic Ability test in Arabic Scores declining steadily with linguistic and cultural loading, as in the pattern of Figure 14.5 A pattern consistent with a language effect, but one that cannot by itself distinguish a second language from a language weakness Family interview with an interpreter He reads Urdu well and was a high achiever at his previous school Important information, but it rests on the family’s report alone Reading sample in Urdu, with help from a teacher at the school who speaks it fluently He read a grade-level passage accurately and fluently and summarized what he read Direct, though unstandardized, evidence of sound reading in his first language Dynamic assessment in Arabic reading Rapid improvement after two sessions of training in decoding strategies An initial indicator of learning potential that needs further corroboration Decision: Zain is not diagnosed with a learning disability at this point. A genuine learning disability usually shows itself in both languages, and the direct evidence from the reading sample, beyond what the family reports, indicates that he reads soundly in Urdu. He will receive eight weeks of focused support in academic Arabic, including explicit teaching of subject vocabulary, with weekly measurement of his reading progress compared against that of peers who have been learning Arabic for the same length of time. If he grows as they do, the language explanation is confirmed. If his growth stalls despite the support, his case will be revisited through a more comprehensive evaluation, and the possibility of a learning disability remains open. What evidence could change the decision? If, after the eight weeks of focused support, his growth in Arabic reading remained clearly slower than that of peers with the same length of exposure, or if a closer assessment of his Urdu reading revealed difficulties with accuracy or fluency, the possibility of a learning disability would return to the fore, and the comprehensive evaluation would be completed. Case two: Waad, age 9 Horn effect The story: On a gifted nomination scale, Waad’s teacher rated her academic ability low, writing: “Her handwriting is very poor, and her notebook is a mess.” The program coordinator, however, asked two other teachers to rate Waad’s answers on a problem-solving task after they had been retyped on a computer, without telling them whose work it was. Both placed her among the top 10% of girls in the class. Decision: Waad was referred for gifted assessment. Her case illustrates the negative face of the halo effect, known as the horn effect ( Horn effect ): one conspicuous negative trait, here her handwriting, colored the judgment of her ability as a whole. Rating work without knowing whose it is offers a simple way to curb it. An assessment of her fine motor skills and handwriting was also requested, and for a reason that goes beyond the handwriting itself. The wide gap between her problem-solving ability and her written performance may be a sign of twice-exceptionality : giftedness combined with a writing difficul

The central argument of this chapter is that fairness means an equal chance of being identified for those who need it, freedom from misdiagnosis for those who do not, and valid score interpretation for every group, which runs deeper than equal percentages. It follows that a risk ratio should be treated as a question that calls for verification, read alongside raw counts and across several years, and that bias should be sought at its four points of entry: referral, instrument, interpretation and decision. It follows, too, that conversational language should not be confused with academic language, that the pattern of scores across cultural and linguistic loading should be read as a hypothesis requiring independent evidence, and that assessor biases should be curbed through alternative hypotheses, multiple raters and a return to the criteria. Some questions in this chapter nonetheless remain open. Cummins’s time frames are estimates drawn from a different context; the Culture-Language Interpretive Matrix discriminates poorly between second language learning and language impairment; and part of the representation gap in gifted programs arises before identification itself, so identification tools alone cannot close it. In the Saudi context, optional registration for the national test makes the family’s decision the first gate, and no data are published that would allow comparison across regions or between boys’ and girls’ programs, so system-level monitoring of fairness remains limited by whatever data are available.

Chapter summary Fairness means an equal chance of being identified for those who need it, freedom from misdiagnosis for those who do not, and valid score interpretation for every group; it runs deeper than equal percentages. The risk ratio is a simple tool for detecting disproportionality, but it raises a question rather than proving bias, and it becomes unstable when numbers are small, so it is read alongside raw counts and across several years. Bias enters at four points: referral, instrument, interpretation and decision. Instrument bias is detected statistically through analyses of differential item functioning and measurement invariance. In gifted programs, underrepresentation is the dominant problem. The representation index and the fair minimum detect it, and universal screening and local norms reduce it, but part of the gap arises before identification. In the Saudi context, optional registration for the national test makes the family’s decision the first gate, and no data are published that would allow comparison across regions or between boys’ and girls’ programs. Conversational language is acquired much faster than academic language, and confusing the two is a common source of misdiagnosis. Cummins’s time frames are estimates drawn from a different context. The pattern of scores across cultural and linguistic loading is more telling than their level, but the Culture-Language Interpretive Matrix discriminates poorly between second language learning and language impairment, so the pattern it shows is a hypothesis that needs independent evidence. Assessor biases are to be expected; they are reduced by alternative hypotheses, rating work without knowing whose it is, multiple raters and a return to the criteria. Glossary of terms Disproportionality A clear difference between a group’s share of a category or program and its expected share. Risk index The number of students in a group who have been diagnosed, divided by the group’s total number. Risk ratio The risk index of one group divided by the risk index of a comparison group. Representation index A group’s share among program students divided by its share among all students; a value of 1 indicates proportionate representation. Equity formula A rule that sets the minimum acceptable representation of a group in a gifted program at its share among students multiplied by 0.8. Excellence gaps Differences between groups in the proportions of students who reach advanced levels of performance. Universal screening Administering an initial instrument to all students in a grade or school level, rather than waiting for nomination or a family request. Differential item functioning Differential item functioning (DIF) A difference in two groups’ performance on an item among individuals of equal standing on the ability being measured, indicating that the item measures something else besides that ability. Measurement invariance The property of a scale measuring the same construct in the same way in two groups, so that their scores can be compared and a single cut-off score applied to both. Basic Interpersonal Communicative Skills (BICS) The language of everyday conversation, in which a second language learner reaches fluency close to that of peers in about two years. Cognitive Academic Language Proficiency (CALP) The language of learning and abstract concepts, which takes roughly five to seven years to develop. Culture-Language Interpretive Matrix (C-LIM) A method for interpreting the pattern of scores according to their cultural loading and linguistic demands, by comparing them with the range expected for students whose exposure to the language resembles the student’s own. Confirmation bias Seeking evidence that supports a hypothesis while overlooking evidence that contradicts it. Anchoring Allowing the first idea that occurs to the assessor to govern the interpretation of everything that follows.
