15 Chapter 15 From diagnosis to decision A diagnosis is worth what follows from it: a report the family can take in, a plan built on its findings, goals against which progress is measured, and periodic review that asks whether the judgment still holds and whether the services still fit. In this chapter we examine the links that connect a diagnostic judgment to an educational decision. Scene from a meeting room Mazen's father and mother sat facing a thirty-page report. His mother leafed through it quickly: tables, standard scores, percentile ranks, and terms such as “phonological processing” and “rapid automatized naming.” On the last page was a single line: “He meets the criteria for specific learning disorder in reading.” His father looked up and asked two questions: “Does this mean something is wrong with our son?” And then: “So what do we do now?” The report was accurate, yet it did not answer the two questions the family had come with. In this chapter we look closely at the distance between a correct finding and a useful decision, and at ways of bridging it. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Classify a set of decisions as a diagnostic judgment, an eligibility decision or a service decision, and justify each classification with an example. Reorganize a test-by-test report around the referral question, and phrase its findings in language parents can understand. Turn a general recommendation into a specific one that states what will be done, who will do it, how much and how often, and how success will be judged. Apply the steps of a feedback meeting in a role-play with a family. Build a chain linking an assessment finding to a need, a measurable goal, a service and a method of progress monitoring in the individualized education program (IEP). Calculate a goal from the baseline and the rate of growth, and decide from a given progress graph whether the intervention should be changed, taking the number of data points into account. Choose the appropriate type of decision for a gifted student (enrichment, single-subject acceleration, whole-grade acceleration or a domain-specific program), specify the evidence it requires, and write a measurable goal for the student. Compare what Saudi regulations stipulate on eligibility, the plan, reevaluation and family rights with what US law stipulates, and identify what the published documents leave unaddressed. Judge whether the evidence in a new case is sufficient for reevaluation or exit from services, and justify that judgment.

The team's task extends beyond the diagnostic judgment, because the value of a diagnosis lies in what follows from it. A report crowded with tables and terminology that ends with a single line about criteria, like Mazen's report in the opening scene, may be technically sound and still fail to answer the family's question: What does this mean for our son, and what will we do? Moving from diagnosis to decision requires distinguishing among the diagnostic judgment, the eligibility decision and the service decision; writing a report organized around the referral question; building a plan whose goals can be measured; and conducting periodic review that asks whether the judgment is still correct and whether the services are still appropriate. We open the chapter with the eligibility decision and what is actually decided in it (Section 15.1), then turn to writing the report and its recommendations, with a sample report (Section 15.2); the meeting with the family (Section 15.3); and the move from the report to the individualized education program, including how to write measurable goals (Section 15.4). We then address progress monitoring, reevaluation and exit from services (Section 15.5); decisions for gifted learners, from identification to placement (Section 15.6); the regulatory framework in Saudi Arabia compared with US law (Section 15.7); and ethics and the student's voice (Section 15.8). We apply all of this to three cases (Section 15.9) and close with principles drawn from the book as a whole (Section 15.10).

search.s: 15.1 The eligibility decision: what is actually being decided?
search.t: At the end of an assessment, three distinct decisions are made, and they are often confused: The diagnostic judgment: Does the student meet the criteria for a category, such as specific learning disorder, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder or giftedness? (The chapters of Part Three discuss the criteria for these categories in detail.) The eligibility decision (Eligibility): Is the student entitled to special education services or to a gifted program under the regulations of the agency that provides them? It usually requires two conditions: the presence of the category, and the student's resulting need for specially designed instruction. In Saudi Arabia, this decision is made by the school's assessment and diagnosis team, which, according to the Special Education Organizational Guide, includes the school principal, the vice principal for student affairs, the special education teacher, the general education teacher, the student counselor or social worker, specialists relevant to the category, and the student's parent or guardian where possible (Ministry of Education, 1436 AH [Arabic]). Saudi regulations define a student with a disability as one whose impairment reaches “the extent that requires the provision of special education services” (Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif], 1422 AH [Arabic]), so need is built into the definition itself. The same logic applies in US law, namely the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), reauthorized in 2004 as the Individuals with Disabilities Education Improvement Act: the presence of a disability must be accompanied by the student's need, because of it, for special education (Code of Federal Regulations, 34 C.F.R. §300.8; Yell, 2019). The service decision: What exactly will the student receive, where, how much, and how will we know it is helping? This decision rests on the details of the student's profile more than on the name of the category. A student may be diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder while succeeding in class and needing only minor accommodations. Another may meet the criteria for no category at all yet need Tier 2 support within response to intervention (RTI), a model that provides students with graduated support across tiers that grow more intensive as their response diminishes. The label does not determine the service: two students diagnosed with the same specific learning disorder may need entirely different plans. Key idea The question with which an assessment begins, “Does the student have X?”, must end with another: “What does the student need, and how will we know that what we provide is helping?” An assessment that answers only the first has done only half its job.

The report is what remains of the assessment. It will be read by the parents, the teacher, the planning team, and perhaps another specialist years later. Most weak reports get the numbers right; they fall short in three ways: they are organized by test rather than by question, they are written in professional jargon, and they end with general recommendations that no one knows how to carry out (Harvey, 2006; Schneider et al., 2018). Organize the report around the question A test-by-test report presents each instrument in its own section: the Wechsler results, then the achievement test results, then the behavior rating scale, leaving readers to pull the threads together themselves. A question-driven report, by contrast, begins with the referral question and gathers evidence from all sources under each sub-question, as Figure 15.1 illustrates. Organized by test Student information and reason for referral Wechsler results: a table of ten indexes with a description of each Achievement test results: a table of fifteen subtests Phonological processing test results: a table Teacher rating scale: a table Summary: criteria are met Recommendations: remedial instruction and follow-up Organized around the question Why does Mazen struggle with reading despite good comprehension? What are his strengths? Oral comprehension and reasoning: from testing, the teacher and the family Where does the difficulty lie? Decoding and fluency: from the achievement test, reading of classroom texts and error analysis What explains it? Weak phonological awareness and rapid naming What was ruled out? Hearing, vision, intellectual disability and limited opportunity to learn What does this mean? The judgment and the degree of confidence in it What do we do? Specific recommendations tied to each finding Figure 15.1: Two structures for the same report. On the left, the instruments are presented one after another; on the right, evidence from all sources is gathered under the questions the reader cares about. Full score tables move to an appendix at the end of the report. Principles of clear writing Write for the least specialized reader: If the parents understand the report, the specialist will too; the reverse does not hold. Describe the behavior before naming the term: “He has difficulty linking letters to their sounds, confusing letters that sound alike, such as sīn and ṣād, and dropping a syllable from long words” is clearer than “weakness in phonological processing” (that is, the processing of speech sounds). If you need the term, explain it the first time it appears. Present numbers with their meaning: Pair “his standard score is 76” with what it means: “he performs below roughly 95% of peers his age.” This is what the percentile rank expresses: the percentage of the student's age peers in the norming sample who scored lower than he did. A percentile rank of 84 means he outperformed 84% of them, and a standard score of 76 corresponds to a percentile rank of about 5. Report the confidence interval as well, that is, the range within which the student's true score most likely falls, since every score carries some measurement error. Begin with strengths: Strengths are an integral part of the picture, and they are often the key to the plan. Separate what was observed from what was inferred: “I observed that he left the task four times in ten minutes” is an observation. “The task appeared to be above his level” is an inference. Both are useful, provided the reader can tell one from the other. State the limits of the assessment: If the norms were developed elsewhere, if the student was ill on the day of testing, or if the assessment was conducted in the student's second language, say so and note its likely effect. Table 15.1: Statements from diagnostic reports in professional language, rephrased in language parents and teachers can understand. In professional language In language everyone can understand He obtained a composite score of 72 on the Working Memory Index

This may be the first time the family hears the word “disability” or “disorder” attached to their child's name. What is said in this meeting, and how it is said, stays with them for years. The task is to present the findings honestly, clearly and compassionately all at once, without softening them to the point that they are lost. Start with what they know Ask: What have you noticed? What worries you? Let the conversation build on their observations. “You mentioned that he avoids homework. Is that true for every subject?” Present strengths first With specific examples from the student himself. “His explanation of how bees work in the hive was more precise than that of many of his classmates.” Explain the difficulty and the judgment In plain language, then the name if there is one, with what it means and what it does not mean. “This does not mean he is lazy or less intelligent.” Pause and listen Leave time for silence, questions and feelings. Do not move on to the plan before they are ready. “What is the first thing that comes to mind for you right now?” Move to the next step What will happen, when, what their role is, and whom to contact. “We will meet in two weeks to write the plan together.” Figure 15.2: Five steps for a feedback meeting. Beneath each step is a sentence that might be said during it. The parents are given a copy of the report, ideally early enough before the meeting to read it, or a one-page summary in plain language. For the teacher: reactions to expect Denial: “He's smart; he just doesn't want to study.” Do not argue. Return to the shared evidence: samples of his work, his progress graph, and what the parents themselves have observed. Guilt: “We should have noticed long ago.” Explain that many of these difficulties surface only with the demands of school, and that identifying them now is better than identifying them later. Relief: Some families feel relieved that the difficulty has a name and an explanation, after years of blaming the child or themselves. This, too, is a legitimate reaction. Fear of stigma: “Will this be written in his file?” Answer honestly about who will have access to the report and about their rights in this regard.

search.s: 15.4 From the report to the individualized education program
search.t: The individualized education program (IEP) is the document that turns assessment findings into instruction. Its components are set by each country's regulations. In Saudi Arabia, the Regulations for Special Education Institutes and Programs specify eight components and make it one of the plan's foundations that “the family must participate in preparing, implementing, evaluating and following up the plan” (Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif], 1422 AH [Arabic], Articles 83–85). Table 15.4 sets these alongside the components of the plan under US law (34 C.F.R. §300.320). Table 15.4: Components of the individualized education program in the Saudi Regulations and their counterparts in US law. Component in the Regulations (1422 AH) Counterpart in US law (a) Description of the present level of performance: strengths and areas of need Present levels of academic achievement and functional performance, and how the disability affects the student's involvement and progress in the general curriculum (b) Long-term and short-term goals, “provided that they are written in behavioral, measurable terms” Measurable annual goals. Short-term objectives or benchmarks are required only for students assessed on alternate assessments aligned to alternate achievement standards (§300.320(a)(2)(ii)) (c) Educational services and related services Special education, related services and accommodations, and any supports needed for school personnel (d) Start and end of services Projected start date of services, and their frequency, location and duration (e) Appropriate educational placement options A statement of the extent to which the student will not participate with peers in the general education class, with an explanation (f) Objective criteria for measuring performance, and procedures and periodic schedules for evaluating the plan (daily, weekly, monthly or annual) How progress toward annual goals will be measured, and when the family will be informed of it (g) Identification of those participating in implementing the plan Members of the IEP team are specified in a separate section and include the parents and, when appropriate, the student (§300.321) (h) Identification of instructional materials No separate counterpart, although the team must consider the student's need for assistive technology No corresponding component among the eight The student's participation in statewide assessments and the accommodations provided in them, and transition services beyond school beginning no later than the first plan in effect when the student turns sixteen, or earlier if the team deems it appropriate (§300.320(b)) The comparison reveals a difference worth noting: the Saudi Regulations require short-term objectives for every student, whereas US law, since the 2004 amendments, has required only annual goals and limited short-term objectives to a narrow group. A reader who adopts an American IEP template may therefore omit a component required under their own system. A good assessment feeds every one of these components. The following chain is what links the report to the plan. If any link breaks, the assessment becomes a document in a file, and the plan becomes a set of goals with no grounding. Link 1 Finding Mazen reads 28 words correct per minute from a grade-level passage, and most of his errors involve letters that look and sound alike. Link 2 Need He needs to master letter–sound correspondence and to have enough practice to build fluency. Link 3 Goal By the end of the second semester, he will read 60 words correct per minute from a grade-level passage on three consecutive measurements. Link 4 Service and accommodation Structured phonics instruction, 30 minutes daily, and test questions read aloud to him in science. Link 5 Progress monitoring Weekly fluency measurement with a grade-level passage, graphed and reviewed every four weeks. search.s: 15.5 Progress monitoring, reevaluation and exit from services
search.t: Progress monitoring A plan is a hypothesis: we hypothesize that this service will bring the student to this goal. Repeated measurement is what tests the hypothesis. Among its common tools is curriculum-based measurement (CBM), a brief, repeated measure of a basic skill using material from the curriculum itself, such as the number of words a student reads correctly in one minute (Deno, 2003; Chapter 4 discusses it in detail). One common decision rule is the consecutive data-point rule: if four consecutive points fall below the aimline, the intervention is changed; if four consecutive points fall above it, the goal is raised. A systematic review of decision rules in reading fluency measurement, however, found that consecutive data-point rules are of low reliability when used alone, because a single measurement fluctuates with the difficulty of the passage and the day of testing. They are therefore supplemented by the trend line ( Trend line ) rule: the line of best fit is drawn through the student's data points, and its slope is compared with that of the aimline. The slope estimate cannot be trusted until enough measurements have accumulated, usually over six to ten weeks or more, depending on the quality of the passages and their equivalence in difficulty (Ardoin et al., 2013). Here the slope behaves like a score: a slope is a range of plausible values . A slope calculated from five fluctuating measurements may in reality be much larger or much smaller than it appears, and judging it “insufficient” requires more data or other evidence. In Saudi schools, a recent study described teachers applying practices close to the response to intervention model, but in a way that was “largely informal,” lacking systematic progress monitoring, diagnostic tools and regulatory guidance (Almulla & Mahama, 2026). In another study, learning disabilities teachers cited lack of data, limited time and the absence of formal adoption of the model among the barriers to implementation (Altheiabi et al., 2025). Without repeated data, the plan comes to be judged by the teacher's impression at the end of the year. 0 20 40 60 80 0 5 10 15 20 Weeks Words correct per minute Initial intervention Intervention after modification Goal: 60 Baseline: 28 Aimline Figure 15.4: Mazen's progress graph with hypothetical values. The square represents the baseline, the dashed line the aimline (Aimline), and the star the goal. In the first eight weeks, all data points fell below the aimline, and their slope was clearly lower than that of the aimline, so the team modified the intervention: it increased the time and added repeated reading practice. Eight measurements are usually enough to judge the slope, whereas four alone are not. After the modification, the slope of the progress line grew steeper, and the points approached the aimline and then rose above it. The decision here was not “Mazen is not learning” but “this intervention is not enough for Mazen.” Reevaluation A diagnosis is a judgment tied to the moment it is made. Children grow, intervention has effects, and instruments improve. For this reason, most systems require reevaluation. In Saudi Arabia, the Special Education Organizational Guide states that “students with disabilities must be rediagnosed no less than 6 months and no more than 18 months after the initial diagnosis,” and it permits further reassessment and rediagnosis later “if the need arises” (Ministry of Education, 1436 AH [Arabic]). We found no fixed periodic schedule in it beyond the first rediagnosis. The Regulations add a right for the family: “rediagnosis of the pupil if the family considers that he was not placed in the appropriate program based on his previous diagnosis, should it request this” (Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif], 1422 AH [Arabic], Article 76). Under US law, by contrast, reevaluation takes place at least once every three years unless the family and the school agree it is unnecessary, no more than once a year unless both agree, a

search.s: 15.6 Decisions for gifted learners: from identification to placement
search.t: Most of this chapter so far has been built on the disability model: a category, a need, and a plan that addresses a deficit. Yet the value of a judgment of giftedness, too, depends on the service decision that follows it, and the question is essentially the same: What does this student need, and how will we know that what we provide fits? The label “gifted” does not determine the service any more than a disability label does. Of two students classified as gifted, one may need acceleration in mathematics and the other a program in creative writing. A growing strand of the literature therefore calls for asking whether the service matches the student's need in a particular domain before asking about the label (Peters et al., 2014; Worrell et al., 2019). Types of decisions and the evidence each requires Table 15.6: Types of decisions for gifted learners, the evidence each decision requires, and what to ask before making it. Decision What it means Evidence required What to ask before deciding Enrichment Broadening and deepening the curriculum without changing the student's grade or pace of progress, either within the classroom or in a separate program Ability or interest that exceeds what the classroom offers: an ability measure, teacher ratings, and the student's products Is the enrichment tied to the student's area of strength, or is it a general activity suitable for any student? Subject acceleration The student studies a single subject using a higher grade's curriculum or alongside a higher grade, while remaining with his own grade for all other subjects Advanced achievement in that same subject: above-level testing showing that the ceiling is masking the student's ability, followed by a test on the higher grade's curriculum showing what he already knows of it and what he does not, so that only the unknown material is taught Can his timetable be arranged? And who will teach him the following year so that he does not repeat what he has already mastered? Whole-grade acceleration Skipping an entire grade, or early entrance High general ability, advanced achievement in more than one subject, social and emotional maturity, and the student's own wish together with the support of the family and teachers. A structured tool such as the Iowa Acceleration Scale is used How does the student himself see it? How will the new class receive him? And who will follow up with him after the move? Talent-domain program A program specialized in a particular domain, such as science, mathematics, scientific research, or the arts Evidence from the domain itself (a test, a product, or a performance in it) added to the overall score Does the admission criterion measure what the program actually offers? Exit from the program or change of service Ending a student's enrollment in a program, or moving him to another service Performance data from the program covering at least one semester after the service has been modified, and an assessment that rules out an undetected learning disability or a temporary circumstance, with the reason documented Does the problem lie in the student, or in how well the program fits him? And do the student and his family know when and how he can return? The acceleration decision is among the most thoroughly studied decisions in gifted education, and among the least used. The report A Nation Empowered summarized decades of research and concluded that acceleration is one of the most effective options available for academically advanced students; that accelerated students generally achieve at least as well as their older peers; that the evidence shows, on average, no social or emotional harm from it; and that the greatest obstacle to it is the beliefs of educators, which run contrary to the research findings (Assouline et al., 2015). This does not mean that acceleration suits every gifted student. The Iowa Acceleration Scale ( Iowa Acceleration Scale ) was therefore developed to guide the team in whole-grade acceleration decisions

search.s: 15.7 The regulatory framework in Saudi Arabia compared with US law
search.t: So far this chapter has presented general principles of eligibility, planning, and reevaluation. The procedures binding on the school and the family, however, are set by each country's own regulations. In this section we present what we found in the published Saudi documents, and we place US law in a parallel column for comparison, since it is among the most detailed systems and among the most prominent in the literature (Yell, 2019). The presentation rests on four Saudi documents: the Regulations for Special Education Institutes and Programs, issued by the Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif] in 1422 AH; the Special Education Organizational Guide, issued by the Ministry of Education in its first edition for the 1436–1437 AH school year, which names the Regulations among its foundations; the Law on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, issued by Royal Decree No. (M/27) dated 11/2/1445 AH, which replaced the Disability Welfare Law of 1421 AH (Article 32); and the Personal Data Protection Law. At the time of writing we found no published edition of the Organizational Guide more recent than the first, so readers should verify which edition is in force at the time they consult it. Table 15.7: Principles of eligibility, planning, and family rights in the Saudi regulations, and their counterparts in US law. Sources: the Regulations (Ministry of Education [Al-Ma'arif], 1422 AH [Arabic]), the Organizational Guide (Ministry of Education, 1436 AH [Arabic]), the Law on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (1445 AH), and the Personal Data Protection Law (1443 AH); and 34 C.F.R. pt. 300. Principle In the Saudi regulations In US law (34 C.F.R. pt. 300) Who determines eligibility The assessment and diagnosis team: the school principal, the vice principal for student affairs, the special education teacher, the general education teacher, the student counselor or social worker, specialists according to the category, the physician or nurse where available, and the parent or guardian where possible (Organizational Guide). In the Regulations: the relevant special education teacher, the behavioral training teacher (psychologist), the parent or guardian, and anyone whose participation the case requires (Article 81) A team that includes the parents and qualified professionals (§300.306(a)(1)) Assessment requirements “Not relying solely on the results of a single measure,” using “the tools and measures approved by the Ministry of Education,” administered and interpreted by “qualified specialists” (Organizational Guide), with tests that are “appropriate to the child's environment” (Regulations, Article 80) No single procedure is used as the sole criterion; tools are valid for the purposes for which they are used and are administered by trained personnel (§300.304) Informed consent Written consent from the parent or guardian after formal notification, with a response due within a period “not exceeding (14) days from the date of the written notification”; if no response is received, “this is considered permission granting consent” (Organizational Guide; the Regulations say “within two weeks,” Article 80). The parent's permission is sought “for the purpose of diagnosis, program preparation, and approval of any modifications” (Article 76) Informed written consent before the initial evaluation, and separate consent before services begin. Silence does not count as consent, except for reevaluation when the school can show that it made reasonable efforts and the parents did not respond (§300.300) Participation The family is invited “to take part in diagnosis, program preparation, and evaluation” (Article 76); the parent or guardian is a member of the assessment team (Article 81); and “the family must participate in preparing, implementing, evaluating, and monitoring the plan” (Articles 83–85) The right to attend eligibility and plan meetings and to participate meaningfully in the decision (§300.322) Access and explanation The parent or guardian is enabled

The following principles are established in the professional codes for assessors, among them the standards of the National Association of School Psychologists (National Association of School Psychologists [NASP], 2020) and the Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct of the American Psychological Association (American Psychological Association [APA], 2017). In essence they are general principles applicable to any system. In Saudi Arabia, the Organizational Guide requires that tools be administered and interpreted “by qualified specialists” (Ministry of Education, 1436 AH [Arabic]), and psychologists practicing in the health sector are subject to professional classification and licensure by the Saudi Commission for Health Specialties, including a licensing examination whose content covers psychological assessment and diagnosis (Saudi Commission for Health Specialties, 2024 [Arabic]). We found no published text specifying the levels of qualification required to administer each category of standardized tests. Ethics for the assessor (NASP, 2020; APA, 2017) Boundaries of competence: Assessors do not administer a tool they have not been trained on, nor do they issue a judgment in an area outside their specialty. Referral to another specialist is a sign of competence. Test security and the right of access: Items from standardized tests are not copied, nor are they given to the family or the teacher for practice, because doing so destroys their validity for that student and for others. This is why no actual items appear in this book. Test security, however, does not justify withholding results from the family: the family has the right to know what was measured, what the result was, and what it means, even if it does not see the items themselves. Understood consent: Consent given through silence, or through a signature on a form that was never explained, is not informed consent in the professional sense. Whatever may suffice from a regulatory standpoint, the assessor's duty is to make sure the family understands what will happen and why. No pressure on the outcome: A judgment is neither made harsher nor softened so that a student will receive a service or be denied one, or because the school wants a certain number. The judgment follows the evidence. Independence and conflicts of interest: If some party asks for a particular result, the assessor's duty is to write what was found and to make clear the limits of what is known. Assessors also disclose any interest that might influence their judgment, such as assessing a student at a center they own and then recommending its services. The student's voice It is often forgotten that a diagnosis belongs to someone. A student who understands his own profile (what he does well, what he finds hard, and what helps him) is better able to ask for what he needs and less likely to explain his difficulty by deciding that he is “stupid.” Students are involved in a way that fits their age: a young child hears a simple explanation of his strengths and of what will help him, an older child attends part of the plan meeting, and an adolescent takes part in writing his own goals. Under US law, the student is invited to the plan meeting whenever postsecondary goals are discussed, beginning no later than the first plan to be in effect when the student turns sixteen, or earlier if the team sees fit (34 C.F.R. §300.321(b), §300.320(b)). Among the eight plan elements in the Saudi Regulations, we found no explicit provision for the student's own participation, although the element “identifying the participants” is broad enough to accommodate it. Adolescents moving from one school level to the next need this participation more than any other students, as the case of Tamim in the next section shows.

All three cases are hypothetical, written for teaching purposes, and their figures are illustrative. Case 1: Mazen, 8 years 6 months From report to plan The story: Mazen is the student from the opening scene, and his full report was presented in Section 15.2: he understands what is read to him and explains his ideas well orally, but he has struggled with reading since first grade. After the first meeting, at which his parents did not understand the report, the specialist went over it with them again. She began by asking them what they had noticed, then read them what the teacher had written about his explanation of how bees work in the hive, and then explained the difficulty in a single sentence: “Mazen understands well, but in his mind the letters don't link to their sounds quickly enough, so reading tires him out. This has a name, and there is teaching that helps with it.” The team then wrote the following plan together with the family. Table 15.9: Mazen's individualized education program. Plan element What was written Present level Strengths: oral comprehension and reasoning in the average range, and clear intellectual curiosity. Needs: reads 28 words correct per minute in grade-level text, whereas his schoolmates read about 70. Avoids reading aloud and complains of fatigue. Long-term goal Will read 60 words correct per minute in grade-level text, on three consecutive measurements, by the end of the second semester. Short-term goals (1) Will read 44 words correct per minute in grade-level text by the end of week 10. (2) Will read two-syllable words containing letters that are similar in sound or in shape with 90% accuracy, on a list of twenty words, by the end of week 8. Service and setting Structured phonics instruction with the learning disabilities teacher in the resource room, 30 minutes daily; he remains in his regular class for the rest of the day. Accommodations Questions are read aloud to him in science and social studies. He is not asked to read aloud in front of the class without preparation. Progress monitoring Weekly fluency measurement, review of the graph every four weeks, and a graph sent to the family every two weeks. Participants The learning disabilities teacher, the classroom teacher, the parents, and Mazen himself, through a simple explanation of his plan. What we learned: The same report, with the same numbers, became useful once it was organized around the family's question and led to goals that could be judged. We saw in Figure 15.4 how progress monitoring led to a change in the intervention rather than to blaming Mazen. What evidence could change the decision? If, after the adjustment, the slope of his trend line remained clearly below the slope of the aimline across eight or more measurements, the team would review the intensity and type of service and reconsider the picture of the difficulty itself. If his oral comprehension proved to weaken as the language demands of later grades increased, the assessment would be broadened to oral language, as happened in Tamim's case. Case 2: Tamim, 14 years 9 months, grade 9 Reevaluation changes the picture The story: Tamim was diagnosed in fourth grade with specific learning disorder in reading: he struggled with decoding, and his nonverbal ability was in the average range. Rediagnosis a year later confirmed his continued eligibility, and he received resource room services for five years; the decoding goals in his plan were met two years ago. In the second semester of ninth grade, before his move to secondary school, his parents requested a reevaluation: he was struggling in science and social studies and said, “I read the whole page, and I don't know what it said.” The special education teacher requested it as well, because he no longer knew what the service was offering Tamim now that he had mastered decoding. Rather than simply renewing eligibility, the team asked the question afresh and added to the assessment what had not been asked the first time: listen

search.s: 15.10 Principles to take with you from this book
search.t: Across this book we have covered many categories, a variety of tools, and numerous cases. Even if the names of instruments and the numbers in the criteria fade from memory, these are the principles we hope will endure: No single measure settles the question Judgment rests on converging evidence from multiple sources, tools, and settings. A score is a range, not a point Every score carries measurement error, and a cutoff is a wide zone. Rule out before you rule in Check hearing, vision, language, and opportunities to learn before attributing a difficulty to the student. Functional impact is a requirement A low score is not enough without a real effect on the student's life and learning. Differential diagnosis is the heart of the work Alongside the question “Are the criteria met?” comes the question “What is the best explanation?” Giftedness and difficulty can coexist Look at the student in comparison with peers and in comparison with himself. A tool is a product of its culture Norms, items, and language carry assumptions, and fairness needs someone to ask about them. The family is a source and a partner Its knowledge of the child is evidence, and its decision is part of the decision. Diagnosis serves instruction Its value lies in the measurable goals and services that change after it. Every judgment is provisional The child grows, the evidence is renewed, and the judgment is revisited.

The central argument we have sought to develop in this chapter is that a diagnosis is measured by what follows from it, and that it is the student's profile, more than the label, that determines the service. A connected chain follows from this: a report organized around the referral question, describing behavior before terminology and presenting numbers with their meaning; recommendations that specify what is to be done, by whom, to what extent, and how success will be recognized; and an individualized education program that moves from finding to need to goal to service to measurement. The plan is a hypothesis tested by repeated measurement: if the student does not progress, the intervention is changed and the student is not blamed. Reevaluation, in turn, is a new question about the student's picture now, one that goes beyond renewing eligibility. The same logic applies to gifted students: each placement decision has its own evidence, and no gifted student should be removed from a program without a search for the cause of the decline. Within the Saudi regulatory framework, however, there remain issues for which we found no published text, such as the right to an independent evaluation and criteria for continuation in and exit from gifted programs; in these matters judgment rests on professional discretion until they are settled by regulation. The student, for his part, retains a right to understand his own profile and to take part in the decision about him, a right that grows in importance at transitions between school levels and a reminder that the purpose of all assessment is a decision that serves the student at its center.

Chapter summary The diagnostic judgment, the eligibility decision, and the service decision are three different decisions. It is the profile, more than the label, that determines the service. In Saudi Arabia, the eligibility decision is made by the school's assessment and diagnosis team. A useful report is organized around the referral question, begins with strengths, describes behavior before terminology, presents numbers with their meaning, states its own limitations, and places tables in an appendix. A good recommendation specifies what is to be done, by whom, to what extent, and how success will be recognized, and it is tied to a finding in the report. The feedback meeting with the family begins with what the family knows, presents strengths, explains the judgment clearly, and leaves time for listening before moving on to the plan. A chain running from finding to need to goal to service to measurement links assessment to the individualized education program. The Saudi Regulations specify eight elements for the plan, including long-term and short-term goals. The plan is a hypothesis tested by repeated measurement. Consecutive data-point rules are complemented by the trend line, and a slope is a range that requires enough data points. Lack of progress calls for changing the intervention rather than blaming the student. Reevaluation is a new question about the student's picture now, going beyond renewal of eligibility. The Organizational Guide sets the first reevaluation at six to eighteen months after diagnosis. Exit from services is a decision that requires assessment and planning. Decisions for gifted students take several forms (enrichment, subject acceleration, whole-grade acceleration, and talent-domain programs), each with its own evidence. Gifted students have goals that measure growth beyond their grade level, and they are not removed from a program without a search for the cause of their decline. A twice-exceptional student has a single plan with two tracks. Under the Saudi regulations, the family has rights to consent, participation, access, confidentiality, and requesting rediagnosis, and its silence for fourteen days counts as consent. We found no published provision for the right to an independent evaluation, nor for criteria for continuation in and exit from gifted programs. Students have a right to understand their own files and to take part in the decisions made about them, and this right matters all the more at transitions between school levels. Glossary of terms Eligibility determination The decision on whether a student is entitled to services; it usually requires both a qualifying category and a need for specially designed instruction. Assessment and diagnosis team The school team that determines eligibility under the Saudi regulations; it includes members from school administration, special education, general education and counseling, along with relevant specialists and the parent or guardian. Individualized Education Program (IEP) A document that sets out the student’s present level, goals, services and accommodations, and how progress will be measured. Present levels of performance A description of what the student can do now, with both strengths and areas of need; it is the starting point for writing goals. Measurable goal A goal that specifies the behavior, the conditions, the criterion and the time frame, so that one can judge whether it has been met. Baseline The level of performance before intervention, usually measured three times, with the median taken. Aimline A line on the progress graph connecting the baseline to the goal, against which data points are compared. Trend line The line of best fit through a student’s data points on the progress graph; its slope is compared with the slope of the aimline. Decision rule A rule agreed upon in advance for changing the intervention or the goal, such as four consecutive data points below the aimline, or a trend-line slope lower than the aimline slope. R

A Appendix A Guide to instruments A concise reference guide to the instruments presented in this book (54 tools and procedures), grouped by purpose, with a pointer to where each is discussed in the chapters. Before using this guide This appendix brings together the instruments presented in the book's instrument profiles and in its tables of instruments and their Arabic versions, arranged in eight tables by purpose. For each instrument it records only what the book itself reports: purpose, age range, examiner qualification level and the status of its Arabic version, followed by the chapter in which it is presented. Age ranges, qualification levels and Arabic versions are all given as they stood when the book was prepared; they change as new editions, new Arabic standardizations and new publisher requirements appear, so the publisher and the instrument's own manual should be consulted before any professional use. This guide is no substitute for the full instrument profile in the relevant chapter. Purpose: Screening Rating Diagnosis Identification Monitoring . A dash (—) means the book does not give this information for the instrument. An asterisk (*) marks an instrument mentioned in the body of a chapter rather than in a profile or table. The chapter number points to the profile or table in which the instrument first appears in that chapter.

B Appendix B Glossary The terms from the chapter glossaries, gathered into a single alphabetical glossary that defines each term and lists the chapters that address it, followed by an English–Arabic index.

search.s: B.1 Terms in alphabetical order (218 terms)
search.t: Above-level testing Administering a test designed for older students to an advanced student to gauge how far ahead the student is. ( Ch. 12 ) Acceleration Delivering content to a student at a younger age or a faster pace than usual, such as taking a subject with a higher grade. ( Ch. 12 Ch. 15 ) Accommodation A change in presentation or response mode that does not alter what a test measures. ( Ch. 3 Ch. 15 ) Adaptive behavior The conceptual, social and practical skills a person performs in everyday life. ( Ch. 3 Ch. 7 ) Advanced Learning Plan (ALP) An individual document for a gifted student that specifies areas of strength, measurable goals in those areas, social-emotional goals, and how progress will be monitored. ( Ch. 15 ) Age equivalent The age at which the average raw score of children equals the student's raw score; it does not mean that the student's skills resemble those of children of that age. ( Ch. 2 ) Aimline A line on a progress-monitoring graph that connects the starting level to the goal, against which the student's data points are compared. ( Ch. 4 Ch. 15 ) Alternate assessment In the U.S. system: an achievement test based on alternate achievement standards for students with the most significant cognitive disabilities; it is not what Chapter 5 means by “alternative methods.” ( Ch. 5 ) Anchoring Allowing the first idea that occurs to the evaluator to govern the interpretation of everything that follows. ( Ch. 14 ) Arithmetic fluency Performing basic arithmetic facts and operations both accurately and quickly. ( Ch. 8 ) Assessment and diagnosis team The school team that determines eligibility under Saudi regulations; it includes members from the school leadership, special education, general education and counseling, along with specialists and the parent. ( Ch. 15 ) Assessment protocol A preplanned set of tools and procedures, each of which answers a specific assessment question. ( Ch. 13 ) Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) A neurodevelopmental disorder marked by a persistent pattern of inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, or both. ( Ch. 10 ) Audiogram A graph showing the softest sound a person can hear at different frequencies in each ear. ( Ch. 11 ) Auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder A disorder in which the inner ear functions but the signal is not transmitted to the brain in a synchronized way, so speech understanding is poorer than the audiogram would predict. ( Ch. 11 ) Augmentative and alternative communication Means that supplement or replace speech, such as signs, pictures and speech-generating devices. ( Ch. 11 ) Authentic assessment Assessment that asks students to perform tasks resembling real-life tasks, scored with rubrics. ( Ch. 5 ) Basal The number of consecutive correct responses after which the student is assumed to know the preceding items and is credited with them. ( Ch. 3 ) Base rate The proportion of the norming sample showing a given difference or pattern, which indicates whether the difference is rare or common. ( Ch. 2 ) Baseline The initial measurements gathered before new instruction begins, against which later progress is compared. ( Ch. 4 Ch. 15 ) Basic Interpersonal Communicative Skills (BICS) The language of everyday conversation, in which a second-language learner reaches fluency close to that of peers in about two years. ( Ch. 14 ) Behavior function What a behavior achieves for the person, such as gaining attention or escaping a task. ( Ch. 5 ) Behavior intervention plan A plan based on the results of a functional assessment that teaches the student a replacement behavior serving the same function and changes the conditions that trigger the problem behavior. ( Ch. 5 ) Biopsychosocial model A model that views disability as the outcome of an interaction between an individual's health condition and environmental and personal factors. ( Ch. 1 ) Bone conduction Transmission of sound to the inner ear through the bones of the skull, bypassing the outer and middle ear.
